question: It is 1 November 2019. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved Act text gives a tenant a retaliation defence only for certain notices. If your notice is a no-reason notice, the Act says it has no effect when given in response to your exercise of a right. The documents don't cover retaliation for other notice types, and they don't say whether asking for repairs counts as exercising a right.

**Document used:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (file "rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf", dated 2 July 2019) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The filename shows "v088," but the text doesn't state an Authorised Version number, so I can't confirm that label. I found no later version in the documents.

## What the law says

- **Retaliation:** A notice under section 263 (no specified reason) "is of no effect if it was given in response to the exercise, or proposed exercise, by the tenant of a right under this Act" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Section 263 notice periods:** For a periodic tenancy, the termination date must be "not less than 120 days after the date on which the notice is given" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). A notice given today cannot validly end the tenancy today.
- **Form:** A notice to vacate is not valid unless it is in the prescribed form, addressed to the tenant, signed, and specifies a termination date. It must also state reasons, except for notices under section 263 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Repair rights:** The landlord must ensure premises are "maintained in good repair" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). If you give written notice of non-urgent repairs and the landlord doesn't carry them out within 14 days, you may apply to the Director to investigate [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). You can then apply to the Tribunal for a repair order [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **No self-help eviction:** A landlord must not require the tenant to vacate "except in accordance with this Act" (penalty: 60 penalty units for a natural person) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

## What to check

1. **Which section the notice relies on.** A month-to-month tenancy can't use the fixed-term end ground in section 261, so a notice given without a stated reason is likely a section 263 notice. Check whether it states a reason.
2. **The termination date.** For a section 263 notice on a periodic tenancy, it must be at least 120 days after the notice date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
3. **Form and signature.** Check it is in the prescribed form, addressed to you, signed, and states a termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
4. **Timing of your repair request.** Compare the date of your written repair request with the notice date. The documents don't set a timing test for retaliation, so this is evidence for the Tribunal, not a rule.

## What you can do

- **Keep records:** your written repair request, any reply, photos, and the notice itself.
- **Challenge the notice within 60 days.** A person "is not entitled to apply to the Tribunal challenging the validity of a notice" under section 263 "after the end of 60 days after the date on which the notice is given" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). If the notice was given on 1 November 2019, that is 30 December 2019 (my calculation).
- **Consider the 30-day rule.** For notices under sections 255–260, 285, 286 or 310, a tenant may apply to the Tribunal challenging the notice "within 30 days after the notice to vacate is given" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Section 263 isn't on that list, so check which section applies. If in doubt, act within the 30-day window too (by 1 December 2019, my calculation).
- **Stay in the home until a possession order is made.** A tenancy ends when a possession order takes effect, or when the tenant vacates on or after the termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The Tribunal must not make a possession order unless it is satisfied the landlord was entitled to give the notice and it hasn't been withdrawn [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Pursue the repairs separately.** Use the section 74 route (Director investigation) and then the section 75 Tribunal application [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

## Gaps in the documents

- The documents don't contain a general retaliation rule covering section 255 or other notice types.
- The documents don't say whether a request for repairs counts as exercising a right for section 266(2).
- The text of sections 91ZZ onward appears in the document's endnotes, which is where the newer residential rental provisions are set out. The documents don't say when those provisions commenced, so I haven't relied on them.
- This is general information from the Act text, not legal advice. For a specific notice, consider contacting the Victorian tenancy advice service or VCAT.

---

**Sources:**
[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf, 2 July 2019), Part 6 provisions including ss 219, 263, 266, 319, 321B.
[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf, 2 July 2019), Part 2 provisions including ss 68, 74, 75, 229.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are stated. (1) A no-reason s 263 notice applies to the periodic tenancy, with a termination date "not less than 120 days after the date on which the notice is given". (2) The hardest point: such a notice "is of no effect if it was given in response to the exercise, or proposed exercise, by the tenant of a right under this Act". The answer notes the documents don't expressly say a repair request counts, but it sets out the tenant's statutory repair rights, so the rule is not hedged into ambiguity. (3) The tenant cannot challenge the notice at the Tribunal "after the end of 60 days after the date on which the notice is given", and the answer names VCAT.

must-not-say.reason: No: although the answer gives the correct 60-day deadline, it also presents a 30-day deadline as one that may apply to this notice, saying "Consider the 30-day rule... check which section applies. If in doubt, act within the 30-day window too (by 1 December 2019, my calculation)," rather than rejecting it as inapplicable to a section 263 notice.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 with its version, both by file name "rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf" (dated 2 July 2019) and by the link "97-109aa088", and it relies only on that version's rules (ss 263, 266, 74, 75 and others); it expressly declines to rely on the later s 91ZZ provisions.

question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved law prohibits the conduct you describe, so you have grounds to challenge it. The documents don't say how to lodge a complaint or what evidence to keep, so I can't give you those steps from them.

## What the law says

The governing document is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 110, incorporating amendments as at 6 August 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). It is the most recent version in my search results, and I haven't confirmed whether a later version applies on 1 October 2025.

- **Advertised price:** A provider or agent must not advertise or offer premises unless the rent is advertised or offered as a fixed amount [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). This is a penalty offence: 60 penalty units for a natural person, or 300 penalty units for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Higher offers:** A provider or agent must not solicit or otherwise invite an offer of rent higher than the advertised amount [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The same penalties apply [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **False or misleading rent statements:** A provider or agent who promotes or advertises premises must not make a false or misleading representation about the rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Misleading conduct to induce a tenancy:** A provider or agent must not induce a person to enter an agreement through misleading or deceptive conduct, or through a false or misleading representation about the rent payable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). This applies to providers not acting in trade or commerce, and the section does not limit the *Australian Consumer Law (Victoria)* [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

The documents don't address a renter's withdrawal of an application, so they don't say whether the withdrawal email was legally effective.

## What you can do or ask

- **Ask the agent or provider in writing** to explain the withdrawal email and whether any offer above the advertised rent was solicited or accepted. Keep the request factual.
- **Seek a remedy through the Tribunal.** The Act's notes say that orders may be made by the Tribunal for contraventions of s 30E [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The retrieved excerpts don't set out the orders available, the time limits, or the application process. Check VCAT directly.
- **Discrimination, if relevant:** If you think you were refused because of a protected attribute, the Regulations' Form 3 says you may apply to VCAT for compensation under section 210AA of the Act if you suffered loss [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). It also gives a complaint route to VEOHRC (1300 292 153) and free advice from Victoria Legal Aid (1300 792 387) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). The Form also lists VCAT's contact number as 1300 018 228 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

## Evidence to keep

The documents don't list what evidence to keep, so the following is my own suggestion, not from the sources:

- The original listing showing the advertised rent.
- Your application and all messages with the agent or provider.
- The withdrawal email, with its full headers and date.
- The current listing showing the higher rent, with screenshots dated and the URL.
- Anything that shows who made the higher offer or what it was, such as written statements from anyone who heard it directly. What you were told secondhand is weaker evidence.

This isn't legal advice. Consider speaking to Victoria Legal Aid or a tenancy lawyer before lodging anything.

---

[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf, dated 2025-08-06 (Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 110)
[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) rt-regs-2021-v004-2025-07-01.pdf, dated 2025-07-01 (Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Form 3)

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
**Short answer:** Probably not, at least not on the owner's allergy alone. Under the Act, the owner can't unreasonably refuse, and if they didn't go to the Tribunal within 14 days of your request, the law treats them as having consented. Whether the refusal is reasonable, and whether they applied in time, are the points to check.

**What the law says**

- A renter may keep a pet if the provider has consented in writing or the Tribunal has ordered it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The request must be made in the form approved by the Director, and given to the provider [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You used the official form, so that requirement appears to be met.
- A provider "must not unreasonably refuse to consent" to a pet [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The provider is taken to have consented unless, within 14 days of getting the request, they apply to the Tribunal for an order that refusal is reasonable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The Tribunal may consider matters such as the type of pet, the character of the premises, and any other relevant matter [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether an owner's allergy counts as a reasonable ground, or how the "owner hardly visits" fact affects that. I can't answer that from the retrieved material.

**Applying this to your situation (as of 15 October 2026)**

Your request was made about three weeks ago, so the 14-day window has likely closed. If the agent or owner did not lodge a Tribunal application in that window, the law treats consent as given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A verbal or written "no" doesn't by itself stop that deemed consent. Only a Tribunal application does.

**What you can do**

1. Ask the agent in writing whether an application was made to the Tribunal (VCAT), and on what date. Keep a record of the date you sent the form.
2. If no application was made, say in writing that you treat the request as consented to under the Act.
3. The documents don't set out a step-by-step route for a renter to challenge a refusal. For advice, Consumer Affairs Victoria's number in the forms is 1300 55 81 81 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf), and Victoria Legal Aid's number for discrimination-related advice is 1300 792 387 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**Other points to check**

- **Assistance dog:** The Act defines "pet" as any animal other than an assistance dog under the Equal Opportunity Act 2010 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If your dog is an assistance dog, different rules apply, and the Regulations list refusing accommodation to someone with an assistance dog as unlawful discrimination [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The documents don't set out those rules in full.
- **Discrimination:** If the refusal is connected to a protected attribute, such as a disability, the Regulations say you can apply to VCAT for compensation [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**Sources**

- [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Residential Tenancies Act 1997, file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf" (dated 13 October 2026). This is the latest version in the retrieved documents, so I've applied it. The file label shows version "v115"; the documents don't otherwise state an "Authorised Version No."
- [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, file "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf" (dated 30 June 2026). The file label shows version "v009".

This is general information based only on those documents, not legal advice.

It then applies this to the three-week timeline: "the 14-day window has likely closed. If the agent or owner did not lodge a Tribunal application in that window, the law treats consent as given." question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
**Short answer:** Based on the retrieved documents, the notice still stands unless the landlord has withdrawn it in the way the Act requires. The buyer pulling out does not, by itself, withdraw the notice. The documents don't say whether a notice to vacate for a sale lapses when the sale falls through, so that point is unresolved.

**What the law says**

- The Act allows a landlord to give a notice to vacate if the premises are to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession immediately after the termination date. The termination date must be at least 60 days after the notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- A notice to vacate is withdrawn only if a notice of withdrawal is given. That withdrawal must be in writing, signed by the person who gave the notice, and signed by the person it was given to [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Nothing in the retrieved provisions says a notice is withdrawn when a sale falls through.
- A landlord can apply to VCAT for a possession order only if the notice has not been withdrawn [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). VCAT must also be satisfied that the notice was properly given and that the renter is still in possession after the termination date [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- The notice is only valid if it is in the relevant prescribed form, signed, addressed to you, states the reasons, and, for a sale notice, is accompanied by the approved documentary evidence [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Form 6 also says that a notice may be challenged at VCAT if it was not given to you properly or the reason is incorrect or incomplete .

**What you can do or ask**

1. **Check the notice itself.** Confirm it is on the prescribed form, has a termination date at least 60 days after it was given, and includes the documentary evidence where required [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
2. **Ask the landlord in writing** to confirm whether they are withdrawing the notice. A withdrawal only counts if both of you sign it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Do not sign anything that you do not understand, and seek advice first.
3. **Stay in the property until a VCAT order says otherwise.** Only Victoria Police can carry out a forcible eviction, and only under a VCAT warrant. The landlord cannot personally use force to remove you . The Act also makes it an offence to require or compel a renter to leave, or to take possession, except in accordance with the Act .
4. **Get advice promptly if you want to challenge the notice.** Form 6 says you should apply to VCAT within 30 days if you experienced family or personal violence that caused the behaviour in the notice . The retrieved provisions do not give a specific deadline for challenging a sale notice under section 91ZZB, so check that with a community legal service.
5. **Watch what the landlord does next.** If the landlord gets possession after giving a sale notice, they must not let the premises for use as a residence within 6 months after the notice was given, unless an exception applies .

**Limits of the documents:** The retrieved material does not say whether the landlord's sale notice lapses when the sale falls through. It also does not cover your specific notice's wording or dates. Given the date of 1 October 2025, the Act version I found is the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, file labelled "v110" (dated 6 August 2025), and the regulations are the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, file labelled "v004" (dated 1 July 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). The documents do not state an "Authorised Version" number on their face. Those labels come from the file names, so please check them against the official Authorised Version before relying on them.

**Sources**
- [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) Residential Tenancies Act 1997, rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf (6 August 2025): ss 91ZZB, 91ZZO, 91ZZQ.
- [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) Residential Tenancies Act 1997, rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf (6 August 2025): s 330 (Possession orders) and related provisions.
-  Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, rt-regs-2021-v004-2025-07-01.pdf (1 July 2025): Form 6.
-  Residential Tenancies Act 1997, rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf (6 August 2025): s 91P.
-  Residential Tenancies Act 1997, rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf (6 August 2025): s 91ZZH.

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
**Short answer:** Probably not, unless you received a valid written notice of the increase. Negotiating or an email from your agent is not enough under the documents I found.

**What the law says**

- A rental provider must give at least 60 days' notice in the prescribed form of a proposed rent increase, and the notice may provide for only one increase [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The Regulations also say the notice must be at least 60 days' written notice [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

Form 5 says a valid notice is required for all rent increases [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- Rent cannot be increased at intervals of less than 12 months [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- A rent increase made in contravention of section 44 is invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

- **Ask for the formal notice.** Ask your agent or landlord to give you a written notice in the prescribed form (Form 5). The form must name the rental provider, not the agent, and must give the current rent, the new rent, the start date and the calculation method [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

Form 5 says you can apply in writing and that the request is free [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Apply to VCAT if needed.** After the Director's report, you may apply to VCAT within 30 days of receiving the report. If you have not requested a report, you may apply to VCAT with leave, but only after 30 days have passed since the notice was given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Form 5 says you will need to pay the increased amount from the date on the notice unless VCAT decides otherwise [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:
**Short answer:** No. The Act doesn't let you arrange a repair without telling the owner, and the documents I found don't address insurance.

**What the law says (as at 15 October 2026)**

- You must give the owner written notice "as soon as practicable after becoming aware" of damage to the premises [1, *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, 2026-10-13]. Electronic written notice is allowed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Damage caused by the renter or a visitor is not fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Chewed skirting boards are likely to count as damage.
- You must leave the premises "as far as practicable" reasonably clean and in the same condition as when you moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Repairs, urgent or non-urgent, may only be done by a suitably qualified person [2, *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, 2026-06-30].

**What you can do or ask**

- **Arrange your own repair only in limited cases.** You may arrange urgent repairs only if you have taken reasonable steps to get the owner or agent to carry them out immediately and you cannot get them to do so [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Urgent repairs cover things like a burst water service, a gas leak, a dangerous electrical fault, or flood or storm damage [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Chewed skirting boards don't appear on that list, so this route probably doesn't apply.
- **Notify the owner in writing now.** Tell them what happened and the nature of the damage [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Expect a repair notice.** If the owner chooses, they can give you a written repair notice. It must state the nature of the damage, that it was caused by a failure to take care, and that you must repair it within 14 days in a tradesman-like manner [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If you don't, the owner may do the repairs at your expense [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You would then be liable for the reasonable costs, which you must reimburse within 14 days of the repairs being completed, once the owner gives you written particulars of the cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Offer to fix it with the owner's agreement.** Agreeing a repair in writing before doing it is the safest route. Any repair must still be done by a suitably qualified person [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Check the bond position before moving out.** The documents I found don't cover how the bond would be affected by this damage, so I can't say more on that.

**Insurance:** The retrieved documents don't say anything about the owner's insurance, or whether your actions would affect it. You would need to ask the owner or their insurer, or check the policy.

**Limits of this answer:** The retrieved material is extracts from the Act and Regulations. It doesn't include the Authorised Version number on the documents. The file names identify the Act as v115 (dated 2026-10-13) and the Regulations as v009 (dated 2026-06-30) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). I haven't confirmed these numbers from the documents' own text. Please check them against the official Authorised Version before relying on them.

Chewed skirting boards are likely to count as damage," together with the duty to leave the premises "in the same condition" and liability for the reasonable repair costs.

question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents I found don't set a minimum number of circuits for a rental. They do require the landlord to have electrical safety checks done and to provide the check date on request. A new rule on circuit breakers and safety switches starts on 29 March 2023, four weeks after your date.

**Which document:** The retrieved text is the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, S.R. No. 3/2021, in a reprint dated 1 June 2022 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). It doesn't carry a separate "Authorised Version" number, so I can only identify it by its S.R. number. The *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* itself wasn't retrieved.

**What the law says now (1 March 2023):**
- The landlord must ensure an electrical safety check of all electrical installations, appliances and fittings they provide is done every 2 years by a licensed or registered electrician. On your request, they must give you the date of the most recent check in writing [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- If no electrical safety check has been done in the last 2 years when you move in, the landlord must arrange one as soon as practicable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

**What starts on 29 March 2023:**
- All power outlets and lighting circuits must be connected to a switchboard-type Circuit Breaker complying with AS/NZS 3000, and a switchboard-type Residual Current Device complying with one of the listed standards (AS/NZS 3190, AS/NZS 61008.1 or AS/NZS 61009.1) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). This is a standard about protection, not a specific number of circuits. The documents don't say whether it would address your overloading problem.
- A fixed heater rule also changes on 29 March 2023. For a Class 1 building, an energy efficient fixed heater in good working order must be installed in the main living area [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). This matters if your heater is the appliance tripping the breaker.

**What you can ask for:**
1. **A written electrical safety check date.** Ask your landlord in writing for the date of the most recent electrical safety check [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
2. **A check now, if none was done in the last 2 years.** If you can't confirm one was done within 2 years of when you moved in, ask for one to be arranged [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
3. **A repair, in writing.** Notify the landlord in writing as soon as practicable about damage or a breakdown of facilities or equipment they supplied. The landlord must carry out non-urgent repairs within a reasonable time, and you may apply to VCAT if they haven't done the repairs within 14 days of notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The documents I retrieved don't list a circuit-tripping fault as an urgent repair, so I can't confirm which category applies.

**What the documents don't cover:** They don't set a minimum number of circuits for a rental, or say how many power points a circuit should serve. A licensed electrician would be the right person to assess whether the load is safe for the existing circuit. For how the rules apply to your specific situation, check the Act or speak to Consumer Affairs Victoria.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved documents don't say whether a rooming house operator can charge for coin-operated washing machines. They don't expressly allow or prohibit it. The rules that do apply are about how service charges must be disclosed.

## What the law says

- **Utility charges:** An operator may charge for electricity, gas and water only if the operator pays for them, the room is separately metered, and the charge is no more than the supplier's charge. This doesn't apply to a shared room [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Laundry isn't mentioned.
- **Service charges:** If an operator charges for services, they must give the resident a separate schedule of those charges before the resident moves in. If the resident uses the services, the operator must give an itemised account of the resident's individual use [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Homes Victoria and registered agencies:** A separate provision allows these bodies (not private operators) to impose a service charge for laundry services where it isn't practicable to measure use. The charge must not exceed the cost of providing the service [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Laundry standard:** From 26 February 2024, rooming houses must provide, for every 12 or fewer residents, laundry facilities in good working order, including a washing machine [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether that machine must be free.

The most recent Act version retrieved is the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version v115 (file dated 13 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). That is in force on 15 October 2026. The Regulations are the Residential Tenancies (Rooming House Standards) Regulations 2023, S.R. No. 10/2023, Authorised Version v002 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

1. **Check the schedule of services.** Ask whether you were given a written schedule of charges before you moved in. If the washing machines are charged for and you weren't given one, the operator may not have complied with the Act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Ask for an itemised account.** If you're being charged for machine use, you can ask for an account showing your individual use of the service [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Check the laundry standard.** Ask whether the house has a washing machine for every 12 or fewer residents, as the Regulations require [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf).
4. **Get more information.** The Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 point to consumer.vic.gov.au/renting for more information [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say how to resolve a dispute over laundry charges specifically.

If you tell me whether the operator is Homes Victoria, a registered agency, or a private operator, and whether you share a room, I can check which provisions apply. The documents don't cover whether a coin-operated machine counts as a "service" under s 109 for a private operator.

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved documents set a mould standard, but they don't say whether advertising photos that show mould are allowed. They also don't say whether a photo is enough to prove a breach.

## What the law says

- **The standard:** "Each room in the rented premises must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). The rental provider must ensure the premises comply with the rental minimum standards and are "vacant and reasonably clean when the renter moves in" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs:** Mould is listed as urgent only where it makes the premises unsafe or insecure. The definition covers "any fault or damage that makes rented premises... unsafe or insecure, including... the presence of mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The definition also includes "a failure to comply with any rental minimum standards" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Advertising photos:** The Act lets a rental provider enter to produce advertising images or video after giving notice, and they must make a reasonable attempt to agree a suitable time [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). A renter can object only on specified grounds, such as identifiable or valuable possessions or family violence risk [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Nothing in the retrieved sections addresses showing a defect like mould in an advertisement.
- **Is the photo enough?** The documents don't say. The standard turns on whether the mould is "caused by or related to the building structure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf), and a photo alone doesn't show cause. The retrieved documents don't cover evidence rules or how VCAT weighs photos.

## What the renter can do or ask

- **Notify in writing:** The renter must notify the rental provider in writing, as soon as practicable, of damage to the premises [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repair (if it makes the premises unsafe):** The rental provider must carry out urgent repairs after being notified. The renter may arrange them if they have taken reasonable steps and the provider hasn't acted, and may be reimbursed up to $2500 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Non-urgent repair:** The provider must carry out repairs in a reasonable time. The renter may apply to VCAT if repairs aren't done within 14 days of notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **VCAT orders:** The renter may apply to VCAT for an urgent repairs order if they cannot meet the cost, the cost is more than $2500, or the provider refuses to pay for repairs the renter arranged [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

- **Advertising:** The retrieved documents don't say whether it is lawful to advertise a property with visible mould. They also don't cover general advertising rules or the Australian Consumer Law beyond a reference in a form about unfair additional terms [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

The text doesn't state an "Authorised Version" number, so these labels come from the file names.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I let a friend move into my rental without telling the agent. Now I want them out. What do I have to do?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved documents do not say how a renter removes a friend who moved in without consent. They do cover the related situation where a renter assigns or sub-lets without consent.

**What the law says**

- Under the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (file "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf", dated 30 June 2026), a renter "must not assign (transfer to another person) or sub-let the whole or any part of the premises without the written consent of the rental provider." The rental provider "may give the renter notice to vacate if the renter assigns or sub-lets the premises without consent" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- Under the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", dated 13 October 2026, the most recent version retrieved), a provider may give a notice to vacate for assignment or sub-letting without consent. The notice "must specify a termination date that is not less than 14 days after the date on which the notice is given" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- A notice to vacate is not valid unless it is in the relevant prescribed form, addressed to the renter, signed by the provider or their agent, states the reasons, and specifies the termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The provider cannot unreasonably withhold consent to sub-let, and must not charge a fee for consent beyond reasonable expenses [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- Only the rental provider can give a notice to vacate. The renter cannot end the friend's occupancy through a notice under these provisions.

**What you can do or ask**

- Tell the agent or provider now, in writing, that someone is living there. Ask whether they will consent. Because consent cannot be unreasonably withheld for sub-letting, this is the most direct route to resolving the situation [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- If the provider refuses and you still want the friend out, ask the friend to leave. The documents do not set out a renter's process for removing another person. If they will not leave, the documents say that a possession order must come from VCAT, and only Victoria Police can carry out a forcible eviction under a VCAT warrant. Rental providers cannot use force . That passage is from the Form 6 information sheet, so check it applies to your situation.

**What the documents don't cover**

- Whether a friend living in the property without paying rent counts as "sub-letting" or "assignment" under these provisions. The documents do not define "occupant" or address this case.
- Whether retrospective consent can cure the breach.
- Any notice or process a renter must follow to remove a non-party occupant.
- Your specific lease terms, which may contain clauses on occupants.

For advice on your particular situation, contact a community legal centre or Consumer Affairs Victoria (1300 558 181), which the Form 6 information sheet lists .

question: It is 1 November 2019. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?
answer:
**What the law says**

Your notice is most likely a notice to vacate for no specified reason under section 263. The retrieved text of the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (file "rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf," dated 2 July 2019) says a landlord may give that notice "without specifying a reason" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). For a periodic agreement, the termination date must be "not less than 120 days after the date on which the notice is given" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Under section 319, a notice under section 263 does not need to state a reason [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

The key protection is section 266(2): "A notice under section 261 or section 263 is of no effect if it was given in response to the exercise, or proposed exercise, by the tenant of a right under this Act" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). This is the retaliation rule that applies to you.

**What to check**

1. **Timing and the reason for the notice.** Did you request repairs before the notice, and did the landlord give the notice the same day? The retrieved excerpts do not say how a tribunal decides whether a notice was given "in response to" a tenant's exercise of a right, so I can't tell you how strong your case is.
2. **Whether repairs were requested in writing.** Section 74 says a tenant may ask the Director to investigate non-urgent repairs if "the tenant has given the landlord written notice" and "the landlord has not carried out the repairs within 14 days" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Whether a request counts as the "exercise of a right under this Act" is not explained in the excerpts.
3. **The termination date.** It must be at least 120 days after the notice is given for a periodic agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). A shorter date is a defect to raise.
4. **The form.** A notice to vacate is not valid unless it is in the relevant prescribed form, addressed to you, signed by the landlord or agent, and specifies the termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
5. **Whether the notice cites a reason.** If it cites repairs, renovation, sale, or another reason, the rules for that section apply instead, including the 30-day challenge period in section 321B [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**What you can do**

- **Apply to the Tribunal to challenge the notice.** For a section 263 notice, the time limit is "after the end of 60 days after the date on which the notice is given" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). For a notice on a listed ground (sections 255–260, 285, 286, 310), section 321B requires an application "within 30 days after the notice to vacate is given" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). If the notice was given on 1 November 2019, the 60-day period ends around 31 December 2019. Confirm the exact date.
- **Wait for a possession application.** A landlord can apply for a possession order only after giving a notice to vacate, and not later than 30 days after the termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The Tribunal "must make a possession order" only if, among other things, the landlord "was entitled to give the notice" and "the notice has not been withdrawn" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). A notice that is "of no effect" under section 266(2) would not meet that test.
- **Keep your repair requests.** Your duty-side rights come from section 68, which requires the landlord to "ensure that the rented premises are maintained in good repair" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). You may apply to the Tribunal for an order requiring repairs under section 75, but that application must be made "within 60 days of receiving the report of the Director" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**What the documents don't cover**

- The retrieved excerpts don't show how a tenant proves that a notice was given in response to a repair request, or what evidence the Tribunal accepts.
- They don't state the Authorised Version number in the text. The file is named "v088," and it is the only version I retrieved, so I can't confirm from the documents alone that it is the version in force on 1 November 2019.
- They don't include the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal Act provisions that section 330 refers to, or any Tribunal guidance on retaliation.

For advice on your specific facts, contact a tenancy advice service or Victoria's Tribunal before the deadline.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered: a no-reason notice is allowed under s263 with 'not less than 120 days' notice for a periodic agreement; s266(2) makes such a notice 'of no effect if it was given in response to the exercise... by the tenant of a right under this Act'; and the hardest point, the 60-day challenge, is covered by 'Apply to the Tribunal to challenge the notice... the 60-day period ends around 31 December 2019.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer says the notice may be given "without specifying a reason" and gives the challenge deadline for this section 263 notice as "after the end of 60 days after the date on which the notice is given"; the 30-day period it mentions under section 321B is assigned only to a different notice type ("If it cites repairs, renovation, sale, or another reason"), not to this notice.

version-cited.reason: Yes: the answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 with its version, via the file name "rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf," "dated 2 July 2019," and the link "97-109aa088", and every rule it applies (ss 263, 266(2), 319, 74, 68, 75, 321B) is cited to that in-force version 088 with no reliance on any other version.

question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved law prohibits the conduct you describe, so you have grounds to challenge it. The documents don't set out a complaint process, a deadline, or a list of evidence, so those points need checking elsewhere.

**Version applied:** The Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 110, incorporating amendments as at 6 August 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). This is the latest version in my search results. I can't confirm whether it was amended between 6 August and 1 October 2025.

## What the law says

- **Rent must be advertised as a fixed amount.** A provider or agent "must not advertise or otherwise offer premises unless the rent under the residential rental agreement is advertised or offered as a fixed amount." The penalty is 60 penalty units for a natural person or 300 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **No inviting higher offers.** A provider or agent "must not solicit or otherwise invite an offer of an amount of rent that is higher than the advertised amount of rent." The same penalties apply [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **No false or misleading rent representations.** A provider or agent "must not make a false or misleading representation in relation to the rent for the premises," with the same penalties [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Misleading conduct that induces you to enter an agreement.** A provider or agent "must not induce a person to enter into a residential rental agreement by engaging in conduct that is misleading or deceptive." This covers false or misleading representations about the rent payable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). This section applies to a provider who is not acting in trade or commerce, which may be relevant to your case. The Act notes that the Tribunal can make orders for contraventions of this section under section 472(1A) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

Your situation raises two separate questions:
1. **The "withdrawn" email.** If it was false, it may be misleading conduct that induced you to stop pursuing the rental, which section 30E addresses [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
2. **The higher offer.** Section 30F(3) prohibits *soliciting or inviting* higher offers. The text doesn't say whether accepting an unsolicited higher offer is caught, so you would need to show the provider or agent invited it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

- **Ask for a written explanation** of the withdrawal email and the reason for the change to the rent.
- **Consider a Tribunal application.** The documents say the Tribunal can make orders for contraventions of sections 30E and 30G, but they don't set out the application steps or time limits [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Seek compensation if you suffered loss.** The Act's note refers to section 210AA, but only for discrimination claims, and the text of that section isn't in my results [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). I can't confirm it applies to your situation.

## Evidence to keep

The documents don't list specific evidence requirements. Practically, you should keep:
- The original advertisement showing the fixed rent (screenshot with date and URL).
- Your application and all correspondence, especially the withdrawal email with its full headers.
- Any notes of phone calls or messages, including dates, times, and names.
- The current listing showing the higher rent.
- Anything showing the other applicant's offer, or what you were told about it.

## What the documents don't cover

- The complaint or Tribunal application process, forms, or deadlines for sections 30E or 30F.
- Whether an unsolicited higher offer breaches section 30F.
- The full text of sections 472 and 210AA.

I can search for these if you want the procedural details.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
**Short answer:** Probably not, at least not on the basis of the allergy alone. Under the Act as it stood on 15 October 2026, a provider must not unreasonably refuse, and if they didn't apply to the Tribunal in time, your request is treated as approved. The documents don't say whether an allergy is a reasonable ground, so that part is uncertain.

**What the law says**

- A renter may keep a pet if the provider has consented in writing or the Tribunal has permitted it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- A renter must make the request in the form approved by the Director, and give it to the provider [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You say you used the official form.
- The provider "must not unreasonably refuse to consent" to a pet [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The provider is taken to have consented unless, within 14 days of getting the request, they apply to the Tribunal for an order that refusal is reasonable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The Tribunal may consider the type of pet, the character of the premises, the fittings, whether refusal is permitted under any other Act, prescribed matters, and any other matter it considers relevant [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What this means for you**

- **Timing:** If you gave the request about three weeks ago (around 24 September 2026), the 14-day window would have closed around 8 October 2026. This is my calculation, so check the exact date you delivered it. If the agent didn't apply to the Tribunal in that window, the documents indicate consent is deemed given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **The agent's "no":** A refusal letter alone doesn't appear to end the matter. The Act's process runs through the Tribunal [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **The allergy:** The documents don't say whether an owner's allergy, especially where the owner rarely visits, is a reasonable ground for refusal. The Tribunal factors listed don't mention allergies specifically [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), so I can't say how it would be treated.

**What you can do**

1. Check the date you gave the request and whether you received any written consent or Tribunal application notice.
2. Ask the agent in writing whether an application was made to VCAT and, if so, when.
3. If no application was made within 14 days, you can rely on the deemed consent. Seek advice if they still refuse, such as from Consumer Affairs Victoria (1300 55 81 81) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) or Victoria Legal Aid.
4. If an application was made, the Tribunal decides whether refusal is reasonable, so you may need to respond to it.

**Documents used:** The Act is *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (No. 109 of 1997), in the file rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf, dated 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The file name suggests Authorised Version v115, but the text itself doesn't state an Authorised Version number, so please confirm that on the official source. The pet clause in the regulations is in the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (S.R. No. 3/2021), in the file rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf, dated 30 June 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

This is general information, not legal advice.

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
**Short answer:** Based on the documents, probably yes. The sale falling through does not by itself cancel the notice. Unless the landlord gives you a signed withdrawal, the notice appears to remain in effect. However, the documents do not say what happens to a notice when a sale collapses, so there may be other grounds to challenge it.

I've applied the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, reprint v110 (file dated 6 August 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, v004 (dated 1 July 2025) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). I can't confirm from the documents that no amendments took effect between those dates and 1 October 2025.

## What the law says

- **The landlord's right:** A landlord may give a notice to vacate if the premises are, immediately after the termination date, to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession. The notice must give at least 60 days' notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 91ZZB(1), (4)).
- **Timing rules for sales:** If the landlord has a contract of sale with conditions, the notice must be given within 14 days after the last condition is satisfied. If the contract has no such conditions, it must be given within 14 days after the contract was entered into [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 91ZZB(2), (3)). If your notice was given outside these windows, it may be invalid.
- **Form and evidence:** The notice must be in the prescribed form, signed, and accompanied by documentary evidence supporting the reason for the notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 91ZZO). The prescribed form is Form 6 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Withdrawal:** A notice to vacate "is withdrawn only if a notice of withdrawal is given." The withdrawal must be in writing and signed by both the person who gave the notice and the person it was given to [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 91ZZQ).
- **Possession:** The landlord can apply to VCAT for a possession order after the notice is given. The Tribunal must not make the order if the notice has been withdrawn [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (ss 322(1), 330(1)(a)(ii)).

## What you can do or ask

1. **Ask the landlord to withdraw in writing.** A withdrawal only takes effect if it is in writing and signed by both the landlord and you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 91ZZQ(2)). Don't sign anything without reading it first.
2. **Check the notice's validity.** Look at the date it was given against the 14-day rules above, whether it is on Form 6, whether it has the required evidence, and whether the termination date is at least 60 days after it was given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
3. **Challenge it at VCAT.** You may apply to VCAT challenging the notice's validity. The application must be made within 30 days after the notice was given, and on or before the hearing of any possession application [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 91ZZS). Because of this deadline, act quickly. Note that the documents do not say whether a failed sale is itself a ground for challenge.
4. **Wait for any possession application.** If you don't leave, VCAT decides whether you must leave and on what date. Only Victoria Police can carry out a forced eviction, and only under a VCAT warrant [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) (Form 6, cl. 4).
5. **Seek advice promptly.** Form 6 advises contacting a community legal organisation listed on the Consumer Affairs Victoria website, or calling 1300 558 181 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

## What the documents don't cover

- Whether a notice to vacate for a sale lapses automatically when the sale falls through.
- How VCAT would weigh a failed sale when deciding whether a possession order is "reasonable and proportionate."
- The date your notice was given, which determines your 30-day challenge window.

The hardest, dependence on the ground and its evidence, is covered by distinguishing a sale 'to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession' from the contract-of-sale 14-day timing rules, by requiring 'documentary evidence supporting the reason for the notice', and by telling the reader to check the notice against these. The answer also states the 60-day minimum, that withdrawal must be 'in writing and signed by both', and gives next steps (ask for a written withdrawal, or challenge at VCAT within 30 days).

must-not-say.reason: Yes. None of the failure conditions is asserted: the answer says "The sale falling through does not by itself cancel the notice," requires a withdrawal "signed by both the person who gave the notice and the person it was given to," and states "The notice must give at least 60 days' notice."

The only other document it relies on is the in-force "*Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, v004 (dated 1 July 2025)" (21-3sra004). It applies no rule from a version that was not in force on 1 October 2025.

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
**Short answer:** Based on the retrieved documents, an email saying rent is going up is unlikely to be a valid rent increase. A rent increase that doesn't follow the rules is invalid. The documents don't say exactly what you must pay in the meantime, and I can't confirm that from them.

**Which versions I relied on:** The Residential Tenancies Act 1997 file is labelled "v110" and dated 6 August 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 file is labelled "v004" and dated 1 July 2025 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). Both predate 1 October 2025. The retrieved text doesn't spell out an "Authorised Version No.", so the v110 and v004 labels are the only version identifiers I can point to.

---

### What the law says

- **Notice is required.** A rental provider "must give a renter at least 60 days notice in the prescribed form of a proposed rent increase" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The Regulations say a "valid notice of a proposed rent increase is required for all rent increases" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Required contents.** The notice must include the amount of the increase, the method used to calculate it, and a statement of your right to apply to the Director within 30 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). It must be on Form 5, which asks for the current rent, the new rent, the start date and the calculation method [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Timing limits.** Rent can't be increased "at intervals of less than 12 months" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Under a fixed-term agreement, rent can't rise before the term ends unless the agreement provides for it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Consequence.** "A rent increase in contravention of this section is invalid" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

### Applying this to your situation

An emailed statement that rent is going up, followed by a refused negotiation, doesn't appear to meet these requirements. The documents don't list an email as a prescribed form. Unless you receive a notice in Form 5 that meets the requirements above, the increase appears to be invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). The documents don't state directly whether you must keep paying the old rent in the meantime, so please check that with Consumer Affairs Victoria.

**From when:** If a valid notice is given, the increase can't take effect until at least 60 days after notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). For example, a notice given on 1 October 2025 would allow an increase no earlier than 30 November 2025. The start date must appear on the notice itself [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

### What you can do

- **Ask for a proper notice.** Ask the rental provider in writing for a notice in the prescribed form. The rental provider's name must be on it, and it "cannot be the agent's name", though the service address can be the agent's [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Ask for a Director's investigation.** If you receive a valid notice and think the proposed rent is excessive, you can apply to the Director "within 30 days after the notice is given" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The request must be in writing [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Apply to VCAT.** After a Director's report, you can apply to VCAT within 30 days of receiving it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). You may also apply to VCAT without a report, but only with its leave, and only after the 30 days have passed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). VCAT may also ask you to pay the increased rent from the date on the notice "unless VCAT decides otherwise" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Get more information.** Consumer Affairs Victoria can be reached on 1300 558 181 or at renting@justice.vic.gov.au [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

The documents don't address whether an informal email counts as a notice in every circumstance, or what happens to rent already paid. A tenancy advice service would be the right place to check those points.

question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:
**Short answer:** The Act doesn't let you quietly arrange the repair without telling the owner. You must give written notice of the damage. The documents don't address insurance.

## What the law says

- **Damage liability:** A renter and their visitors must not intentionally or negligently cause damage to rented premises, but fair wear and tear is excluded [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Whether a dog chewing skirting boards counts as negligence depends on the facts, such as whether reasonable care was taken [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Notice is required:** A renter who becomes aware of damage must, as soon as practicable, give the provider written notice of the fact that the damage occurred and its nature. Electronic written notice is allowed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Repairs must be done by a qualified person:** The Regulations state that only a suitably qualified person may do repairs, both urgent and non-urgent [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Exit condition:** At the end of the agreement, the renter must leave the premises reasonably clean and in the same condition as when they moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Modifications:** A renter must not make alterations without the provider's written consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether replacing skirting boards is a "repair" or an "alteration," so I can't say which applies.

## What the renter can do or ask

1. **Give written notice now.** Tell the owner or agent in writing what the dog damaged and what kind of damage it is [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This is required "as soon as practicable," so waiting until move-out is risky.
2. **Offer to fix it, or let the owner choose.** If the owner gives a repair notice, it must be in writing and must state the nature of the damage and that the damage was caused by the renter's failure to ensure care was taken. It can require repair within 14 days, in a tradesman-like manner [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If the renter doesn't repair it in that time, the owner may do the repair at the renter's expense [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The renter is liable for reasonable costs only if the owner gives written particulars of the cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Repairing it yourself with the owner's agreement, using a suitably qualified person, is the cleanest route [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3. **Don't rely on the urgent-repair route.** Under the Regulations, a renter may arrange urgent repairs and be reimbursed up to $2500 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The Act's definition of urgent repairs lists items such as burst water services, gas leaks, and serious fault in a staircase; skirting boards are not on that list [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't show that this route applies here.
4. **Check the end-of-tenancy inspection.** The owner must complete the final inspection and condition report within 10 days after the agreement ends, give you an opportunity to attend if possible, and allow for fair wear and tear .

## Insurance

The documents don't say anything about the owner's insurance or how a renter's damage affects it. You'd need to ask the owner or check the policy directly.

## Documents and versions

- [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (file labelled "rta-1997-v115," dated 13 October 2026). The excerpts don't show an Authorised Version number explicitly, so I can't confirm it beyond the file label.
- [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, S.R. No. 3/2021 (file labelled "rt-regs-2021-v009," dated 30 June 2026).
-  Form 4 (Condition Report) under the same Regulations. The same file applies.
