question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
**Short answer:** The regulations require a specific circuit protection setup from 29 March 2023, which is four weeks after today. They don't set a number of circuits, and I found nothing that addresses overloading from running a kettle and heater together.

## What the law says

- **The new rule starts 29 March 2023.** From then, "all power outlets and lighting circuits in the rented premises are to be connected to" a switchboard-type circuit breaker complying with AS/NZS 3000, and a switchboard-type residual current device complying with one of several listed AS/NZS standards [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Your power points being on one circuit is not, by itself, a breach of the text.
- **The rule doesn't specify circuit numbers.** The regulation I found doesn't say how many circuits a rental needs or limit how many outlets can share one [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Heating from 29 March 2023.** For a Class 1 building, an energy efficient fixed heater in good working order must be installed in the main living area [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether a portable heater counts or how this interacts with circuit capacity. Fixed heaters are defined as heaters "not designed or manufactured to be portable" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Electrical safety checks.** The rental provider must ensure an electrical safety check of the electrical installations, appliances and fittings they provide is conducted every 2 years by a licensed or registered electrician, and must give the renter the date of the most recent check in writing on request [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). They must also provide a copy of the most recent check within 7 days after a written request from the renter [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Repairs.** Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs, both urgent and non-urgent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The renter must notify the rental provider in writing as soon as practicable of damage or a breakdown of facilities or equipment supplied by the provider [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

## What you can ask for

1. **Written confirmation of the electrical safety check:** the date of the most recent check, and a copy of the report within 7 days of your written request [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
2. **A repair, in writing:** Tell the provider in writing about the tripping breaker so there is a written record [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The provider must carry out non-urgent repairs in a reasonable time [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
3. **VCAT if nothing happens:** You may apply to VCAT for an order requiring non-urgent repairs if the provider hasn't done them within 14 days of receiving notice of the repair [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
4. **Urgent repairs:** The documents list failure of heating or cooking appliances supplied by the provider as urgent repairs, and the provider must carry out urgent repairs after being notified [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). I couldn't confirm from these documents whether a circuit or breaker fault counts as urgent, so check the Consumer Affairs Victoria urgent repairs list [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

## Limits of this answer

- The only source I retrieved is the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, **Authorised Version No. 002, incorporating amendments as at 1 June 2022** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). I couldn't check later amendments, so confirm the current version on legislation.vic.gov.au.
- I didn't retrieve the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* itself, so the definition of urgent repairs and any statutory notice rules are not covered here.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved documents don't directly say whether a rooming house operator may charge for coin-operated washing machines. They do set out limits on charges generally, and what a resident can ask for.

**What the law says**

- **Separately metered utilities:** An operator may charge for electricity, gas and water used in a room only if the operator pays for those utilities, the room is separately metered, and the charge is no more than the supplier's charge [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Laundry is not mentioned in this section.
- **Charges for services:** If an operator charges for services, it must give the resident a separate schedule of those charges before the resident moves in. If the resident uses a service, the operator must provide an itemised account of that individual use [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Laundry service charges:** Section 109A allows a service charge for laundry or utility services, but only for Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency, and only where use can't practicably be measured. The charge must not exceed the cost of providing the service [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This provision doesn't clearly cover a private operator, and the documents don't say whether it applies to your house.
- **Laundry facilities:** From 26 February 2024, laundry facilities must include a washing machine in good working order for every 12 or fewer residents [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf). The standard doesn't say whether the machines must be free.
- **Urgent repairs:** Urgent repairs include failure or breakdown of an essential service or appliance for laundering supplied by the operator [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do**

1. **Check your paperwork.** Ask whether you were given a written schedule of charges before you moved in, as section 109 requires if the operator charges for services [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If the washing machines are listed as a charged service, the operator must also give you an itemised account of your individual use [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Ask for an itemised account** if you are being charged, to show your own use [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Ask about the machines' condition.** If a machine breaks down, it may count as an urgent repair. Notify the operator, and if they don't act, you may be able to arrange repairs and seek reimbursement [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
4. **Seek advice.** If there is no written schedule or the charges are unclear, contact Consumer Affairs Victoria (the forms refer to 1300 55 81 81 for general information) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf), or apply to VCAT.

**Gaps and version note**

- The documents don't state whether a private operator may charge for coin-operated laundry, or what the maximum price would be.
- The Act copy I found is labelled "rta-1997-v115" and dated 13 October 2026, which is before your date of 15 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The text doesn't show an Authorised Version number, so please confirm the current version on the official legislation website.
- The rooming house standards are dated 1 December 2024 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf). The forms are dated 30 June 2026 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved documents don't say whether a rental ad showing mould is allowed. They also don't say whether a photo is enough to prove a breach. They do set out the minimum standard for mould and the rules on advertising photos.

**Which versions apply (1 October 2025):** The Regulations are the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (S.R. No. 3/2021), reprint dated 2025-07-01 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). The Act is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (No. 109 of 1997), dated 2025-08-06 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Both were in force on 1 October 2025. The file names give the version numbers as v004 (Regulations) and v110 (Act). The text I retrieved doesn't print a separate "Authorised Version No." label, so please confirm those numbers against the official source.

### What the law says about the condition

- **Minimum standard:** "Each room in the rented premises must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). This is in Schedule 4, clause 8.
- **Provider's duty:** The rental provider must ensure the premises comply with the rental minimum standards and are vacant and reasonably clean when the renter moves in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Disclosure to applicants:** The provider must disclose if the premises comply with the rental minimum standards. From 31 December 2021, the provider must also disclose any repair notice received in the last 3 years relating to mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

### Advertising photos

- The Act lets a provider enter to produce advertising images and video, after notice, and must make a reasonable attempt to agree a suitable time with the renter [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (ss 85(b)(ii), 86(1)(ab), 89A(1)–(2)).
- A renter can object in writing to photos that show certain possessions, such as identifying, sensitive or high-value items [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 89A(3)).
- If the renter asks, the provider must not advertise images containing their possessions until the renter has reviewed them and given written consent [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 89A(4)–(5)).
- The documents don't say whether a photo showing mould may be advertised.

### Is the photo enough to prove a breach?

The documents don't cover this. They don't say what evidence proves a breach, how much weight a photo carries, or whether a photo alone shows the mould is "caused by or related to the building structure." That is a factual question the documents don't resolve.

### What the renter can do or ask

- **Ask for information:** Ask the provider whether the premises meet the rental minimum standards, and whether they have received a mould or damp repair notice in the last 3 years [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) (reg 16).
- **Before moving in (not yet in possession):** A renter can terminate the agreement, by notice, if the premises "do not meet any rental minimum standards" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 91L(f)). Termination takes effect only if the renter does not take possession and the agreement terminates under the Act (s 91L(b) read with s 334 is cross-referenced in the Act's text).
- **After moving in:** Notify the provider in writing of damage as soon as practicable. The provider must carry out non-urgent repairs in a reasonable time, and the renter may apply to VCAT if repairs are not done within 14 days of notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) (Schedule 1, Part D, cl 26).

The documents don't say whether a mould issue in an ad would qualify as an urgent repair. If you're a renter facing this, get advice from Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy service.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I let a friend move into my rental without telling the agent. Now I want them out. What do I have to do?
answer:
**Short answer:** Under the Act, you can't simply remove the friend yourself. The landlord can give a notice to vacate for unauthorised sub-letting or assignment, but only in a prescribed form with at least 14 days' notice. If the friend won't leave, the matter goes to VCAT. The documents don't say whether a friend living in the property counts as a sub-let or assignment, and they don't say whether you are the landlord or the renter.

**What the law says (as at 15 October 2026)**

- The governing document is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- A residential rental provider may give a notice to vacate if the renter "has assigned or sub-let or purported to assign or sub-let the whole or any part of the premises without the residential rental provider's consent." The termination date must be at least 14 days after the notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Renters must not assign or sub-let without the rental provider's written consent. The rental provider "cannot unreasonably withhold consent" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- A notice to vacate is not valid unless it is in the prescribed form, addressed to the renter, signed by the giver (or their agent), states the reason, and specifies the termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Under the Act, documentary evidence is required only for certain other notice types, not this one [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The rental provider must give the notice before applying to VCAT for a possession order. Only Victoria Police can carry out a forcible eviction, and only under a VCAT warrant. Rental providers cannot use force themselves [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do or ask**

- **If you are the renter:** Ask the friend to leave, or seek consent from the rental provider if you want them to stay. Be aware that the rental provider can give a notice to vacate for unauthorised sub-letting, and that you may have breached your duties by allowing the friend to move in without consent [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Talk to the agent or landlord promptly, and consider getting legal advice.
- **If you are the rental provider:** Serve a notice to vacate on the renter (not the friend) in the prescribed form, with the reason stated and a termination date at least 14 days after service [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). If the friend does not leave by that date, you would need to apply to VCAT for a possession order [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Challenging the notice:** The documents say a 30-day VCAT challenge right applies to certain notice types (sections 91ZX–91ZZC), not to this one [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The notice form does say the renter may seek advice and may challenge the notice at VCAT [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Check with VCAT or a community legal centre about this.

**Not covered by the documents**

- Whether a friend staying in the property is a "sub-let" or "assignment" under the Act.
- The rights and position of the friend as an occupant.
- The Authorised Version number for the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*. The retrieved file shows only S.R. No. 3/2021 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

question: It is 1 November 2019. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved documents don't contain a retaliation provision for rented premises. They do show when a notice to vacate is invalid, how long you have to challenge it, and what the landlord must include in it. The document is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf," dated 2 July 2019 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The "v088" in the filename is the only version reference I found, and I can't confirm from the text alone that it was the version in force on 1 November 2019.

### What the law says

- **Form and content:** A notice to vacate is not valid unless it is in the relevant prescribed form, addressed to the tenant, signed by the landlord or agent, states the reason(s) for giving it (unless it is a specified notice type), and specifies a termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Notice period:** If the notice is for repairs or renovation (s 255), the termination date must be not less than 60 days after the notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Other grounds have different minimums, such as 14 days for non-payment of rent (s 246) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Your right to challenge:** A tenant who receives a notice to vacate under certain sections (including s 255) may apply to the Tribunal challenging its validity. The application must be made within 30 days after the notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The Tribunal can decide whether the notice is valid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). If it finds the notice valid, you generally cannot challenge it again unless exceptional circumstances exist [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Repairs duties:** The landlord must ensure the premises are maintained in good repair [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). You can ask the Director to investigate non-urgent repairs if you gave the landlord written notice and the landlord did not carry out the repairs within 14 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Possession orders:** The Tribunal must not make a possession order before the termination date stated in the notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). It also cannot order possession unless the landlord was entitled to give the notice and the notice has not been withdrawn [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

### What to check

1. **The termination date.** If the notice is under s 255 and gives less than 60 days, it may be invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
2. **The stated reason.** Check that a reason is given and that it matches a ground the landlord can actually use [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
3. **The form and signature.** Check that it is in the prescribed form, addressed to you, and signed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
4. **Whether the reason is real.** For a repairs or renovation ground, the landlord must have all necessary permits and consents, and the work must be unable to proceed unless you leave [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
5. **Timing.** Note the date you gave the repair request and the date you received the notice.

### What you can do

- **Apply to the Tribunal within 30 days** of the notice being given. If the notice was given on 1 November 2019, that is about 1 December 2019 (my calculation from the 30-day rule in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)).
- **Keep records** of the repair requests, the written notice you gave, and the notice to vacate.
- **Keep paying rent** and avoid any breach that could give the landlord a separate ground.

### What the documents don't cover

- The retrieved text contains **no retaliation provision for rented premises**. The retaliation-type rules I found apply to caravans (s 315, which covers notices given in response to a resident exercising a right under the Act) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) and Part 4A sites (s 317ZH) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). I cannot say from these documents whether a comparable rule applies to your tenancy.
- I don't have the **termination date, stated reason, or form** of your notice, so I can't say whether it is valid.

If you share the notice's termination date and stated reason, I can check it against the sections above.

question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved law prohibits some of what you describe, including soliciting an offer above the advertised rent and misleading rent representations. The documents don't cover how to lodge a complaint, the time limits, or what the Tribunal can order, so I can't give you those steps.

**Governing document:** The Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 110, incorporating amendments as at 6 August 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). I found no later version in the search results, so I've applied it to 1 October 2025.

## What the law says

- **Bidding above the advertised rent is prohibited.** A rental provider or agent "must not solicit or otherwise invite an offer of an amount of rent that is higher than the advertised amount of rent for the rented premises." The penalty is 60 penalty units for a natural person or 300 penalty units for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Your report that someone offered more than the advertised price is relevant to this rule, but the documents don't show whether that offer was solicited.
- **Rent must be advertised as a fixed amount.** Premises must not be advertised or offered unless the rent is "advertised or offered as a fixed amount" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **False or misleading rent representations are prohibited.** A provider or agent who advertises rented premises "must not make a false or misleading representation in relation to the rent for the premises" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Misleading conduct that induces you to enter an agreement is prohibited.** This includes misleading or deceptive conduct, or a false representation about "the rent payable under the agreement" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). This section applies to providers not acting in trade or commerce, and it does not limit the Australian Consumer Law (Victoria) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

- **Check the rules against your facts.** The documents support a challenge if the provider or agent solicited a higher offer, or if the advertised rent or the email was false or misleading. Whether your "withdrawal" email was itself unlawful isn't addressed in the documents.
- **Tribunal orders.** The Act notes that section 472(1A) provides for orders the Tribunal may make for a contravention of section 30E [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The text of section 472(1A) is not in the retrieved documents, so I can't tell you what orders are available.
- **Deposits.** If you paid any money as a sign of good faith, the provider must refund it if the agreement isn't entered into within 14 days (or on the next business day after that period) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

## Evidence to keep

The documents don't list what evidence is needed. Generally useful items include:

- The original listing showing the advertised rent.
- The "withdrawn" email, with full headers and dates.
- Any messages about your application, and any mention of other offers or higher rent.
- Any receipts or proof of payment, if you paid anything.
- The current listing showing the higher rent.

## Not covered by the documents

- Complaint procedures, time limits, and who enforces sections 30E–30G.
- The text of section 472, and what the Tribunal can order.
- Whether the Australian Consumer Law (Victoria) provides a separate remedy.

I'd recommend checking with Consumer Affairs Victoria or VCAT for the procedure and deadlines, and getting advice if you intend to pursue a claim.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
**Short answer:** Probably not on the allergy ground alone. Under the Act, the agent's "no" does not end the matter. The owner's allergy is not a listed reason in the documents I found, and the law gives the landlord a set process to follow.

## What the law says

- A renter may keep a pet if the landlord has consented in writing or the Tribunal (VCAT) has ordered it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The request must be made in the form approved by the Director, and given to the landlord [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You used the official form, so that requirement appears to be met.
- A landlord **must not unreasonably refuse** consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations say the same: "The rental provider must not unreasonably refuse a request to keep a pet" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- The landlord is **taken to have consented** unless, within 14 days after receiving the request, they apply to VCAT for an order that refusing is reasonable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- When deciding such an application, VCAT may consider the type of pet, the character of the premises, and any other relevant matter [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't mention allergies of an owner specifically.

## What this means for you

- **Timing:** Your request was made about three weeks ago, so the 14-day window has probably closed. If the agent did not apply to VCAT within 14 days, the Act treats consent as given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). I can't confirm from the documents whether an application was filed, so check with the agent or VCAT.
- **The agent's refusal:** A refusal letter alone does not stop the deemed consent. Only a VCAT application does [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Allergy:** The documents don't say whether an owner's allergy is a reasonable ground to refuse. The fact that the owner rarely visits is also not addressed. Those points would be for VCAT to weigh, if an application is made.

## What you can do

1. **Keep records:** Save your signed request form, proof of when it was given, and the agent's refusal in writing.
2. **Check for a VCAT application:** Ask the agent in writing whether one was lodged. If not, you can point to the deemed consent in section 71C(2) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Get advice:** Consumer Affairs Victoria can be reached on 1300 55 81 81 . Victoria Legal Aid can advise on discrimination issues on 1300 792 387 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

This is general information based on the retrieved documents, not legal advice.

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents don't say whether a notice to vacate lapses when the sale falls through, so I can't confirm that you must leave. Under the law as the documents describe it, the notice stays in place unless it is withdrawn in the prescribed way, and you have options to check.

**Version relied on:** The Act is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf", dated 6 August 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). That was the version in force on 1 October 2025. The text does not state an Authorised Version number, so "v110" is taken from the file name only.

**What the law says**

- **Sale notices:** A landlord may give a notice to vacate if the premises are to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession immediately after the termination date. The termination date must be at least 60 days after the notice is given. If a sale contract is conditional, the landlord may give the notice within 14 days after the last condition is satisfied. If the contract is not conditional, the notice must be given within 14 days after the contract is entered into [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Validity of the notice:** A notice to vacate is not valid unless it is in the relevant prescribed form, addressed to the renter, signed, states the reasons, and, for a sale notice, is accompanied by the documentary evidence approved by the Director [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Withdrawal:** A notice to vacate is withdrawn only if a notice of withdrawal is given. That notice must be in writing, signed by the person who gave the notice, and signed by the person to whom it was given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). A buyer pulling out does not, by itself, withdraw the notice under these provisions.
- **Challenging the notice:** A renter who receives a notice to vacate under the sale provisions may apply to the Tribunal challenging its validity, on or before the hearing of any possession order application. The application must be made within 30 days after the notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Landlord's restriction:** If the landlord obtains possession after a sale notice, they must not let the premises for use as a residence within 6 months of the notice date, unless an exception applies [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Possession:** The regulations' notice form states that if you do not leave by the termination date, the landlord may apply to VCAT for a possession order. Only Victoria Police can carry out a forcible eviction, and only under a VCAT warrant [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do or ask**

1. **Check the notice against the requirements above:** the 60-day minimum, the 14-day timing relative to the sale contract, the prescribed form, the documentary evidence, and the signature. Any defect may make it invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
2. **Ask the landlord in writing to withdraw it.** A valid withdrawal needs a signed written notice of withdrawal from the landlord and your signature [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
**Short answer:** Based on the documents, you don't have to pay a rent increase unless your agent gives you a valid written notice. A notice that doesn't follow the rules is invalid, and a conversation or email exchange doesn't count as a notice.

**What the law says**

- The landlord must give you "at least 60 days notice in the prescribed form of a proposed rent increase" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- The notice must state the amount of the increase, the method used to calculate it, and your right to apply within 30 days to the Director to investigate the proposed rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- The notice can only provide for one rent increase [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- Rent can't be increased at intervals of less than 12 months [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- If you're on a fixed-term agreement, the rent generally can't go up before the term ends unless the agreement already provides for an increase [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- A rent increase that doesn't comply with these rules "is invalid" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- The prescribed form is Form 5, the "Notice of Proposed Rent Increase to Renter of Rented Premises." It must be sent personally, by post, or by email if you have consented to email [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do or ask**

- **Ask for the formal notice.** If you haven't received a Form 5 notice, the increase isn't valid yet. Ask the agent to confirm in writing whether they are issuing one.
- **Check the timing.** If a valid notice were given today (1 October 2025), the 60-day period would end on 30 November 2025. The new rent could not start before 60 days after the notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Check the start date stated on any notice you receive.
- **Check the last increase.** Confirm when rent last increased. Another increase within 12 months would be invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Check your agreement type.** If you're in a fixed term, the agreement must already provide for an increase [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Challenge it if needed.** Within 30 days after receiving a valid notice, you can apply in writing to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria to investigate whether the proposed rent is excessive. This is free [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). You can also apply to VCAT for an order declaring the rent excessive. Under the Form 5 notice, you will need to pay the increased amount from the date on the notice unless VCAT decides otherwise [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

**Limits of the documents**

- The documents don't say whether your agent's email could count as a Form 5 notice if it contained the required details. Form 5 requires the prescribed form, so an informal email is unlikely to be enough, but I can't confirm that from the documents.
- The documents don't state an official "Authorised Version number." The file names indicate the Act is version 110 (dated 6 August 2025) and the Regulations are version 004 (dated 1 July 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). Please check the official source to confirm the version number.
- I don't have information about your specific agreement, so I can't say whether your rent increase is lawful without seeing it.

question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:
**Short answer:** No. The law requires you to tell the owner in writing about the damage as soon as practicable, and the documents don't allow you to arrange the repair without them. The documents don't address insurance.

**Which versions I applied:** For 15 October 2026, I relied on the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* file labelled "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* file labelled "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The documents don't state an "Authorised Version" number in those words, so the "v115" and "v009" in the filenames are the only version identifiers I can point to.

### What the law says

- **Notice is required.** A renter must give written notice to the owner (the "residential rental provider") as soon as practicable after becoming aware of damage to the premises [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations say the same, adding that where damage occurs the renter must notify the rental provider in writing [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **You have a duty to avoid damage and to leave the property in good condition.** The renter must avoid damaging the premises [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). At the end of the agreement, the renter must leave the premises in the same condition as when they moved in, taking fair wear and tear into account [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Fair wear and tear does not include damage caused by a renter or visitor [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Repairs must be done by a suitably qualified person.** The Regulations state that only a suitably qualified person may do repairs, both urgent and non-urgent [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Skirting boards are unlikely to be "urgent repairs."** The Act's list of urgent repairs covers things like burst water services, gas leaks, and serious storm damage [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Chewed skirting boards do not appear on that list.

### What you can do or ask

1. **Tell the owner or agent in writing now**, describing the damage (what was damaged and how). Email may count as written notice if the parties have agreed to electronic service [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
2. **Ask whether they want you to repair it.** The owner can give you a repair notice requiring you to repair the damage at your expense within 14 days, in a proper and tradesman-like manner. If you don't, the owner may repair it and charge you the reasonable cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Consider a quote from a suitably qualified tradesperson** to share with the owner, so they can decide whether they want you to fix it or whether they'll claim the cost from your bond.
4. **Expect a possible bond deduction.** An owner can claim from the bond the reasonable cost of repairs for damage caused by the renter, taking fair wear and tear into account [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Before claiming, they must give you bond claim evidence at least 3 days in advance, and that evidence must not conflict with the condition report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**Gap:** The documents do not say whether a renter can carry out their own repair to damage they caused without the owner's knowledge. They only say that the notice must be given and that repairs must be done by a suitably qualified person [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Because you're moving out, the cleanest route is to notify the owner now and agree on who does the repair and how it's paid for.

### Insurance

The documents I retrieved don't address the owner's insurance, so I can't say whether the damage would affect it. You should ask the owner or check the policy directly.

The repair-notice and bond-deduction points add that the renter pays. (3) Insurance: 'The documents I retrieved don't address the owner's insurance.' question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved documents don't set a minimum number of circuits for a rental, and they don't address kettle-and-heater loads. The electrical rule that is in the documents takes effect on 29 March 2023, after your date of 1 March 2023.

## What the law says

- **Electrical circuit rule (not yet in force):** Schedule 4, clause 9 says that "On and from 29 March 2023," all power outlets and lighting circuits must be connected to a switchboard-type circuit breaker complying with AS/NZS 3000 and a switchboard-type residual current device complying with one of several listed AS/NZS standards [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The text doesn't specify a number of circuits.
- **Minimum standards apply from move-in:** A rental provider must ensure the premises comply with the rental minimum standards on or before the day the renter moves in [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **General repair duty:** The provider must ensure the premises are "in good repair" and "in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). Repairs must be done by a suitably qualified person [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Electrical safety checks:** The provider must arrange an electrical safety check every 2 years by a licensed or registered electrician [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

## What you can ask for

1. **A written repair request.** Notify the provider in writing "as soon as practicable" about a breakdown of facilities or equipment supplied by the provider. The provider must carry out non-urgent repairs "in a reasonable time" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
2. **Urgent repair, if applicable.** If the premises didn't meet the minimum standards on or immediately after move-in, you may request urgent repairs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The documents list urgent repairs as including failure of an essential service for hot water, cooking, heating or laundering [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). They don't say whether a tripping circuit counts, so I can't confirm that it is urgent.
3. **A copy of the latest electrical safety check.** On written request, the provider must give you a copy of the most recent electrical safety check within 7 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The record must include the electrician's name and licence number, the date, the results, and a report under AS/NZS 3019 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
4. **VCAT.** If the provider hasn't carried out a non-urgent repair within 14 days of receiving notice, you may apply to VCAT for an order requiring the repair [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

## Gaps in the documents

- The documents don't say how many circuits a rental must have.
- They don't say whether the circuit-breaker requirement applies to a tenancy that began before 29 March 2023.
- The Regulations are labelled "v002" in the filename and dated 1 June 2022, and the text cites S.R. No. 3/2021. The text doesn't show a separate "Authorised Version" number, so I can't confirm one.

This is general information based on the retrieved documents, not legal advice. For your specific situation, Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy advice service would be useful.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved documents don't clearly say whether a private rooming house operator can charge for coin-operated washing machines. The one express laundry charging power applies to Homes Victoria and registered housing agencies, not to most operators.

## What the law says

I applied the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* file labelled Authorised Version v115, dated 13 October 2026, which is in force on 15 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

- **Laundry charges:** A service charge for "laundry or utility services or facilities" may only be imposed by Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency, and only in a rooming house declared under section 19(2) or (3). It applies only if it is not possible or practicable to accurately measure the resident's use. The charge must not exceed the cost of providing the service [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Utility charges:** An operator may charge separately for electricity, gas and water, but only if the room is separately metered, and the charge must not exceed the supplier's charge. This provision does not mention laundry [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Disclosure:** If an operator charges for services, it must give the resident a separate schedule of those charges before the resident moves in, and an itemised account if the resident uses them [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Invalid terms:** A term in an agreement that is inconsistent with the Act is invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Washing machines:** From 26 February 2024, the rooming house standard requires one washing machine for every 12 or fewer residents, in good working order [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf). The standards document says nothing about whether residents may be charged for it.

**Gap:** The documents do not say whether coin-operated machines run by a private operator count as a "service charge" or are otherwise lawful. They also don't say whether the operator may charge for them at all.

## What you can do or ask

1. **Ask for the charges in writing.** Ask your operator for the separate schedule of services and, if you use the machines, an itemised account [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Check your agreement.** If a term requires you to pay for laundry and is inconsistent with the Act, it may be invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You can apply to the Tribunal to declare a term invalid or vary it if it is harsh or unconscionable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **If Homes Victoria or a registered agency runs your house**, you can apply to the Tribunal to withdraw or vary a service charge. The Tribunal can order it withdrawn or varied [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Report faults.** You must report broken facilities to the operator [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), and the operator must keep facilities in good repair [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) and comply with the rooming house standards [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

The documents don't cover whether a particular operator can charge for coin machines, so check your agreement and the operator's written schedule, and consider getting advice from a tenancy service.

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved documents don't say whether a rental ad may show mould. They also don't say whether a photo is enough to prove a property breaches the minimum standards.

**Version applied:** The documents are the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (file titled "rt-regs-2021-v004", dated 1 July 2025) and the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (file titled "rta-1997-v110", dated 6 August 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Both predate 1 October 2025, so I've applied them. The file names suggest Authorised Version numbers 004 and 110, but the text doesn't label them that way, so please confirm the numbers on the official source.

---

### What the law says

- **Mould is a minimum-standards breach.** "Each room in the rented premises must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" [1, Sch 4 cl 8].
- **The provider must meet the standards.** The provider "must ensure that the premises comply with the rental minimum standards" [1, Sch 1 cl 26].
- **Disclosure before signing.** Before entering an agreement, the provider must disclose prescribed information, including whether the premises comply with the rental minimum standards, and, from 31 December 2021, whether they have received a repair notice in the last 3 years relating to mould or damp caused by the building structure [2, s 30D; 1, reg 16(2)(b)–(c)]. A breach of s 30D carries a penalty of 60 penalty units for a natural person, or 300 for a body corporate [2, s 30D].
- **Misleading advertising.** A provider must not induce someone to enter an agreement by misleading or deceptive conduct, including a false or misleading representation about "the characteristics of the premises" [2, s 30E(2)–(3)(d)]. The penalties are the same as above [2, s 30E].
- **Advertising photos.** The regulations allow a provider to enter "to take images or video for advertising a property that is for sale or rent" [1, Sch 1 cl 34]. The documents don't say whether ads may show defects.

### Can they advertise it like that?

The documents don't answer this directly. What they do show is that the provider must still meet the minimum standards [1, Sch 1 cl 26], and must not mislead about the premises' characteristics [2, s 30E]. Showing the mould in the photos is not, on its face, misleading. The problem would be advertising the room in a way that hides the mould, or omitting the disclosures in s 30D.

### Is the photo enough to prove a breach?

The documents don't say what evidence is needed or how a breach is proven, and they don't say whether a photo alone is sufficient. A photo showing mould is relevant to the "free from mould" standard, but the documents don't say whether the mould is "caused by or related to the building structure", which is part of the standard [1, Sch 4 cl 8]. Assessing that would require further facts, and the documents don't cover how it is established.

### What the renter can do or ask

- **Ask for disclosure.** The renter can ask whether the premises comply with the rental minimum standards and whether there has been a mould or damp repair notice in the last 3 years [2, s 30D; 1, reg 16(2)].
- **Treat mould as urgent.** Mould or damp "caused by or related to the building structure" is listed as an example of a fault that makes premises unsafe or insecure, which falls within the definition of urgent repairs. The definition also includes "a failure to comply with any rental minimum standards" [2, s 3(1) def. of urgent repairs (ib), (k)].
- **Urgent repairs process.** The provider must carry out urgent repairs after being notified. If the renter has taken reasonable steps to get the provider to act immediately and the provider hasn't, the renter may arrange the repairs and be reimbursed "for the reasonable cost of repairs up to $2500". The renter can apply to VCAT if they cannot meet the cost, the cost exceeds $2500, or the provider refuses to pay [1, Sch 1 cl 30].
- **Non-urgent repairs.** The renter must notify the provider in writing "as soon as practicable". If repairs aren't done within 14 days of notice, the renter may apply to VCAT [1, Sch 1 cl 31].

**Not covered by the documents:** how to prove a breach, whether a photo is enough, and the specific VCAT process and evidence requirements. A tenancy advisor such as Consumer Affairs Victoria would be the next step.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I let a friend move into my rental without telling the agent. Now I want them out. What do I have to do?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved documents don't give a direct procedure for a renter to remove a friend who moved in without consent. The closest provision is a landlord's notice to vacate for unauthorised sub-letting, and the documents don't say whether a friend living there counts as a sub-letting.

**What the law says**

- Under the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, a landlord may give a renter a notice to vacate if the renter "has assigned or sub-let or purported to assign or sub-let the whole or any part of the premises without the residential rental provider's consent." The notice must give a termination date "not less than 14 days" after it is given [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't define "sub-let," so I can't confirm that a friend living there without paying rent falls within it.
- The Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 say the renter "must not assign... or sub-let the whole or any part of the premises without the written consent of the rental provider" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The rental provider "cannot unreasonably withhold consent" to a sub-letting [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- A notice to vacate is not valid unless it is in the prescribed form, addressed to the renter, signed, states the reason, and specifies the termination date [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- If the renter doesn't leave by the termination date, the landlord may apply to VCAT for a possession order. VCAT decides whether it is "reasonable and proportionate" to make one, and "Only Victoria Police can carry out a forcible eviction, and only when they are acting on a VCAT order" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do or ask**

- **Talk to the rental provider or agent.** They may be the party who would need to act, and they may ask for the friend to leave or for a consent process. The documents don't set out what happens if they refuse.
- **Ask for written consent** if you want the friend to stay. The rental provider cannot unreasonably refuse a sub-letting consent, but the documents don't say how this applies to a friend who isn't paying rent.
- **Check your agreement.** Any term about occupants or sub-letting may matter, but the documents don't cover what your agreement says.
- **Seek advice.** Consumer Affairs Victoria's renting line is 1300 558 181 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**What the documents don't cover**

- Whether a friend who is not a party to the agreement can be removed by you directly, and how.
- Whether a friend's occupation without consent is a breach that justifies a notice to vacate, beyond the sub-letting provision.
- Any time limits or steps for a renter to remove a co-occupant.

**Document versions:** The Act file is labelled v115 and dated 13 October 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations file is labelled v009 and dated 30 June 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Neither document states an "Authorised Version" number in its text, so I've relied on the file labels.

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both points are covered. The sub-letting point is plainly stated: the renter "must not assign... or sub-let the whole or any part of the premises without the written consent of the rental provider." The harder point, that the answer depends on the arrangement, is covered less directly. The answer never says "it depends on the arrangement", and it assumes the friend pays no rent. But it does make the outcome turn on a named deciding fact, what the friend pays: "I can't confirm that a friend living there without paying rent falls within it" and "the documents don't say how this applies to a friend who isn't paying rent."

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer says none of the listed things. The only fixed period, "not less than 14 days," is a landlord's notice to vacate given to the renter for unauthorised sub-letting, not a process for ending the friend's occupancy, and the answer adds that the documents don't say whether a friend "falls within it." The answer also never suggests a lock-out or removing the friend's belongings, never says the friend has no rights, and never says the friend can apply to VCAT to be added to the lease.

question: It is 1 November 2019. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved documents don't include the 2019 wording of a retaliation rule for rented premises, so I can't confirm exactly when a retaliatory notice is of no effect. They do set out the challenge route and a 30-day deadline.

## Which law applies

The file labelled version 088 of the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (dated 2 July 2019) is the version in force on 1 November 2019 [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The excerpts don't print the Authorised Version number, so I can't state it. The next version is dated 4 December 2019 [[11]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf), so I haven't applied it. The later versions from 2021, 2022 and 2025 [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa098%20authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) postdate your notice.

## What the 2019 Act says

- **Challenge right:** A renter who receives a notice to vacate may apply to VCAT challenging its validity. The application must be made on or before the hearing of a possession application and within 30 days after the notice is given [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The Tribunal may determine whether the notice is valid [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Which notices:** This challenge right covers notices under sections 255–260, 285, 286 or 310 [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The excerpts don't say which reasons fall under which section, so check the section number on your notice.
- **Re-challenge:** If the Tribunal finds the notice valid, you can't challenge it again unless exceptional circumstances exist [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Form:** A notice to vacate for rented premises is not valid unless it is in the prescribed form, addressed to the renter, signed, states the reason(s), and states the termination date [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Possession:** A landlord can apply for a possession order after giving a notice to vacate, no later than 30 days after the termination date [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The Tribunal can't decide the application before the termination date [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). It must make a possession order only if the landlord was entitled to give the notice, the notice was not withdrawn, and the landlord complied with section 72 of the VCAT Act [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

## What the documents don't cover

- **Retaliation rule in 2019:** The 2019 excerpts don't show the wording of a provision making a notice of no effect if it was given because the renter exercised a right. A later version does have such a rule, which says a notice "is of no effect" if given in response to the renter's exercise of a right under the Act [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa098%20authorised.pdf). That wording isn't in the 2019 excerpts, so I can't say it applied on 1 November 2019.
- **Notice period for month-to-month tenancies:** The retrieved 2019 text doesn't give the minimum notice period for your tenancy.
- **Regulation forms:** The prescribed forms I found are from 2021 onward [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)[[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf), so they may not match the forms used in 2019.

## What to check and do

1. **Deadline:** Challenge within 30 days after the notice was given. For a notice given on 1 November 2019, that is about 1 December 2019. Confirm how the notice was served and how the 30 days is counted.
2. **Reason and section:** Check whether the stated reason and section number are among those listed in the challenge provision [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
3. **Validity:** Check that the notice is in the prescribed form, signed, addressed to you, states reasons, and states a termination date [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
4. **Evidence for retaliation:** Gather a dated record of your repair requests, the leaking-fixture problems, any written correspondence, and the notice itself. The timing (same day as your follow-up) is relevant, but the excerpts don't set out how a retaliation claim must be proved.
5. **Don't ignore the notice:** A landlord still needs a VCAT possession order to remove you, and the Tribunal decides the matter [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
6. **Get advice quickly:** Given the short deadline, speak to a tenant advice service promptly. The retrieved documents don't list specific services for 2019.

must-not-say.reason: No. The answer states a 30-day challenge deadline rather than 60 days ('Challenge within 30 days after the notice was given... that is about 1 December 2019'), and it says a notice is not valid unless it 'states the reason(s)', which asserts that the landlord needed to give a reason.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Act in force on 1 November 2019 by version and date: "The file labelled version 088 of the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (dated 2 July 2019)", with the 97-109aa088 link. It still counts as named despite the odd remark that the excerpts don't print the version number. Every rule it applies comes from version 088, including the challenge right, the 30-day deadline, the form requirements and the possession order rules. The later version 098 retaliation rule and the 2021+ Regulations forms are mentioned only to say they may not have applied in 2019, not presented as law or as steps to take.

question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?
answer:
**Short answer:** Yes, the Act prohibits rental bidding and misleading rent representations, and it may give you grounds to challenge what happened. But the retrieved documents don't say how to challenge a withdrawn rental application, and they don't set out what evidence to keep.

**Version applied:** For 1 October 2025, I used the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (No. 109 of 1997), file "rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The retrieved text doesn't show an Authorised Version number beyond that file label. Later versions (dated 25 November 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)) are after your date, so I didn't rely on them.

---

### What the law says

- **Advertised rent must be a fixed amount.** A provider or agent must not advertise or offer premises unless the rent is advertised or offered as a fixed amount. The penalty is 60 penalty units for a natural person or 300 for a body corporate [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **No soliciting higher offers.** A provider or agent must not solicit or otherwise invite an offer of rent higher than the advertised amount [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **No accepting unsolicited higher offers, but only in the later text.** The November 2025 version says a provider or agent must not accept an unsolicited offer of higher rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). That paragraph was inserted by No. 6/2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The 1 October 2025 version I retrieved stops at the solicitation rule [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), so I can't confirm this prohibition applied on your date.
- **Misleading rent statements are prohibited.** Providers and agents must not make false or misleading representations about rent in advertising [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). They also must not induce someone to enter an agreement through misleading conduct or false representations about the rent payable [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The Tribunal can make orders for contraventions of this section [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

### What you can do or ask

1. **Ask the agent in writing** why the application was recorded as withdrawn, and ask for the withdrawal record. The retrieved documents don't provide a procedure for this.
2. **Raise the advertised price.** If the agent solicited or accepted a higher offer, that conduct falls within the prohibitions above [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
3. **Consider the Tribunal.** Section 472(1A) provides for orders the Tribunal may make for misleading-conduct contraventions [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The retrieved excerpts don't say what compensation or orders are available for bidding or for the withdrawal email, and they don't set out a time limit.

The documents don't cover whether the withdrawal email itself is a legal breach. The rules on withdrawing notices in the Act apply to notices to vacate, not rental applications [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), so I can't apply them to your situation.

### What to save as evidence

The documents don't list evidence to keep, so these are general practical suggestions, not drawn from the sources:

- The original advertisement or listing showing the advertised rent (screenshots with dates).
- Your application and all emails or messages with the agent.
- The withdrawal email, with full headers, and any proof you did not withdraw.
- The current listing showing the higher rent, with dates and screenshots.
- Anything showing the other offer, such as messages or a statement from the agent. Note who told you and when.

### Gaps

- The documents don't confirm whether No. 6/2025 was in force on 1 October 2025, so the ban on accepting unsolicited higher offers is uncertain for your date.
- The documents don't cover the process for disputing a withdrawn application or the time limits for doing so.
- The regulations' rental application rules, which cover bidding [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf), are dated after 1 October 2025, so I didn't rely on them.

For advice on your specific facts, contact a tenancy advice service.
