question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
**Short answer:** Probably not. Under the Act, the owner cannot unreasonably refuse, and if they didn't apply to the Tribunal within 14 days, the law treats your request as approved. The documents don't say whether an allergy is a reasonable ground for refusal.

**Version used:** The most recent Act in the retrieved documents is *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf," updated 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The title says "v115," but the text doesn't state an Authorised Version number explicitly, so please confirm the number on the official source. The retrieved *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (updated 30 June 2026) covers the form and related rules [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**What the law says**

- **The request:** You must make it in the form approved by the Director, and give it to the rental provider [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Your form appears to meet this.
- **No unreasonable refusal:** "A residential rental provider must not unreasonably refuse to consent to the renter keeping a pet on the rented premises" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Deemed consent:** The provider is "taken to have consented" unless, "within 14 days after being given the request, the residential rental provider applies to the Tribunal" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Your request was about three weeks ago, so that 14-day window has likely passed.
- **Tribunal route:** A provider who wants to refuse must apply to VCAT for an order that refusal is reasonable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Tribunal may consider the type of pet, the character of the premises, and "any other matter the Tribunal considers relevant" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do**

1. **Check whether an application was filed.** Ask the agent in writing whether the owner applied to VCAT within 14 days of your request. If they didn't, the documents indicate your consent is taken to be given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Respond in writing.** Point out the 14-day rule and that the refusal must be reasonable. Keep copies of your request, the refusal, and any dates.
3. **Get advice.** Consumer Affairs Victoria can be reached on 1300 55 81 81 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Victoria Legal Aid gives advice on discrimination issues on 1300 792 387 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). VCAT can be reached on 1300 018 228 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**What the documents don't cover**

- Whether an owner's allergy is a "reasonable" ground for refusal. The Act doesn't address allergies specifically.
- Whether the agent can refuse on the owner's behalf.
- Whether the dog's breed, size, or building rules (such as strata or body corporate rules) affect the answer.
- Whether the owner's infrequent visits matter legally.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. Deemed consent is stated: the provider is 'taken to have consented' unless 'within 14 days after being given the request, the residential rental provider applies to the Tribunal'. The three-week application, the hardest point, is covered by 'Your request was about three weeks ago, so that 14-day window has likely passed' together with 'If they didn't, the documents indicate your consent is taken to be given'. The next step is 'Ask the agent in writing whether the owner applied to VCAT within 14 days of your request.'

But its advice step "Consumer Affairs Victoria can be reached on 1300 55 81 81" is sourced from 97-109aa111, Authorised Version No. 111 (November 2025), which was not in force on 15 October 2026. question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
**Short answer:** Based on the retrieved documents, the notice does not stop applying just because the sale fell through. The documents don't say what happens when a sale collapses, so I can't confirm whether the notice remains valid. You should get advice before deciding whether to move out.

**Which law applies:** On 1 October 2025, the version in force is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 110, file `rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf` (dated 6 August 2025), as named in its title [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Later versions in the search results (v111 dated 25 November 2025, and v115 dated 13 October 2026) postdate your date, so I haven't relied on them [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### What the law says

- **Sale notices:** A landlord may give a notice to vacate if the premises are, immediately after the termination date, "to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). If there is a conditional contract of sale, the landlord must give the notice within 14 days after the last condition is satisfied. If the contract is unconditional, it must be given within 14 days after the contract is entered into [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Minimum notice:** The termination date must be "not less than 60 days after the date on which the notice is given" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Withdrawal:** A notice to vacate "is withdrawn only if a notice of withdrawal is given." The withdrawal must be in writing, signed by the person who gave the notice, and signed by the person to whom it was given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Since your landlord hasn't withdrawn it, the notice has not been withdrawn under this rule.
- **Possession orders:** The Tribunal can only order you to leave if it is satisfied, among other things, that the notice "has not been withdrawn" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

### What the documents don't cover

The retrieved documents don't say whether a sale-based notice stays valid after the buyer withdraws. They also don't say whether the landlord can still rely on the "to be sold or offered for sale" ground. I can't fill that gap from memory.

### What you can do

1. **Check the notice's validity.** It must be in the prescribed form, addressed to you, signed, state the reason, and, for a sale notice, be accompanied by documentary evidence supporting the reason. It must also state a termination date at least 60 days after it was given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). It should also have been given within the 14-day windows described above [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
2. **Apply to VCAT if you want to challenge it.** You can apply within 30 days after the notice is given to challenge its validity [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Your deadline depends on when the notice was given, so check that date now.
3. **Ask the landlord for a signed withdrawal.** If they agree to withdraw, it must be in writing and signed by both of you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
4. **Consider ending the agreement early.** The Form 6 information sheet lists "the premises are to be sold" as a reason for which you may be able to end the agreement earlier than the termination date, by giving at least 14 days' notice of intention to vacate [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). This comes from the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* version dated 25 November 2025 [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf), which postdates 1 October 2025, so I can't confirm it applied on your date.
5. **Get advice.** Form 6 advises seeking advice immediately from a community legal organisation listed on the Consumer Affairs Victoria website, or calling 1300 558 181 [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered. (1) The answer sets out the sale ground ("to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession"), the separate contract-based timing ("within 14 days after the last condition is satisfied" or after an unconditional contract), and the need for "documentary evidence supporting the reason." It also flags that whether the landlord can still rely on the ground after the buyer pulled out is not covered by the documents. (2) It states the 60-day minimum. (3) It says withdrawal must be "in writing, signed by the person who gave the notice, and signed by the person to whom it was given." (4) It gives next steps: ask for a signed withdrawal, or apply to VCAT within 30 days. Point (1) is the hardest, because the answer presents the planned-sale and contract-based routes and the evidence requirement but never says outright that the outcome depends on which ground was used.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: none of the three failure conditions is asserted. The answer states the notice 'does not stop applying just because the sale fell through', that a withdrawal must be 'signed by the person who gave the notice, and signed by the person to whom it was given', and that the termination date must be 'not less than 60 days after the date on which the notice is given' (the 14-day figures refer only to the landlord's window for giving notice and the tenant's own notice of intention to vacate).

version-cited.reason: No: although the answer correctly names the 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 110', step 4 presents the option to end the agreement early as a step the user can take, sourced from the 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 version dated 25 November 2025'. That version was not in force on 1 October 2025 (Version No. 004, dated 1 July 2025, was), and the caveat does not cure this because deleting the step would change the answer's substance.

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
**Short answer:** Based on the documents, you probably don't have to pay the higher rent yet. An email saying the rent is going up, followed by a refused negotiation, isn't a valid rent increase notice. Without one, the rent can't legally go up.

**Which law applies on 1 October 2025**

- The Regulations version in force on that date appears to be the one dated 1 July 2025 (file "rt-regs-2021-v004-2025-07-01.pdf"). Its Form 5 says the rental provider "must give you at least 60 days notice of any rent increase" [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- A later version (file "rt-regs-2021-v005-2025-11-25.pdf") raised this to 90 days [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). That version postdates 1 October 2025, so it doesn't apply to your situation.
- For the Act, the latest version in my results that predates 1 October 2025 is "rta-1997-v097-2021-03-28.pdf." Section 44(1) requires "at least 60 days notice in the prescribed form of a proposed rent increase" [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa097%20authorised.pdf). The documents don't show whether this section was amended between March 2021 and October 2025, so please check the current Act version.
- The documents don't show a separate "Authorised Version number" beyond the version labels in the file names above.

**What the law says**

- **Prescribed form:** The rental provider "must use this form" (Form 5) to notify you of a proposed rent increase, and "a valid notice of a proposed rent increase is required for all rent increases" [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Required content:** The notice must state the method used to calculate the increase, and the increase "cannot be greater than the amount calculated using this method" [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). It may provide for one rent increase only [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Timing:** Rent can't be increased more than once every 12 months [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf), and not during a fixed term unless the agreement provides for an increase [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). Under the Act, a rent increase that contravenes section 44 "is invalid" [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa097%20authorised.pdf).
- **Who gives it:** The form requires the rental provider's name, which "cannot be the agent's name" [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

**Start date**

If a valid 60-day notice were given on 1 October 2025, the earliest possible increase would be about 30 November 2025. This assumes the notice is given on that date and that the form's start date allows for the full notice period. Any start date earlier than that would not comply.

**What you can do or ask**

1. **Ask for the official notice.** Request a Form 5 notice from the rental provider, not just the agent. Check that it states the current rent, the new rent, the start date, and the calculation method [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
2. **Apply to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria.** You can ask the Director to investigate if you think the increase is excessive. This is free, must be in writing, and must be made within 30 days after the notice is given [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)[[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa097%20authorised.pdf). The form lists GPO Box 123 Melbourne 3001 and renting@justice.vic.gov.au, and the phone number 1300 558 181 for more information [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
3. **Apply to VCAT.** You can also ask VCAT to declare the rent excessive. This must be made within 30 days after receiving the Director's report, or within 30 days after the notice is given if there is no report. You will generally need to pay the increased amount from the date on the notice unless VCAT decides otherwise [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

I can't tell from the documents whether the agent's email itself counts as a notice. It would need to be in the prescribed form and contain the required content. If you have a fixed-term agreement, check whether it allows an increase during the term.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered. The answer says the provider "must use this form" (Form 5) and must give "at least 60 days notice." It also says an email "isn't a valid rent increase notice. Without one, the rent can't legally go up," and that a non-compliant increase "is invalid." Finally, it gives next steps, such as asking for an official Form 5 notice and applying to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria within 30 days. The hardest point is the email's invalidity. It is hedged mildly ("probably," plus the closing caveat), but the reader can still clearly tell which way it falls.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. None of the failing claims are asserted: the answer says "you probably don't have to pay the higher rent yet", does not tie the start date to the email, applies "at least 60 days notice" and raises the 90-day rule only to say it "postdates 1 October 2025, so it doesn't apply", and never says email is barred, only that the email "would need to be in the prescribed form and contain the required content."

version-cited.reason: No. The answer applies the Act's s 44 rules (60 days' notice in the prescribed form, and an increase that breaches s 44 'is invalid') from 'rta-1997-v097-2021-03-28.pdf' (link 97-109aa097), not the in-force Authorised Version No. 110; deleting that material would change its substance, even though it correctly relies on Regulations version 004 ('rt-regs-2021-v004-2025-07-01.pdf').

question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents don't allow you to quietly arrange the repair without telling the owner. They also don't address insurance.

**Which law applies:** Today is 15 October 2026. The most recent Regulations in the results are the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Authorised Version No. 009 (dated 30 June 2026) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The most recent Act text I found is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 101 (dated 7 September 2022) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). I found no later Act version, so I can't confirm that No. 101 is the version in force today.

**What the law says**

- Your dog chewing the skirting boards is damage. A renter must take care to avoid damaging the premises [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- You must give the owner or agent written notice as soon as practicable after becoming aware of the damage [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The Regulations say the same: notify the rental provider in writing of any damage [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- You may arrange urgent repairs yourself only if you have taken reasonable steps to get the owner to do them immediately and they haven't [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The Regulations list the urgent-repair categories, which focus on essential services such as hot water, cooking, heating and laundering [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether skirting boards qualify, and they seem unlikely to.
- Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs, whether urgent or non-urgent [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Any repairer you use would need to be suitably qualified.
- If you don't repair the damage, the owner can give you a repair notice. It must state the nature of the damage, that you caused it, and that you have 14 days to repair it in a tradesman-like manner [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). If you don't, the owner may repair it at your expense and recover the reasonable cost of the repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- At the end of the tenancy, you must leave the premises reasonably clean and in the same condition as when you moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The Regulations also say you must restore the premises to their pre-tenancy condition at the end, excluding fair wear and tear, for modifications [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do or ask**

1. **Give written notice now.** Tell the owner or agent in writing about the skirting-board damage, with a description of it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). This is required, so doing it quietly isn't an option.
2. **Offer to have it fixed, or ask the owner to arrange it.** Ask whether they want you to repair it or whether they'll do it. If they want it fixed, a repair notice would set out the 14-day period and the cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
3. **Get a quote from a suitably qualified person** so you have a cost figure to discuss [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
4. **If the owner wants you to pay**, the Act requires written particulars of the cost before you're liable for it, and you have 14 days after the repairs are completed to reimburse them [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

**Insurance:** The documents don't cover the owner's property insurance, so I can't say whether this damage would affect it. Ask the owner or their insurer directly.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered: (1) written notice 'as soon as practicable after becoming aware of the damage'; (2) responsibility for the dog's damage, since the owner may 'repair it at your expense and recover the reasonable cost', plus the duty to leave the premises 'in the same condition as when you moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear'; (3) 'The documents don't cover the owner's property insurance'; (4) a next step, 'Give written notice now'.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: none of the failing claims appear, since the answer rejects a quiet repair ('The documents don't allow you to quietly arrange the repair without telling the owner'), states no insurance outcome as fact ('I can't say whether this damage would affect it'), and never says the renter must pay the owner's insurance excess.

version-cited.reason: No. The rubric requires Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, but the answer instead names and relies on 'Authorised Version No. 101 (dated 7 September 2022)' and also cites 97-109aa088 (version 088) for rules it applies, including the notice, repair notice and end-of-tenancy duties. Neither version was in force on 15 October 2026, though it does correctly cite Regulations Version No. 009.

question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved documents don't set a number of circuits a rental must have. The electrical rule you're asking about starts on 29 March 2023, about four weeks after today, so it isn't in force yet.

**What the law says**

- The rental minimum standard for electrical safety says that "On and from 29 March 2023... all power outlets and lighting circuits in the rented premises are to be connected to" a switchboard-type circuit breaker complying with AS/NZS 3000, and a switchboard-type residual current device complying with one of several listed standards [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The rule is about protection on each circuit, not how many circuits there are [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- The earliest version I found is the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 reprint dated 1 June 2022 (file "rt-regs-2021-v002-2022-06-01.pdf") [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). I didn't find a version that covers exactly 1 March 2023, and the excerpt I retrieved doesn't show its cover page, so I can't confirm its Authorised Version number. The file name indicates version 002, but that is not verified. The same electrical text appears in later reprints, including Authorised Version No. 004 (as at 1 July 2025) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- For the heater, the regulations required a fixed heater in good working order in the main living area of a Class 1 building for the period 29 March 2021 to 28 March 2023 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). The 2021 Regulations also say a fixed heater is to be in the main living area [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). I couldn't confirm the exact wording of that clause in the 2022 reprint from the excerpt I have.

**What you can ask for or do**

- **Ask for a safety check.** The rental provider must keep records of gas and electrical safety checks and give them to the renter on request [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). You can also ask for the date of the last electrical safety check, which is recorded in the condition report [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Report the problem in writing.** The condition report guidance says renters should "tell the rental provider or their agent about any defect that could be a threat to safety" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). A written notice of the problem is useful evidence.
- **Escalate if repairs aren't done.** If the condition report lists something needing repair and the rental provider doesn't fix it within a reasonable time, you can apply to VCAT for an order requiring the repairs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Check your condition report.** If you find something not working, you may apply to VCAT to correct the report within 30 days after the start date of the agreement [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

**What the documents don't cover**

- Whether a rental must have a particular number of circuits, or whether a breaker tripping under load breaches the standard.
- The rental provider's general repair duties under the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, which aren't in the retrieved excerpts.
- Any version of the rules specifically in force on 1 March 2023, since I couldn't retrieve one.

A licensed electrician can tell you whether the circuit is overloaded or faulty. Consumer Affairs Victoria (www.consumer.vic.gov.au/renting) is the place to confirm current repair obligations.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents don't say whether a rooming house operator can charge for coin-operated washing machines. They don't address that situation directly. They do set out rules on charges that would apply if an operator does charge for a service.

**What the law says**

- **Utility charges in your room:** An operator may charge for electricity, gas and water used in a room only if the operator pays for those utilities and the room is separately metered, and the charge must not exceed the supplier's charge. This section does not apply to residents of a shared room [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Washing machines aren't mentioned, so this rule doesn't clearly cover them.
- **Charges for services:** If an operator charges for services, it must give you a separate schedule of the amounts before you move in. If you use a service, it must give you an itemised account of your individual use [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Laundry service charges:** Section 109A allows a service charge for laundry services, but only for Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency, and only in a rooming house declared under section 19(2) or (3). It applies only where it is not possible or practicable to accurately measure the use of the service. The charge must not exceed the cost of providing it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If your operator is a private company, this provision doesn't appear to apply.
- **Laundry standards:** From 26 February 2024, rooming houses must have laundry facilities in good working order for every 12 or fewer residents, including a washing machine [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf). The retrieved text doesn't say whether these must be free.

**What you can do or ask**

1. Ask the operator in writing what legal basis it relies on to charge for the machines.
2. Ask for the separate schedule of services that section 109 requires, and for an itemised account of your use if you're being charged [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. If your house is run by Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency, check whether they gave you written notice of the service charge, and check that it doesn't exceed the cost of providing the service. You can apply to the Tribunal for an order to withdraw or vary it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. Check how many residents the house has and whether it has at least one washing machine for every 12 or fewer residents [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf).

**Limits of these documents**

I can't confirm from these documents whether your operator is Homes Victoria, a registered housing agency, or a private operator, or whether your house is declared under section 19. I also can't tell from them whether coin-operated laundry charges are lawful for a private operator. For that, you would need to check with the Victorian tenancy authorities or get legal advice.

**Sources:** The current Act text is the 2026 reprint, which appears to be Authorised Version No. 115 based on its file name, dated 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved documents set a mould standard for rentals, and they require landlords to disclose certain mould-related information. They don't say whether a rental ad may show mould, and they don't say whether a photo is enough to prove non-compliance.

**Which version applies:** On 1 October 2025, the version in force is the one dated 1 July 2025, labelled v004 in the file name (*Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, S.R. No. 3/2021) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). I didn't retrieve an Authorised Version number stated in the document itself, so I'm using the v004 label. Versions dated after 1 October 2025 are not used here.

**What the law says**

- **Mould standard:** "Each room in the rented premises must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Disclosure duties:** The rental provider must disclose whether the premises comply with the rental minimum standards, and whether they have received a repair notice in the last 3 years relating to mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The text I retrieved for this is from the 2022 version [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The v004 excerpt I found doesn't include this regulation, so I can't confirm its wording in force on 1 October 2025.
- **Advertising:** The documents don't cover rules about what a rental ad may show or say, so I can't say whether this ad is allowed.
- **Photos as proof:** The documents don't say what evidence is needed to show a property fails the minimum standards. A photo might show visible mould, but the standard only covers mould "caused by or related to the building structure" [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf), and a photo alone doesn't show the cause.

**What the renter can do or ask**

- Ask the provider whether the property complies with the rental minimum standards, and whether any mould or damp repair notice has been received in the last 3 years [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- Ask for the disclosure information in writing. The documents don't say what form it must take.
- The documents don't cover inspections, condition reports for mould, complaint processes, or Tribunal applications, so I can't advise on those steps from these sources.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered: the mould standard is quoted ('free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure'), the photo point is addressed ('a photo alone doesn't show the cause'), and a next step is given ('Ask the provider whether the property complies with the rental minimum standards').

must-not-say.reason: Yes: neither failing claim is made. On the photo, the answer says "a photo alone doesn't show the cause." On advertising, it says "The documents don't cover rules about what a rental ad may show or say, so I can't say whether this ad is allowed," rather than claiming such ads are banned.

It does correctly name the Regulations version 'v004' dated 1 July 2025.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I let a friend move into my rental without telling the agent. Now I want them out. What do I have to do?
answer:
**What the law says**

You are the rental provider, so the rules that apply to you are in the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*. The most recent Regulations in the documents I can access are Authorised Version v009, dated 30 June 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The Act version I can access is v088, dated 2 July 2019 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The documents don't show whether v088 is still the current Act version on 15 October 2026, so please check that before relying on it.

- **Consent is required.** The renter must not assign or sub-let the whole or any part of the premises without the rental provider's written consent. If they do, the rental provider may give the renter notice to vacate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Your ground for ending the tenancy.** A landlord may give a notice to vacate if the tenant has assigned or sub-let, or purported to, without consent. The termination date must be at least 14 days after the notice is given [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Whether a friend moving in is "sub-letting."** The documents don't define this or say whether a friend living there without a separate sub-lease counts. You'll need advice on whether the facts fit this ground.

**What you have to do**

1. **Serve a notice to vacate on the correct form.** The notice must use Form 6 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). It must:
   - give the termination date, allowing at least the minimum notice required under the Act (14 days under s 253) plus time for delivery [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf);
   - name the rental provider, not the agent. The agent's name can only be used for the address for service [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf);
   - state the reason and section number of the Act, with specific details [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Form 6 says a notice may be found invalid if it lacks enough detail [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
2. **If the friend does not leave, apply to VCAT for a possession order.** Form 6 says rental providers must give the appropriate notice before applying for a possession order. VCAT decides whether you were entitled to give the notice and whether a possession order is reasonable and proportionate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3. **Do not remove them yourself.** Rental providers cannot personally use force to remove a renter. Only Victoria Police can carry out a forcible eviction, and only on a VCAT order (a warrant for possession) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**What the renter can do or ask**

- **Challenge the notice.** The renter may challenge it at VCAT, for example if they believe it was not given properly or the reason is incorrect [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Ask for consent instead.** The rental provider cannot unreasonably withhold consent to assign or sub-let, and must not demand or receive a fee for consent beyond reasonable expenses [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). If you would accept the friend as an occupant, you could consider written consent on those terms.

**Not covered by the documents:** whether a friend's occupancy counts as sub-letting in your situation, and whether the 2019 Act text is still current on 15 October 2026. For a specific decision, contact Consumer Affairs Victoria or get legal advice.

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both points are covered, though the answer wrongly treats the user as the rental provider. The dependence on the arrangement is hedged but present, and names a deciding fact about what was agreed: 'The documents don't define this or say whether a friend living there without a separate sub-lease counts. You'll need advice on whether the facts fit this ground.' The consent point is stated directly: 'The renter must not assign or sub-let the whole or any part of the premises without the rental provider's written consent.'

It also wrongly treats the user as the rental provider, so this process does not fit the renter's situation.

question: It is 1 November 2019. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved documents don't contain the provision that bans retaliatory notices to vacate for rented premises, so I can't confirm what protects you on that point. They do cover how to challenge a notice to vacate and the deadline for doing so.

**Version applied:** The most recent reprint dated before 1 November 2019 is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* file labelled v088 (dated 2 July 2019) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The text doesn't print an Authorised Version number, so I can only cite it by that file label. Two other reprints are dated after your date, so I haven't relied on them: v089 (4 December 2019) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf) and v090 (2 March 2020) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf). The *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* form [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf) is dated 2022, so it isn't the law in force on 1 November 2019 and I haven't relied on it.

---

### What the law says

- **Form and validity:** A notice to vacate is not valid unless it is in the relevant prescribed form, is addressed to the tenant, is signed by the landlord or their agent, specifies the reason or reasons for the notice, and specifies the termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Challenging the notice:** A tenant who receives a notice to vacate under certain sections can apply to the Tribunal (VCAT) challenging its validity. The application must be made within 30 days after the notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The listed sections include 255 to 260, 285, 286 and 310 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The excerpts don't show which section your notice relies on, so check the notice.
- **Tribunal powers:** The Tribunal may determine whether the notice is valid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). If it finds the notice valid, you can't bring another challenge unless "exceptional circumstances" exist [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Possession orders:** The Tribunal must make a possession order only if the landlord was entitled to give the notice and the notice has not been withdrawn [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). A landlord can apply for a possession order at any time after the notice is given, but no later than 30 days after the termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

### What you can check

1. **The notice's form and content:** Is it the prescribed form? Is it addressed to you, signed, and does it state a specific reason and termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)?
2. **The stated reason:** Does the notice give a reason, and does it match the section it relies on? The excerpts don't say what the retaliation provision requires, so I can't say whether a reason that refers to your repair request meets that test.
3. **The deadline:** If the notice was given on 1 November 2019, a challenge must be made within 30 days, which is by about 1 December 2019 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
4. **Notice period:** The excerpts don't state the minimum notice period for a month-to-month tenancy under these sections, so I can't tell you whether the termination date is too early.

### What you can do

- **Apply to VCAT within 30 days** if you think the notice is invalid, including on retaliation grounds, and seek advice quickly [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)[[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The 2022 form [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf) lists retaliation as a ground for challenge, but it's a later document, so this is only context.
- **Get advice promptly.** I can't find in the retrieved documents the text of the retaliation provision itself or the minimum notice period for your case, so a legal or tenancy advisor should confirm both.

must-not-say.reason: No: the answer asserts that a notice is invalid unless it "specifies the reason or reasons for the notice" (telling the user to check whether it states "a specific reason"), and it gives a 30-day challenge deadline ("The application must be made within 30 days after the notice is given") instead of 60 days.

version-cited.reason: No. The answer correctly names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 version in force, citing it as "v088 (dated 2 July 2019)" with the 97-109aa088 link. However, it also relies on the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 form (21-3sra002, dated 2022), which was not in force on 1 November 2019, to tell the user to "Apply to VCAT within 30 days... including on retaliation grounds" because "The 2022 form lists retaliation as a ground for challenge." This presents a later document's rule as a step the user can take, which counts as relying on it despite the 'only context' caveat. Deleting that material would remove the only support for retaliation as a ground for challenge, so the substance of the answer would change.

question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?
answer:
**Short answer:** The law in force on 1 October 2025 prohibits rental bidding and misleading rent advertising, but the documents I can access don't say how to challenge a withdrawal email, and they don't include the regulations in force on that date.

## What the law says

The version in force on 1 October 2025 is the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 110 (dated 6 August 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Later versions are not in force on that date, so I haven't relied on them, except to note what changed.

- **Fixed advertised rent:** A provider or agent must not advertise or offer premises unless the rent is advertised or offered as a fixed amount [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **No soliciting higher offers:** A provider or agent must not solicit or invite an offer of rent higher than the advertised amount [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **No false or misleading rent advertising:** A provider or agent must not make a false or misleading representation about the rent in advertising [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **No misleading conduct to induce an agreement:** A provider or agent must not induce a person to enter a rental agreement through misleading or deceptive conduct, or a false or misleading representation about the rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Not in that version:** A later version (dated 25 November 2025) adds a ban on accepting an unsolicited higher rent offer, inserted by No. 6/2025 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The version you asked about does not include this ban [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

## What you can ask or do

- **Challenge the process:** The Act's note says the Tribunal may make orders for a contravention of the misleading-conduct section (s 30E) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The documents I can access don't say which Tribunal orders apply to the bidding or advertising sections.
- **Ask the agent in writing** why the application was recorded as withdrawn, and to confirm whether they solicited or accepted a higher offer. This is general practice, not something the documents require.
- **Note on the withdrawal email:** The Act's withdrawal rules in the documents concern notices to vacate, not rental applications [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). They don't apply to your situation.

## What to save as evidence

The documents don't list evidence requirements for this situation. Based on general practice, consider keeping:

- The original advertisement showing the fixed rent (with the date you saw it).
- Your application and all emails or messages with the agent.
- The "withdrawn" email, with its full headers and date.
- Screenshots of the new listing showing the higher rent and its date.
- Anything that shows what the other offer was or how it was made.

## What the documents don't cover

- Whether the agent actually solicited or accepted the other offer. This depends on facts I don't have.
- How to dispute a withdrawn rental application.
- The Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 in force on 1 October 2025. The regulation versions I found are dated 25 November 2025 [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) and 30 June 2026 [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

This isn't legal advice. For a formal challenge, contact Consumer Affairs Victoria or VCAT.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
**Short answer:** Probably not, unless the owner has already taken the request to the Tribunal. Under the Act, the owner must not unreasonably refuse, and if they don't apply to VCAT within 14 days, consent is taken to have been given. Your request was about three weeks ago, so that 14-day window has likely closed.

Based on the most recent version of the Act in the documents (dated 13 October 2026, the file is named v115, but the text does not print an Authorised Version number), I'm applying that version as in force on 15 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **Consent is required, and the owner can't unreasonably refuse.** A renter may keep a pet if the provider has consented in writing or the Tribunal has ordered it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The provider "must not unreasonably refuse to consent" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Deemed consent after 14 days.** The provider "is taken to have consented" unless, "within 14 days after being given the request," they apply to the Tribunal under section 71D [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Only a Tribunal application stops this. A verbal or written refusal does not, on its face, do so [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **If the owner does apply to VCAT.** The Tribunal may order that it is reasonable to refuse consent, or may permit the pet [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). In deciding, it may consider the type of pet, the character and nature of the premises, the fittings, whether refusal is permitted under any other Act, and any other relevant matter [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Discrimination.** Refusing to rent because of a protected attribute can be unlawful. The regulations list "disability" and "assistance dog" among protected attributes, and state that refusing accommodation "because you have an assistance dog" is an example of unlawful discrimination [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Allergy of the owner is not on that list in the excerpts I found, so I can't say from the documents whether it is protected.

## How this applies to you

1. **Timing:** Three weeks ago is roughly 24 September 2026, so the 14-day period would have ended around 8 October 2026. Confirm the exact date you gave the request.
2. **Did the owner apply to VCAT by then?** This is the key question. If they did not, consent is likely taken to have been given under section 71C(2) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't tell me whether an application was filed, so you need to check with VCAT.
3. **The owner's allergy.** The Act doesn't list allergy as a ground to refuse. The factors the Tribunal considers are about the pet, the premises and fittings, and "any other matter" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Whether an allergy is a reasonable ground, and how much weight the owner's rare visits carry, is not answered in the documents.

- If no application was made within 14 days, you can rely on deemed consent, but get advice before keeping the dog.
- If they did apply, the Tribunal decides. Contact VCAT (1300 018 228, vcat.vic.gov.au) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) or Victoria Legal Aid (1300 792 387) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). For general tenancy questions, Consumer Affairs Victoria is listed at 1300 55 81 81 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

This is general information based on the retrieved documents, not legal advice. The documents do not say how a Tribunal would weigh an allergy against a rarely-present owner, and they don't confirm whether any VCAT application was filed.

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
**Short answer:** Based on the documents, the notice is still in effect unless it is formally withdrawn. The documents do not say whether a notice lapses when the sale falls through, so I can't confirm that you can ignore it.

## What the law says

- **Withdrawal requires a formal document.** A notice to vacate "is withdrawn only if a notice of withdrawal is given." That notice must be in writing and signed by both the person who gave the notice and the person it was given to [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). A landlord's decision not to proceed with the sale is not, on the text, a withdrawal.
- **The sale ground.** A landlord may give a notice to vacate if the premises are to be "sold or offered for sale with vacant possession" immediately after the termination date. The termination date must be at least 60 days after the notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The landlord must also attach documentary evidence supporting the reason [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Which version applies.** On 1 October 2025, the version in force is the one labelled v110 (file dated 6 August 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). A later version, v111 (dated 25 November 2025), exists but postdates your date, so I haven't applied it [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Gap in the documents.** Nothing in the retrieved documents addresses whether a sale-based notice lapses when the contract falls through. The sale provisions only set timing rules for notices given around a contract of sale [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

1. **Ask the landlord for a signed notice of withdrawal.** If they agree, it must be in writing and signed by both parties [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
2. **Check the notice's validity.** Look at the termination date (at least 60 days after the notice was given), whether it is in the prescribed form, whether it states the reason, and whether documentary evidence was attached [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
3. **Apply to VCAT within 30 days.** A renter who receives this kind of notice may apply to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) challenging its validity. The application must be made within 30 days after the notice was given, on or before the hearing of any possession order [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
4. **Know what happens if you don't leave.** An older version of the regulations says that rental providers cannot personally use force to remove a renter, and only Victoria Police can carry out a forcible eviction under a VCAT warrant for possession [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa098%20authorised.pdf). I can't confirm that this text was in force on 1 October 2025.
5. **Get advice quickly.** The regulations direct renters challenging a notice to contact a community legal organisation listed on the Consumer Affairs Victoria website, or call 1300 558 181 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa098%20authorised.pdf).

**Not covered by the documents:** whether the notice lapses after a failed sale, and the specific termination date and evidence in your notice, which I don't have.

---

**Sources:**
[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version v110, dated 6 August 2025 (rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf).
[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version v111, dated 25 November 2025 (not applied; postdates 1 October 2025).
[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa098%20authorised.pdf) Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version v002, dated 1 June 2022 (rt-regs-2021-v002-2022-06-01.pdf). Applicability on 1 October 2025 is not confirmed.

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
**Short answer:** Based on the documents, you probably do not have to pay a higher rent yet. An agent's email and a refused negotiation are not a valid rent increase notice. But the law does require the landlord to give a proper notice, and that notice sets the start date.

**What the law says**

- A rental provider must give the renter "at least 60 days notice in the prescribed form of a proposed rent increase." [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (*Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf, dated 6 August 2025, s 44(1))
- A rent increase made in contravention of s 44 "is invalid." [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 44(5))
- The increase must be stated on the prescribed form. The Regulations say "A valid notice of a proposed rent increase is required for all rent increases." [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) (*Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, file rt-regs-2021-v004-2025-07-01.pdf, dated 1 July 2025, Form 5)
- The notice may provide for only one increase, must state the amount and how it was calculated, and must not increase rent more than once every 12 months. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) (s 44(2)-(4A); Form 5)

**What you can do or ask**

1. **Ask for a formal Form 5 notice.** It must name the rental provider (not the agent), state the current and new rent, the start date, and the calculation method. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) If the notice doesn't meet these requirements, it may not be valid.
2. **Check the notice period.** On 1 October 2025, the Act and the Regulations I could confirm both say 60 days. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) A later version of the Regulations (dated 25 November 2025) changes Form 5 to "at least 90 days notice." [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf) The documents do not say when that change took effect, so I can't apply it to your situation.
3. **Use your review rights.** Within 30 days after the notice is given, you can apply to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria to investigate if you think the increase is excessive. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) (s 45(2)) You can also apply to VCAT, generally within 30 days after the Director's report, or 30 days after the notice if there is no report. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) (s 46)
4. **Be aware of the payment risk.** Form 5 says you will need to pay the increased amount from the date on the notice "unless VCAT decides otherwise." [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) So if you receive a valid notice and challenge it, you may still have to pay from the notice's start date while the challenge is pending.

**Answer to your question**

- **Do you have to pay?** Not on the basis of an email and a refused negotiation. Without a valid notice in the prescribed form, the increase is invalid. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)
- **From when?** The documents do not give a start date for an increase that has not been validly notified. Once a valid notice is given, the start date is the one stated on the notice, and it must allow at least 60 days (on the documents I could confirm for 1 October 2025). [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

*Note: The documents I found are labelled by version (v110 for the Act, v004 for the Regulations). I can't confirm these are the official Authorised Version numbers. This is general information, not legal advice. For advice on your specific tenancy, contact Consumer Affairs Victoria.*

Without a valid notice in the prescribed form, the increase is invalid'; and it gives next steps, including asking for a Form 5 notice and applying to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria within 30 days after the notice.

It mentions the later Regulations version 005 (90 days, dated 25 November 2025) only as a later change it 'can't apply', so deleting that mention would not change the answer's substance.

question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents don't support fixing the skirting boards without telling the owner. The renter must notify the owner in writing, and only a suitably qualified person may do repairs. The documents also don't say whether the damage affects the owner's insurance.

**Which law applies:** For 15 October 2026, the latest Regulations version I found is *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (file "rt-regs-2021-v009", dated 30 June 2026) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The latest Act version in the results is *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (file "rta-1997-v110", dated 6 August 2025) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The text I retrieved doesn't show "Authorised Version No." labels, so I'm citing the file version labels. The retrieved excerpts of both are partial, so I can't confirm every provision.

**What the law says**

- **Damage must be reported.** The renter must avoid damaging the premises, and where damage occurs, must notify the owner in writing [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). The notice must be given "as soon as practicable" [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Your dog's damage is a notifiable event.
- **Only a suitably qualified person may repair.** "Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs—both urgent and non-urgent" [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- **The owner can require you to pay.** The owner may give a repair notice if damage results from the renter's failure to take care. The notice must be in writing and state the nature of the damage, that it was caused by the renter's failure, and that the renter must repair it within 14 days in a tradesman-like manner, or the owner may do it at the renter's expense [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). If the owner does the repairs, the renter is liable for reasonable costs if the owner gives written particulars of the cost, and must reimburse within 14 days after the repairs are completed [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Fair wear and tear is excluded.** At the end of the tenancy, the renter must restore the premises to their original condition, excluding fair wear and tear [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Chewing is not fair wear and tear.
- **Exit inspection.** At the end of the agreement, the owner or agent must complete the final inspection and fill in the condition report within 10 days after the end date [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

**Your questions**

1. **Can you get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner?** No, not on what the documents say. You'd need to give written notice as soon as practicable and use a suitably qualified person [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Doing the repair without telling the owner would likely breach the notice duty. Repairing without notice also risks the owner treating it as their own repair and charging you for it [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

2. **Would it affect the owner's insurance?** The documents don't say. The Regulations do prohibit a term that makes the renter liable "by default for an insurance excess to be paid under an insurance policy of the rental provider" [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). That shows the excess can't be shifted to you by default, but it doesn't say whether damage affects the owner's policy. You'd need to ask the owner or agent, or check the policy.

**What you can do**

- Give the owner or agent written notice now, describing the damage, and ideally attach photos [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- Offer to arrange or pay for a suitably qualified person to repair it, or ask the owner whether they'd prefer to do it, with written costs.
- Keep a copy of your notice and any quotes or receipts.
- If the owner gives a repair notice, you have 14 days to repair it properly [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Otherwise, ask for written cost particulars before paying.
- For advice on the specific situation, contact Consumer Affairs Victoria (1300 558 181) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

On the hardest point, it says the renter must "restore the premises to their original condition, excluding fair wear and tear" and that "Chewing is not fair wear and tear". It says the insurance question is not settled ("The documents don't say"). It gives next steps such as giving written notice and offering to arrange or pay for repairs.

question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents do not say how many circuits a rental needs. They do set an electrical safety standard that starts on 29 March 2023, four weeks after your date.

**Which version applies:** The earliest version I found is the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (file labelled v002, dated 1 June 2022) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). I found no version dated between then and 1 March 2023, so I have applied it. The retrieved text does not state a formal Authorised Version number, so I can only refer to the file label, v002.

**What the law says:** Schedule 4, clause 9 (Electrical safety) provides that "On and from 29 March 2023... all power outlets and lighting circuits in the rented premises are to be connected to" a switchboard-type circuit breaker complying with AS/NZS 3000, and a switchboard-type residual current device complying with one of AS/NZS 3190, AS/NZS 61008.1 or AS/NZS 61009.1 [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The clause does not mention the number of circuits, and it does not yet apply on 1 March 2023 [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Later versions of the regulations repeat the same wording [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf), but I have not used them to answer your date.

**What you can ask for:**

- **Electrical safety check records.** The rental provider must ensure an electrical safety check of the electrical installations, appliances and fittings they provide is conducted every 2 years by a licensed or registered electrician, and must provide the renter with the date of the most recent check, in writing, on the renter's request [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). You can ask for this date now.
- **Check at the start of a tenancy.** If no electrical safety check was done within the 2 years before you moved in, the provider must arrange one "as soon as practicable" [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Compliant circuits from 29 March 2023.** From that date, you can ask for the outlets and lighting to be on compliant circuit breakers and residual current devices, as clause 9 describes [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

**What the documents don't cover:** They do not say whether a tripping breaker from running a kettle and heater together is a breach, how many circuits are required, or how to request a repair for this problem. The repair and urgent-repair provisions of the Act were not in the retrieved material. A licensed electrician can tell you whether the wiring is overloaded, and Consumer Affairs Victoria (consumer.vic.gov.au/renting) can advise on your options. Put any request to your provider in writing.
