question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents I found don't say directly whether a private rooming house operator may charge for coin-operated washing machines. They do set conditions on any charge for services, and they give you ways to check and challenge one.

**What the law says**

- Charges for utilities are limited. An operator may charge for electricity, gas and water only if the room is separately metered, and the charge can't exceed the supplier's charge [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). That section doesn't mention washing machines.
- If an operator charges for services, it must give you a separate schedule of the amounts before you move in, and an itemised account of your individual use if you use those services [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- Section 109A allows a *service charge* for laundry services, but only where Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency imposes it, in a house declared under s 19(2) or (3). It applies only if it isn't possible or practicable to measure your use accurately. The charge must not exceed the cost of providing the service, and it must be notified to you in writing [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). This section does not cover private operators.
- If the operator stops providing a service, the rent must be reduced by the amount agreed, or by an amount the Tribunal sets [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- The Rooming House Standards require that, for every 12 or fewer residents, there is a washing machine in good working order [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do or ask**

1. Ask the operator for the written schedule of any service charges. If you didn't receive one before moving in, s 109 says it should have been provided [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
2. Ask for an itemised account of your use if you are charged [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
3. Check who runs the house. If it's Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency, you can apply to VCAT to have a service charge withdrawn or varied, and the Tribunal can order it withdrawn or varied [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
4. If a machine breaks down, report it to the operator in writing. Failure of a laundering appliance supplied by the operator is an urgent repair. If the operator doesn't fix it, you can arrange repairs and seek reimbursement of up to $2,500, or apply to VCAT [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**Gaps**

The documents don't say whether a private operator can charge coin-op fees for laundry, what rate would be acceptable, or whether a coin-op fee counts as a "service charge" under the Act. For a definite answer, you would need to check the current Act and the rooming house's agreement, or contact Consumer Affairs Victoria.

**Versions used**

- *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (retrieved copy labelled v111, dated 25 November 2025) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). This is the latest version in my search results, and I can't confirm that no later version applies on 15 October 2026.
- *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (S.R. No. 3/2021, retrieved copy labelled v009, dated 30 June 2026) [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- *Residential Tenancies (Rooming House Standards) Regulations 2023* (S.R. No. 10/2023, retrieved copy dated 1 December 2024) [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: Yes. The answer covers all four points: it says the Standards require 'for every 12 or fewer residents, there is a washing machine in good working order'; it says the documents 'don't say whether a private operator can charge coin-op fees for laundry', which covers the hardest point that the law doesn't require free machines; it says a 'separate schedule of the amounts' must be given 'before you move in'; and it advises 'Ask the operator for the written schedule of any service charges.'

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved documents set a minimum standard for mould, but they don't answer whether the advertising itself is allowed, and they don't say how much weight a photo carries as evidence.

**Version in force:** For 1 October 2025, the applicable document is the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* in the file labelled *rt-regs-2021-v004-2025-07-01.pdf* (dated 1 July 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). Later versions in the search results (dated 25 November 2025 and 30 June 2026) postdate your date, so I haven't relied on them [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)[[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The retrieved text doesn't show a separate "Authorised Version No." beyond the v004 label in the filename.

**What the law says about the mould:**
- Under Schedule 4 (Rental minimum standards), clause 8: "Each room in the rented premises must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- So a bedroom with mould that is caused by or related to the building structure would fall short of this standard. The documents don't say whether surface mould from tenant habits would count.

**Is the photo enough to prove it?**
- The documents don't say what evidence is needed to prove a breach, how a photo should be treated, or who carries the burden of proof.
- A photo may show that mould is present. It doesn't, by itself, show the cause. The standard only covers mould "caused by or related to the building structure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf), so the cause is a separate question.

**Can they advertise it like that?**
- The retrieved in-force text doesn't contain rules on rental advertising or on what a provider must disclose to applicants.
- An earlier version (dated 1 June 2022) lists disclosure items, including whether the premises comply with the rental minimum standards and whether the provider has received a repair notice about mould or damp in the last 3 years [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). That version isn't in force on 1 October 2025, and the retrieved text doesn't show whether the same wording applied then, so I can't rely on it for your date.
- The Act itself (the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*) isn't among the retrieved documents, so I can't say what it requires for advertisements.

**What the renter can do or ask:**
- The documents don't set out a complaint or dispute process for a mould problem in a rented home. I can't confirm what steps are available from these documents.
- A practical step is to ask the provider or agent, in writing, whether the bedroom has mould or damp, whether it complies with the rental minimum standards, and whether any repair notice about mould or damp has been received in the last 3 years. The last two points come from the disclosure items in the 2022 version [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf), so you should check they applied on 1 October 2025.
- Keep dated photos and written replies. The documents don't say whether this evidence would be sufficient.

**Not covered by the retrieved documents:** advertising rules, the Act's provisions on disclosure, the evidential standard for a breach, and the VCAT or other dispute process for a rental property. For these, the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* and the official Consumer Affairs Victoria guidance would need to be checked.

---

**Sources**
[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) rt-regs-2021-v004-2025-07-01.pdf (1 July 2025)
[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf) rt-regs-2021-v005-2025-11-25.pdf (25 November 2025)
[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf) rt-regs-2021-v002-2022-06-01.pdf (1 June 2022)
[[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf (30 June 2026)

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered: the answer quotes the standard that each room 'must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure'; it says the photo 'doesn't, by itself, show the cause' and that the documents don't say what evidence proves a breach; and it gives a next step, 'ask the provider or agent, in writing, whether the bedroom has mould or damp'.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I let a friend move into my rental without telling the agent. Now I want them out. What do I have to do?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents I can access don't contain the provision that governs a friend moving in without the agent's knowledge as of 15 October 2026. The steps below come from the regulations' notice-to-vacate form and an older Act version, so confirm them before acting.

## What the law says

- **Current Act not confirmed:** The only Act text I found is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* as at 2 July 2019 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). I can't confirm it's the version in force on 15 October 2026, so I can't give you the current notice period.
- **Possible ground (2019 Act):** That version lets a landlord give a tenant a notice to vacate if the tenant has "assigned or sub-let or purported to assign or sub-let the whole or any part of the premises without the landlord's consent." The termination date must be "not less than 14 days after the date on which the notice is given" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). This applies to the tenant, not necessarily to a friend who isn't a party to the agreement, and the documents don't address unauthorised occupants directly.
- **Form and content (2026 Regulations):** The notice must be on Form 6 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). It must give a termination date that allows for "the minimum notice required under the Residential Tenancies Act 1997" and the delivery method, and it must state the reason with "specific details" and the relevant section number of the Act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The rental provider's name must be given, not the agent's name [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **If they don't leave:** You may apply to VCAT for a possession order. VCAT decides whether you were entitled to give the notice and will make an order only if it is "reasonable and proportionate to do so" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **No self-help eviction:** "Rental providers cannot personally use force to remove you... Only Victoria Police can carry out a forcible eviction, and only when they are acting on a VCAT order (a warrant for possession)" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What the other party can do or ask

- They can challenge the notice at VCAT if they believe it was not given properly, or if the reason or information is incorrect or incomplete. They can also ask for more time if they would face hardship [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- If they have experienced family or personal violence that caused the behaviour in the notice, they should apply to VCAT within 30 days after the notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What you should do next

1. Check your tenancy agreement and the 2026 Regulations' Form 6 requirements.
2. Get the current *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* text, since the version I found is from 2019 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
3. Confirm whether your friend is a party to the agreement or simply an occupant. The notice-to-vacate form is written for renters who are parties to the agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
4. Give a properly completed Form 6 notice with the correct minimum notice period.
5. If they don't leave, apply to VCAT for a possession order. Don't remove them yourself.

**Version note:** The 2026 Regulations file is labelled "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The Act file is labelled "rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The documents don't state an Authorised Version number in the text, so I can't confirm the official Authorised Version number for either.

This is general information, not legal advice. Consumer Affairs Victoria (1300 558 181) or a community legal centre can help with your specific situation.

question: It is 1 November 2019. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved documents don't contain the rented-premises retaliation rule that was in force on 1 November 2019, so I can't tell you what the law required of your notice on that date.

**What the 2019 document covers**

The only retrieved document dated before 1 November 2019 is the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, version v088, dated 2 July 2019 [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Its excerpts cover Part 6 (termination for caravan parks and site agreements) and Part 7 (possession orders). They don't include the rented-premises notice provisions. The excerpts do show that a tenant or resident may apply to the Tribunal within 30 days after a notice to vacate is given, for notices under sections 255–260, 285, 286 and 310 [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The excerpt doesn't say what those sections cover, so I can't confirm that they apply to a month-to-month rental.

**What the later law says (not in force on 1 November 2019)**

Later versions of the Act say that a notice to vacate is of no effect if it was given in response to the renter exercising a right under the Act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Those versions also allow a renter to apply to the Tribunal challenging the notice, generally within 30 days after it is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). These provisions appear in versions dated 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The earliest version retrieved, dated March 2020, doesn't contain this text in the excerpts I received [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf). I can't say from these documents when the rule was introduced, so don't treat it as the law on 1 November 2019.

**What you can do**

- Check the date on the notice, the reason it gives, and whether it is on the prescribed form. The later version requires a notice to vacate to be in the relevant prescribed form, to specify the reasons, and to specify a termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). I can't confirm that the 2019 Act had the same requirements for your type of tenancy.
- Get advice quickly. The Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 form for a notice to vacate advises renters who think a notice was given because they exercised their rights to seek advice immediately from a community legal organisation [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). That form is from a 2021 version, so it doesn't confirm the 2019 position either.
- Confirm the 2019 provisions from the Authorised Version of the Act in force on 1 November 2019, or ask a tenancy advice service. The retrieved documents don't include that version.

must-mention.reason: No. The answer never states that a no-reason notice is allowed with at least 120 days' notice. It also gives the Tribunal challenge window as 30 days, not 60. The retaliation rule appears only as later law with the warning 'don't treat it as the law on 1 November 2019', which hedges it too far to count.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says a reason was required or that a deadline other than 60 days applies to this notice. It attributes the requirement to "specify the reasons" and the "generally within 30 days" deadline to later versions it says are "not in force on 1 November 2019." It also notes the 2019 30-day provision for sections 255–260, 285, 286 and 310, but says it "can't confirm that they apply to a month-to-month rental."

Caveats do not cure this, and deleting those sources would change the substance of the advice.

question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?
answer:
**Short answer:** The Act in force on 1 October 2025 prohibits a landlord or agent from *soliciting* a higher rent offer, and the penalties are set out below. The documents I found don't clearly say whether accepting an unsolicited higher offer was prohibited on that date, and they don't address a false "withdrawn" record directly. They also don't say what evidence to keep.

**Which version applies:** The version in force on 1 October 2025 is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version 110 (file dated 6 August 2025) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Versions dated later in 2025 and 2026 are not in force on that date, so I haven't relied on them for the answer.

---

### What the law says

- **Rent must be advertised at a fixed amount.** The provider or agent must not advertise or offer premises unless the rent is advertised as a fixed amount [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **No soliciting higher offers.** The provider or agent "must not solicit or otherwise invite an offer of an amount of rent that is higher than the advertised amount of rent" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Penalties.** Breaching these rules carries up to 60 penalty units for a natural person, or 300 penalty units for a body corporate [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Unsolicited offers.** A later version (Authorised Version 111, dated 25 November 2025) adds a rule that the provider or agent must not accept an unsolicited higher offer. That subsection was "inserted by No. 6/2025 s. 7" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Version 110 does not contain it, so it was not in force on 1 October 2025 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). I couldn't find the commencement date of No. 6/2025 in the documents.
- **Misleading conduct.** Section 30E prohibits inducing someone to enter an agreement through misleading or deceptive conduct, with the same penalties [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Section 472(1A) provides for Tribunal orders for contraventions of this section [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). This may be relevant if the false withdrawal and the rent change were used to push you out of the deal, but the documents don't say how it applies to your facts.

---

### What you can do or ask

1. **Ask the agent in writing** to explain the withdrawal record and to say whether a higher offer was solicited or invited. The documents don't set out a formal complaint process.
2. **Apply to VCAT if the conduct is misleading.** The documents show that Tribunal orders are available for contraventions of section 30E [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The documents don't state the filing deadline or what compensation is available for this type of claim.
3. **Get advice on the bidding issue.** Whether it was a prohibited solicitation or acceptance depends on facts the documents don't cover, such as whether the agent invited the offer.

---

### Evidence to keep

The documents don't list what evidence to keep for this situation. As general practice, not from the sources, you could keep:
- the original advertisement and listing showing the fixed rent,
- your application and every message you sent,
- the "withdrawn" email, with headers and date,
- any messages about the other offer or the new listing,
- screenshots of the current listing.

---

### Limits of these sources

- I found no document on how to challenge a false withdrawal record or on the evidence required.
- The Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 contain applicant guidance, such as contacting the provider to check the outcome [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Those versions are dated after 1 October 2025, so I haven't relied on them.

must-mention.reason: No. The answer never states that relisting at a higher fixed rent is not illegal by itself. It covers the soliciting ban, says the unsolicited-acceptance rule was not in force on 1 October 2025 ('Version 110 does not contain it, so it was not in force'), and says the documents 'don't address a false "withdrawn" record directly', but the first point is absent.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: none of the three claims is asserted. On unsolicited offers, the answer says the rule 'was not in force on 1 October 2025', and in its short answer it says the documents 'don't clearly say whether accepting an unsolicited higher offer was prohibited on that date', so it does not call acceptance illegal on that date. It never says relisting at a higher rent is illegal by itself; it only says the agent 'must not solicit or otherwise invite an offer' above the advertised rent. It never says the applicant can force the agent to rent the property to them.

The answer names the 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 110 (file dated 6 August 2025)' and applies only its rules on fixed-amount advertising, solicitation, penalties and s 30E; it mentions Version 111 only to say a rule was added later and was not in force, and it says outright that it does not rely on the later Regulations versions (005, 009).

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
**What the law says**

The Act in force on 15 October 2026 is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, in the reprint labelled **v115** (file dated 13 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The excerpt doesn't print an "Authorised Version No." on its own, so the v115 label comes from the file name.

- A provider **must not unreasonably refuse** consent to a pet [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- If the renter's request is given, the provider is **taken to have consented unless, within 14 days after being given the request, the provider applies to the Tribunal** under section 71D [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- To refuse, the provider must apply to the Tribunal for an order that refusing is reasonable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Tribunal can then permit the pet or, if it is satisfied refusal is reasonable, make orders refusing consent or excluding the pet [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- When deciding, the Tribunal may consider the type of pet, the character of the premises, and "any other matter the Tribunal considers relevant" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Act does not list the owner's allergy or how often the owner visits as factors.
- The Regulations (version dated 30 June 2026) repeat that the rental provider "must not unreasonably refuse a request to keep a pet" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**Applying this to your situation**

- You used the required form. Section 71B requires a request "in the form approved by the Director" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Your request was about three weeks ago, so the 14-day window has probably closed. Unless the owner or agent applied to the Tribunal within 14 days, the request is deemed consented to [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say when your request was received or whether any application was filed, so you should confirm both dates.

- Whether the refusal is "unreasonable" depends on the Tribunal's assessment. The documents don't say how an allergy is weighed against the factors above.

**What you can do or ask**

1. Check the date your request was given and whether the agent or owner has applied to VCAT. If no application was filed within 14 days, you can rely on the deemed consent in section 71C(2) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. Ask the agent in writing to confirm consent, or to say whether a Tribunal application has been made. Keep copies of the request and all replies.
3. Check your lease for any pet clause. Any additional term "must not exclude, restrict or modify any of the rights and duties included in the Act" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
4. If the provider does apply to the Tribunal, you can respond to it. The Tribunal decides whether refusal is reasonable under section 71E [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

The documents don't cover VCAT contact details, fees, or what happens if a provider ignores the 14-day rule. For those, check the Tribunal's or Consumer Affairs Victoria's official sites.

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
**Short answer:** Based on the documents I found, the notice has not been withdrawn, so it appears to remain in effect. The documents do not say whether a notice lapses when a sale falls through, and a notice alone does not force you out. The landlord would need a VCAT possession order. I can't tell from what you've given me whether the notice was valid when it was issued.

**Version used:** The Act version in force on 1 October 2025 is the one in the file *rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf* [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). I'm reading "Authorised Version v110" from the filename, since the text itself doesn't state it. The v111 file dated 25 November 2025 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) postdates your date, so I haven't relied on it.

**What the law says**

- **Sale as a ground:** A landlord may give a notice to vacate if the premises are to be "sold or offered for sale with vacant possession" immediately after the termination date. If a contract of sale exists, the timing depends on whether it has conditions. With conditions, the notice must be given within 14 days after the last condition is satisfied. Without conditions, it must be given within 14 days after the contract is entered into. The termination date must be at least 60 days after the notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Withdrawal:** A notice to vacate "is withdrawn only if a notice of withdrawal is given." The withdrawal must be in writing and signed by the person who gave the notice *and* by the person it was given to [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Validity requirements:** A notice to vacate is not valid unless it is in the prescribed form, addressed to the renter, signed, states the reasons, includes any required documentary evidence, and specifies the termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Gap in the documents:** Nothing in the retrieved excerpts says what happens to a sale-based notice if the buyer withdraws. I can't say whether the notice remains valid in that situation.

**What you can do**

1. **Check your dates.** Confirm when the notice was given, what termination date it specifies, and when the sale contract was entered into or its conditions satisfied. These determine whether the notice was valid from the start.
2. **Challenge it at VCAT within 30 days.** A renter may apply to VCAT challenging the validity of a notice given under section 91ZZB. The application must be made within 30 days after the notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). VCAT may determine whether the notice is valid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). This deadline may already have passed, so act quickly.
3. **Ask the landlord in writing to withdraw it.** A withdrawal only takes effect if it is in writing and signed by both the landlord and you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Without your signature, the landlord's withdrawal is not effective under that section.
4. **If the landlord applies for a possession order,** you can attend the VCAT hearing. The documents I retrieved don't include the possession-order provisions for this version of the Act, so I can't tell you the test VCAT will apply.
5. **Get advice quickly.** A community legal centre or Consumer Affairs Victoria can review your notice and dates, especially given the 30-day deadline.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered. The hardest one, that the answer depends on the ground and its evidence, is met by distinguishing premises 'to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession' from the case where 'a contract of sale exists', and by noting that validity requires the notice to state reasons and include 'any required documentary evidence'. The answer also states 'at least 60 days', says withdrawal must be 'in writing and signed by the person who gave the notice and by the person it was given to', and gives next steps: challenge at VCAT within 30 days or ask for a written withdrawal signed by both.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: none of the three failure conditions appears, since the answer says the notice "appears to remain in effect" because it "has not been withdrawn", says withdrawal must be "signed by the person who gave the notice *and* by the person it was given to" so that "Without your signature, the landlord's withdrawal is not effective", and gives only a 60-day minimum ("at least 60 days after the notice is given"), with the 30-day and 14-day figures being the VCAT challenge deadline and the timing for giving notice rather than notice periods.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Act's in-force version as 'Authorised Version v110' via the file 'rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf' and the link '97-109aa110', and every rule it applies is cited to [1], that v110 document. It mentions v111 only to say it postdates 1 October 2025 and was not relied on.

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
**Short answer:** Probably not, unless the agent gives you a valid written notice. Under the version of the law in force on 1 October 2025, a rent increase needs a proper notice, and an informal email or refusal to negotiate isn't one.

**What the law says**

- A valid notice of a proposed rent increase is required for all rent increases, and it must be in the prescribed form (Form 5). The notice must state the current and new rent, the start date, and how the increase was calculated. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)
- Under the version in force on 1 October 2025, the rental provider must give at least 60 days' notice of any rent increase. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) (The file is titled "rt-regs-2021-v004-2025-07-01.pdf," Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, dated 1 July 2025. The documents don't show an "Authorised Version" label, so I'm relying on that filename for the version number.)
- The Act says a landlord must give at least 60 days' notice in the prescribed form, and a rent increase made in contravention of this section is invalid. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)[[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf) Those Act versions are dated 2019 and 2020. I did not find a 2025 version of the Act, so I can't confirm it's the one in force on 1 October 2025.
- A rent increase can't happen more than once every 12 months, and not during a fixed term unless the agreement provides for it. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)
- A later version (rt-regs-2021-v005, dated 25 November 2025) changes the minimum notice to 90 days. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf) That version postdates 1 October 2025, so it doesn't apply to your question.

**What you can do or ask**

1. **Ask whether a Form 5 notice has been given.** If not, the documents indicate the increase is not valid yet. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)[[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
2. **Check the start date.** A valid notice must state the start date. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) Under the 60-day rule, the increase can't start earlier than 60 days after a valid notice is given. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)[[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) Your question about "from when" can't be answered from the documents without a notice that states a date.
3. **Check the notice's content.** It must include the method used to calculate the increase, and the increase cannot exceed the amount that method produces. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)
4. **Challenge it if one arrives.** You can apply to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria within 30 days after the notice is given, for free, to investigate whether the increase is excessive. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)[[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) You can also apply to VCAT within 30 days after the Director's report, or within 30 days of the notice if there's no report. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) If VCAT is not asked to decide otherwise, you'd pay the increased amount from the date on the notice while the application is pending. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

**Gaps:** The documents don't say what the agent's email contained, whether it was a valid notice, or what the rent increase amount or start date would be. For the Act's 2025 wording, you'd need to check the current Act or get advice from Consumer Affairs Victoria (1300 558 181). [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are present: the answer requires Form 5 and at least 60 days' notice, and it lists next steps, including applying to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria once a notice arrives. The hardest point, that the email is not a valid notice, is covered by 'Probably not, unless the agent gives you a valid written notice... an informal email or refusal to negotiate isn't one' and 'a rent increase made in contravention of this section is invalid.'

None of the fail conditions is asserted: the answer says "Probably not, unless the agent gives you a valid written notice," requires "at least 60 days' notice" for 1 October 2025, mentions 90 days only for a later version that "doesn't apply to your question," and says only that "an informal email... isn't one" rather than that a notice can never be emailed.

question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:
**Short answer:** No, the law doesn't support having the damage fixed quietly without telling the owner. You must notify the rental provider in writing. The documents don't say anything about insurance.

**Which version applies:** On 15 October 2026, the latest Act document I found is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (file tagged v111, dated 25 November 2025) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The latest Regulations are the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (file tagged v009, dated 30 June 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The documents don't print an "Authorised Version No." on their face, so I've taken the version numbers from the file names.

**What the law says**

- Renters must avoid damaging the premises. Where damage occurs, the renter must notify the rental provider in writing [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- A renter must give written notice to the rental provider as soon as practicable after becoming aware of damage to the rented premises [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- If damage is caused by the renter's failure to take care, the rental provider may give a written repair notice. It must state the nature of the damage, that the renter caused it, and either that the renter must repair it within 14 days, or that the provider is doing the repairs and the renter is liable for the cost [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- If the renter doesn't repair it in a proper, tradesman-like manner within 14 days, the rental provider may repair it at the renter's expense. The renter must reimburse reasonable costs within 14 days after the repairs are completed [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs, whether urgent or non-urgent [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**What the renter can do or ask**

1. **Notify the owner in writing now**, describing the skirting board damage, before it is repaired or you move out [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
2. **Offer to repair it yourself, or to pay for a qualified tradesperson**, with the owner's agreement. Ask them to confirm this in writing. If they give a repair notice, you have 14 days to fix it properly or they can do it and charge you [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
3. **Don't rely on "urgent repairs" to cover this.** A renter can arrange urgent repairs and claim reimbursement, but the renter must first take reasonable steps to get the provider to do them immediately, and the renter must give 7 days' written notice of the repairs and cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Skirting boards are unlikely to qualify, though the full list of urgent repairs is on the Consumer Affairs Victoria website, not in these documents [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
4. **Ask for a condition report or inspection.** At the end of a tenancy, the provider must inspect and allow for fair wear and tear, which doesn't count as damage caused by the renter [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

**Insurance:** The documents don't address whether the damage affects the owner's property insurance, so I can't answer that. Check the owner's policy or ask them.

must-mention.reason: No. The second point is only partly covered. The answer shows renter liability through the repair-notice provisions, saying the renter 'is liable for the cost' and that 'fair wear and tear... doesn't count as damage caused by the renter'. But it never states that the renter must leave the home in the same condition as at the start of the tenancy, and it does not tie responsibility to damage caused by a pet. The other three points are covered: written notice 'as soon as practicable', insurance not addressed by the documents, and the next steps.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. None of the three failing claims is made: the answer rejects a quiet repair ("No, the law doesn't support having the damage fixed quietly without telling the owner"), declines to state any insurance outcome ("The documents don't address whether the damage affects the owner's property insurance, so I can't answer that"), and never says the renter must pay the owner's insurance excess.

version-cited.reason: No. The answer identifies the Act as 'file tagged v111, dated 25 November 2025', but Authorised Version No. 115 (dated 13 October 2026) was in force on 15 October 2026. It also applies rules from other superseded versions: the notification and urgent-repair steps come from Act v110 (97-109aa110), and the fair wear and tear step comes from Regulations v005 (21-3sra005).

question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents I found don't set a minimum number of circuits for a rental. They do set a safety standard for how power outlets and lighting circuits must be protected, and that standard starts on 29 March 2023, four weeks after your question date.

## What the law says

- **Electrical safety standard (not yet in force on 1 March 2023):** Schedule 4, clause 9 of the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (S.R. No. 3/2021) provides that "On and from 29 March 2023... all power outlets and lighting circuits in the rented premises are to be connected to" a switchboard-type circuit breaker complying with AS/NZS 3000, and a switchboard-type residual current device complying with one of several listed AS/NZS standards [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The clause does not mention how many circuits a rental must have.
- **Electrical safety checks (in force now):** The rental provider must ensure an electrical safety check of all electrical installations, appliances and fittings they provide is done every 2 years by a licensed or registered electrician. If no check has been done in the last 2 years when the renter moves in, the provider must arrange one "as soon as practicable" [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Repairs:** The renter must notify the provider in writing, as soon as practicable, of a breakdown of facilities or equipment the provider supplied. The provider must carry out non-urgent repairs within a reasonable time [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

The most recent retrieved version of the Regulations is dated 2025 and was not in force on 1 March 2023, so I haven't relied on it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

## What you can ask for

1. **A written date of the most recent electrical safety check.** The provider must give this in writing when you request it [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
2. **An electrical safety check now,** if none has been done in the last 2 years. The provider must arrange it "as soon as practicable" [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
3. **A written repair request** for the tripping circuit. Notify the provider in writing as soon as practicable, because the Regulations require written notice of breakdowns [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The provider must then carry out the repair within a reasonable time. You can apply to VCAT if repairs are not done within 14 days of the provider receiving notice [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
4. **Request that the circuit be brought up to the standard in clause 9 from 29 March 2023.** The documents support this only in general terms: the standard applies from that date, and the documents don't say how a circuit overload issue should be fixed [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

## What the documents don't cover

- The minimum number of circuits or power points in a rental.
- Whether a shared circuit that trips under normal use breaches any standard.
- The exact text of the electrical safety check rules as they read on 1 March 2023. The retrieved copy of the electrical safety check text comes from a later version, so I haven't quoted it as the 2023 position.

Because the breaker trips with normal use of appliances, a licensed electrician should assess the circuit. Ask the provider to arrange this in writing.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved documents don't say whether a rooming house can charge for coin-operated washing machines. They don't mention coin-operated machines at all. Here is what they do cover.

**What the law says**

- **Electricity, gas and water:** An operator may charge for these only if the operator pays the bill and the room is separately metered. The charge can't be more than the supplier's charge, and this doesn't apply to shared rooms [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A washing machine charge isn't clearly within this rule, so it doesn't settle your question.
- **Charges for services:** If an operator charges for services, it must give you a separate schedule of those charges before you move in. If you use a service, it must give you an itemised account of your individual use [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Service charges by Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency:** These bodies may impose a service charge for laundry services in a declared rooming house, but only if it isn't possible or practicable to accurately measure your use. The charge must not exceed the cost of providing the service. They must give you written notice of the charge, and you can apply to the Tribunal to withdraw or vary it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This does not apply to private operators.
- **Minimum equipment:** From 26 February 2024, a rooming house must provide a washing machine in good working order for every 12 or fewer residents [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether residents must use these machines for free.

The version I used is the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 file labelled v115, dated 2026-10-13, which is the latest version before 15 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't include an explicit "Authorised Version" number beyond this v115 label.

**What you can ask or do**

1. **Ask the operator for the schedule of services** and the amount for the washing machines. You're entitled to this before you took up residency [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If there isn't one, ask for it in writing.
2. **Ask for an itemised account** of your individual use if you're charged [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Check who runs the house.** If it's Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency, they may only charge a service charge where your use can't be accurately measured, and the charge can't exceed their cost. You can apply to the Tribunal to challenge it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Get advice on the specific charge.** The documents don't say whether a coin-operated charge is lawful for your house, so a tenancy service or the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal can confirm this for your situation.

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved documents set a mould standard for rentals, but they don't say whether a listing may show mould photos, and they don't say whether a photo is enough to prove a breach.

**What the law says**

- The rental minimum standards require that "each room in the rented premises must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). The 1 July 2025 version of the Regulations is the latest retrieved document dated before 1 October 2025, so I've relied on it. Its filename is "rt-regs-2021-v004-2025-07-01.pdf," but the retrieved text doesn't show an Authorised Version number, so I can't confirm one.
- The standard is limited to mould or damp "caused by or related to the building structure" [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say how that cause is established.
- Providers must disclose certain information to rental applicants. The disclosure list includes whether "the rented premises comply with the rental minimum standards," and whether the provider has received a repair notice in the last 3 years "relating to mould or damp in the premises caused by or related to the building structure" [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). That text comes from the 2022 version. I couldn't confirm from the 1 July 2025 version that it's unchanged, and the later versions are dated after 1 October 2025, so I haven't relied on them.

**Can they advertise it like that?**

The documents don't address advertising or listing photos. They don't say whether showing mould in a listing is allowed, or whether it counts as misleading.

**Is the photo enough to prove a breach?**

The documents don't say what evidence is needed or how a breach is proved. A photo can show mould, but the standard only covers mould caused by or related to the building structure [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf), and the documents don't say how that link is shown. I can't say whether a photo alone would be enough.

**What the renter can ask or do**

- **Ask for disclosure:** The provider must disclose whether the premises comply with the minimum standards and whether they've received a relevant mould or damp repair notice in the last 3 years [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The documents don't say how or when a renter can enforce this.
- **Complaints or VCAT:** The retrieved documents don't cover complaint steps, dispute resolution, or the Act's enforcement provisions (for example, section 30D of the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, which the regulations refer to, but whose text isn't in the results).

I'd check the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 and the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) guidance for the advertising question and the evidence question.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I let a friend move into my rental without telling the agent. Now I want them out. What do I have to do?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved documents don't give a renter a process to remove a friend they let move in. The rental provider (the landlord) is the one who gets a possession order, and only Victoria Police can physically remove anyone. I've assumed you are the renter, since you refer to "the agent" and "my rental."

**What the law says**

- **Sub-letting and assignment:** The renter must not assign or sub-let "the whole or any part of the premises without the written consent of the rental provider." The rental provider "may give the renter notice to vacate if the renter assigns or sub-lets the premises without consent" [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Letting a friend move in without the landlord's written consent may fall under this clause. The documents don't say whether it does on your facts.
- **Notice to vacate:** A rental provider must give a notice to vacate before applying to VCAT for a possession order [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). The notice must state the termination date, and the minimum notice period under the Act must be allowed for [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). The retrieved documents don't state that minimum period, so I can't give you the number of days.
- **VCAT and possession:** If you don't leave by the date in the notice, the rental provider may apply to VCAT for a possession order. VCAT decides whether the rental provider was entitled to give the notice and whether a possession order is "reasonable and proportionate" [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- **Forced removal:** The landlord cannot personally use force. Only Victoria Police can carry out a forcible eviction, and only when acting on a VCAT order (a warrant for possession) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). A warrant must be executed within the time stated in the order, which must not exceed 30 days after the warrant is issued [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **The friend's own position:** Under the Act, a possession order can also be sought against a person "who entered into or remained in occupation without the applicant's licence or consent" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). This route is for a rental provider, and it applies where the occupier is not a renter under a residential rental agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do or ask**

- The documents don't set out steps for a renter to remove an occupant. What they do say is that you should get advice if you think you have grounds to challenge a notice to vacate, by contacting one of the community legal organisations listed on the Consumer Affairs Victoria website [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- Before you act, consider whether you need the landlord's consent after the fact. The documents don't address whether retrospective consent is possible.
- You can contact Consumer Affairs Victoria on 1300 558 181 or visit consumer.vic.gov.au/renting [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

**Which versions I relied on (as of 15 October 2026)**

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997:** The retrieved version is file "rta-1997-v111-2025-11-25.pdf," which I read as Authorised Version v111, dated 25 November 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The documents don't show whether later amendments were made before 15 October 2026, so please check the current reprint.
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021:** The latest retrieved version is "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf," which I read as Authorised Version v009, dated 30 June 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The sub-letting clause (item 27) appears in the 2025 version [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf) but not in the parts of the 2026 version I retrieved, so I can't confirm the 2026 wording of that clause.

**What I couldn't find:** the minimum notice period under the Act, the exact wording of the current sub-letting clause, and any renter-initiated process for removing an occupant. For a decision that could affect your tenancy, get advice from a community legal centre or Consumer Affairs Victoria.

must-mention.reason: No. The sub-letting point is covered by the quote that the renter must not sub-let "without the written consent of the rental provider." However, the answer never says the outcome depends on the arrangement with the friend. It names none of the deciding facts (a space that is only theirs, what was agreed, or what they pay) and says only that "the documents don't say whether it does on your facts."
