It applies rules from v111, including the 30-day warrant execution limit and possession orders against unauthorised occupants. It also applies the sub-letting clause from Regulations version 005 (21-3sra005) rather than the in-force version 009.

question: It is 1 November 2019. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?
answer:
## What the law said on 1 November 2019

The applicable document retrieved is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 88, dated 2 July 2019** (“rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf”). [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

A tenant could arrange **urgent repairs** if they had taken reasonable steps to get the landlord or agent to do them immediately but could not get them to do so; the landlord’s reimbursement limit was **$1,000**, unless a higher amount was prescribed. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) For **non-urgent repairs**, the tenant had to give written notice, and could apply to the Director if the repairs were not done within **14 days**; after receiving the Director’s report, the tenant could apply to the Tribunal. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) The retrieved document does **not** say whether leaking fixtures specifically counted as urgent repairs. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

The Act did **not** contain a general rule in the retrieved provisions making every notice to vacate invalid merely because it followed a repair request. The specific retaliation rule in section 91ZZI(3) applied to a notice under **section 91ZK**—a mortgagee’s notice—if it was given in response to exercising, or proposing to exercise, a right under the Act. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) The separate rule in section 91ZZI(4) concerned notices ending a **fixed-term** agreement, so it does not appear to address your month-to-month agreement. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

## What to check and ask for

1. **Check the reason and section stated on the notice.** A notice was invalid unless it used the prescribed form, was addressed to you, was signed, stated the reason, and specified the termination date. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

2. **Check the notice period.** If the reason was repairs, section 91ZX required the landlord to have the necessary permits and consents and to show that the work could not properly be done unless you vacated; the termination date had to be at least **60 days** after the notice. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

3. **Check supporting evidence.** A repairs notice under section 91ZX had to include documentary evidence approved by the Director supporting the stated reason. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

4. **Preserve proof of the timing and real reason.** Keep your repair requests, photographs, replies, the notice, and any messages showing that the notice was issued the same day. The retrieved document does not state what evidence proves retaliation, but these records directly document the sequence of events.

5. **Ask the landlord or agent to withdraw the notice in writing** if the stated reason is false, unsupported, or the notice is defective. Under the Act, withdrawal required a written notice signed by both the person who gave the notice and the person to whom it was given. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

6. **Consider a Tribunal challenge promptly.** For a notice under section 91ZX, you could apply to the Tribunal challenging its validity within **30 days after the notice was given**, and the Tribunal could determine whether it was valid. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

The retrieved documents do not establish a broader month-to-month “retaliatory eviction” remedy beyond checking the notice’s statutory basis, validity, evidence and notice period.

must-mention.reason: No. All three required points are missing. The answer never says a no-reason notice is allowed with at least 120 days' notice. Instead of stating that a no-reason notice has no effect if given in response to the tenant exercising a right such as requesting repairs, it says the Act 'did not contain a general rule... making every notice to vacate invalid merely because it followed a repair request', which contradicts that point. It also gives a 30-day window for challenging a section 91ZX notice rather than the 60-day VCAT challenge for a no-reason notice.

must-not-say.reason: No. The answer states both prohibited claims. It says the landlord needed to give a reason: "A notice was invalid unless it... stated the reason." It also gives a deadline other than 60 days for a VCAT challenge: "you could apply to the Tribunal challenging its validity within **30 days after the notice was given**."

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 88, dated 2 July 2019' (also given as rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf and the 97-109aa088 link), and every rule it applies is cited to that in-force version, with no reliance on any other version.

question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?
answer:
## What the law says

On **1 October 2025**, the applicable document is the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 110, dated 6 August 2025**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

- A property must be advertised or offered at a **fixed amount of rent**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- The rental provider or agent must not **solicit or otherwise invite** an offer higher than the advertised rent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- They must not make a **false or misleading representation about the rent** when advertising the property. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- Misleading or deceptive conduct, or a false or misleading representation about rent, is prohibited where it **induces a person to enter into a residential rental agreement**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

Therefore, if the agent or rental provider invited higher offers, or advertised the original rent while actually seeking a higher rent, those provisions may be relevant. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) However, the documents do not establish that an offence occurred merely because another applicant independently offered more, or because the property was later listed at a higher rent. The key issue is what the agent or provider said or invited applicants to do. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

The email falsely saying that you withdrew may also be relevant evidence of what happened, but the retrieved provisions do not specifically address falsely recording or communicating a withdrawal before a rental agreement is entered into. The documents also do not provide a general right to require the property to be offered to you at the advertised rent.

## What you can do or ask

You can ask the agent, in writing:

1. why your application was recorded as withdrawn;
2. who made that decision and when;
3. whether the advertised rent was changed, and the date and reason for the change; and
4. whether applicants were invited or encouraged to offer more than the advertised rent.

You can raise the matter with the relevant regulator or apply to **VCAT** if you have evidence of conduct covered by these provisions. The Act states that section 472(1A) provides for Tribunal orders on an application or in proceedings concerning a contravention of the misleading-conduct provision. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) The retrieved documents do not state the precise application procedure, available order, or whether compensation would be available on these particular facts.

The documents do **not** specify what evidence a renter must save. As a practical precaution, retain the original advertisement showing the rent, your complete application and confirmation, the email saying you withdrew, all messages with the agent, screenshots showing any later higher listing, and records of dates and times. Keep originals and export emails or messages where possible. These evidence-preservation steps are practical suggestions, not requirements stated in the retrieved documents.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered. (1) Relisting is addressed: 'the documents do not establish that an offence occurred merely because... the property was later listed at a higher rent.' (2) Inviting higher offers is banned: the agent 'must not solicit or otherwise invite an offer higher than the advertised rent.' (3) The hardest point, unsolicited offers, is covered by 'the documents do not establish that an offence occurred merely because another applicant independently offered more... The key issue is what the agent or provider said or invited applicants to do.' (4) The false email is addressed: 'the retrieved provisions do not specifically address falsely recording or communicating a withdrawal.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer rejects all three claims instead of asserting them, stating that the documents 'do not establish that an offence occurred merely because another applicant independently offered more, or because the property was later listed at a higher rent' and that they 'do not provide a general right to require the property to be offered to you at the advertised rent.'

version-cited.reason: Yes: the output names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as 'Authorised Version No. 110, dated 6 August 2025' with a 97-109aa110 link. That is the version in force on 1 October 2025, and every rule applied (fixed rent, no soliciting higher offers, no misleading representations, s 472(1A) orders) is sourced from that version.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
## What the law says

On **15 October 2026**, the applicable document is **_Residential Tenancies Act 1997_, Authorised Version v115 (13 October 2026)**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

You used the approved request form, as required. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) A residential rental provider must not unreasonably refuse consent to keep a pet. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

Most importantly, the provider is **taken to have consented** unless, within **14 days** after receiving the request, the provider applied to the Tribunal for an order that refusal would be reasonable. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) You sent the request **three weeks ago**, so the 14-day period has passed.

Therefore, the agent’s refusal by itself is not enough if the provider did not apply to the Tribunal within those 14 days. The Act does not specifically say that an owner’s allergy is, by itself, a valid reason for refusal. The Tribunal may consider the type of pet, the character and nature of the premises and fixtures, whether another Act permits refusal, prescribed matters and any other relevant matter. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The documents do not say how much weight must be given to an owner’s allergy or how the owner’s infrequent visits affect the decision.

## What you can do or ask

Ask the agent in writing whether the residential rental provider applied to the Tribunal **within 14 days of receiving your request**, and ask for the application details if they say yes. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

If no timely application was made, you can state that consent is deemed under section 71C(2). The Act says a renter may keep the pet where the provider has consented in writing or the Tribunal has made an order permitting it; the Act’s note and section 71C(2) provide for deemed consent after 14 days without a timely Tribunal application. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

If an application was made on time, the Tribunal—not the agent alone—determines whether refusal is reasonable. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The retrieved documents do not specify a separate procedure for a renter to challenge the refusal, so I cannot state that procedure from these documents.

must-mention.reason: Yes. The output states every required point. Point 1: the provider is 'taken to have consented' unless they apply to the Tribunal within 14 days. Point 2: 'You sent the request three weeks ago, so the 14-day period has passed', so the refusal alone is not enough without a timely Tribunal application. Point 3: it gives a next step, 'Ask the agent in writing whether the residential rental provider applied to the Tribunal within 14 days of receiving your request.' Saying 'Tribunal' instead of 'VCAT' does not change the meaning.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer says none of the three: it rejects the refusal as final ("the agent's refusal by itself is not enough if the provider did not apply to the Tribunal within those 14 days"), puts the Tribunal application on the provider rather than the renter ("the provider applied to the Tribunal"), and says the allergy is not decisive ("The Act does not specifically say that an owner's allergy is, by itself, a valid reason for refusal").

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the required document with its in-force version, 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version v115 (13 October 2026)', and every citation links to 97-109aa115, with no rules drawn from any other version.

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
### What the law says

As at **1 October 2025**, the relevant document is the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 110, dated 6 August 2025** (“rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf”). [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

A notice to vacate because the premises are being sold is permitted if the premises are to be **sold or offered for sale with vacant possession immediately after the termination date**. The notice must generally give at least **60 days’ notice** and include supporting documentary evidence. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

The buyer pulling out does **not automatically withdraw** the notice. Under section 91ZZQ, a notice is withdrawn only if a **written notice of withdrawal** is given, signed by both the person who gave the notice and the person to whom it was given. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

Therefore, if the notice is otherwise valid and its termination date has arrived, you should not assume that you can remain simply because the sale failed. However, the Act’s provisions retrieved here do not say that the notice remains valid if the landlord is no longer selling or offering the property for sale with vacant possession.

### What you can do or ask

Ask the landlord, in writing, to confirm whether the property is still being offered for sale with vacant possession and to provide a signed written withdrawal if they are no longer proceeding.

You may challenge the notice at VCAT: for a sale-based notice, you can apply to challenge its validity within **30 days after it was given**, and you may also challenge it when the landlord applies for a possession order. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) The prescribed notice form also says that you can challenge the notice if you disagree with the reason or believe the information is incorrect or incomplete. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

The retrieved documents do not determine whether **your particular notice** is valid, because that depends on its wording, termination date, timing, attached evidence and the landlord’s current intention.

must-mention.reason: Yes - all four points are covered. The hardest, dependence on the notice's ground and evidence, is met by 'sold or offered for sale with vacant possession' and 'that depends on its wording, termination date, timing, attached evidence and the landlord's current intention'; the answer also states the 60-day minimum, withdrawal by written notice signed by both parties, and next steps of asking for a signed withdrawal or challenging at VCAT within 30 days.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer says the buyer pulling out "does **not automatically withdraw** the notice", that withdrawal requires a notice "signed by both the person who gave the notice and the person to whom it was given", and that the notice must give "at least **60 days' notice**", so it asserts none of the failing claims.

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
## What the law says

On **1 October 2025**, the applicable document is **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, `rt-regs-2021-v004-2025-07-01.pdf` (Authorised Version v004)**. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

The rental provider must use the prescribed **Form 5—Notice of Proposed Rent Increase**; a valid notice is required for every rent increase. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) The notice must state the current rent, new rent, start date, and calculation method. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) It may be sent by email **only if you previously consented to receiving notices by email**. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

Therefore, based on the documents and your statement that you received only an ordinary agent email and never an official notice, **you do not have to pay the higher rent on the information provided**. The documents do not support a rent increase taking effect without a valid notice. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

A valid notice must give at least **60 days’ notice**, so the higher rent cannot start earlier than 60 days after a valid notice is given. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) Because no valid notice has been given, the documents do not establish any start date for the increase. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

You can tell the agent that you will continue paying the current rent until they give a valid Form 5 notice complying with the requirements, including the calculation method and at least 60 days’ notice. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

You can also ask them to provide the prescribed notice and confirm the proposed start date and calculation method. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes. The answer covers all four points: Form 5, at least 60 days' notice, and the next step of continuing to pay the current rent. The hardest point, that the email is not a valid notice and the higher rent isn't payable yet, is covered by 'you do not have to pay the higher rent on the information provided. The documents do not support a rent increase taking effect without a valid notice.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer says the renter does not have to pay now ("you do not have to pay the higher rent on the information provided"), does not date the increase from the email ("the documents do not establish any start date for the increase"), gives only a 60-day minimum ("at least 60 days' notice"), and allows email notices ("may be sent by email only if you previously consented").

version-cited.reason: No: the answer names only the Regulations as 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, rt-regs-2021-v004-2025-07-01.pdf (Authorised Version v004)' and never names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 or its Authorised Version No. 110, which is a required document in the first list.

question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:
## What the law says

Skirting-board damage caused by your dog is likely damage to the rented premises, not fair wear and tear. A renter must not intentionally or negligently cause damage, and must notify the rental provider **in writing as soon as practicable**, stating that the damage occurred and describing its nature. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

The current retrieved Act is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 110, dated 6 August 2025**. The current retrieved regulations are **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 009, dated 30 June 2026**. These are the documents in force for 15 October 2026.

The regulations state that **only a suitably qualified person may do repairs**, whether urgent or non-urgent. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) However, the documents do not say that a renter may arrange a non-urgent repair without notifying the rental provider or obtaining the provider’s agreement. The urgent-repair procedure—which permits a renter to arrange repairs after taking reasonable steps to have the rental provider do them—does not establish a general right to arrange non-urgent repairs, and the documents do not classify damaged skirting boards as an urgent repair. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

- Notify the owner or agent **in writing now**, with a description and photographs of the chewed skirting boards. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- Ask them to arrange the repair, or ask for written agreement to your proposed suitably qualified repairer and the proposed method of repair.
- Do not conceal the damage or have an unqualified person repair it. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- Before leaving, the premises must be left in the same condition as at the start of the tenancy, allowing for fair wear and tear. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

The retrieved documents **do not address whether an undisclosed repair would affect the owner’s property insurance**, so I cannot say what the insurance consequences would be.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered. The hardest is renter responsibility, covered by "Skirting-board damage caused by your dog is likely damage to the rented premises, not fair wear and tear" and "the premises must be left in the same condition as at the start of the tenancy, allowing for fair wear and tear." The answer also requires written notice "as soon as practicable," says the documents "do not address whether an undisclosed repair would affect the owner's property insurance," and gives a next step to "Notify the owner or agent in writing now."

must-not-say.reason: Yes. None of the prohibited claims are made: the answer rejects a quiet repair ("Notify the owner or agent in writing now" and "Do not conceal the damage"), declines to state an insurance outcome ("I cannot say what the insurance consequences would be"), and never says the renter must pay the owner's insurance excess.

version-cited.reason: No: the answer relies on the 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 110, dated 6 August 2025' (link 97-109aa110) for its notification and end-of-tenancy condition rules, but Version No. 115 (dated 13 October 2026) was in force on 15 October 2026, even though it correctly cites Regulations 'Authorised Version No. 009'.

question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
## What the law said on 1 March 2023

The applicable document is **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 002, dated 1 June 2022**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

The retrieved law **does not specify a minimum number of electrical circuits** for a rental. Therefore, having most power points on one circuit is not, by itself, shown in these documents to breach a prescribed circuit-number rule. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

The electrical minimum standard was due to apply **from 29 March 2023**, not on 1 March 2023. From that date, all power outlets and lighting circuits had to be connected to a compliant switchboard-type **Circuit Breaker** and **Residual Current Device (RCD)**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

## What you can ask for

You can make a written request for a copy of the **most recent electrical safety check**. The rental provider must provide it within **7 days** of receiving your written request. The check record must include the electrician’s name and licence or registration number, the inspection date, results, repairs required and action taken, together with a report prepared under **section 2 of AS/NZS 3019**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

The rental provider must ensure an electrical safety check of the electrical installations, appliances and fittings they provide is conducted **every 2 years** by a licensed or registered electrician; if no check was conducted within the previous 2 years when you moved in, they must arrange one as soon as practicable. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

Given the breaker repeatedly trips when the kettle and heater run together, you can ask the rental provider **in writing** to have a licensed or registered electrician investigate the circuit, the breaker/RCD and the provided electrical installation, and to address any repairs identified. The retrieved documents do not say that the provider must install an additional circuit specifically because two appliances trip the breaker. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both points are covered: the answer says 'The retrieved law does not specify a minimum number of electrical circuits,' and its next steps include a written request for a copy of the most recent electrical safety check and asking the provider 'in writing to have a licensed or registered electrician investigate... and to address any repairs identified.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer states the law "does not specify a minimum number of electrical circuits" and that the electrical standard "was due to apply from 29 March 2023, not on 1 March 2023," so it neither asserts a circuit minimum nor says the circuit breaker/RCD standard already applies.

version-cited.reason: No. The answer names only the 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 002, dated 1 June 2022'; it never mentions the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Authorised Version No. 101), which is a required document.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
## What the law says

On **15 October 2026**, the retrieved Act document is **_Residential Tenancies Act 1997_, Authorised Version 111 (25 November 2025)**. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) The retrieved standards document is **_Residential Tenancies (Rooming House Standards) Regulations 2023_, Authorised Version 2 (1 December 2024)**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf)

A rooming house must provide **one washing machine in good working order for every 12 or fewer residents**, based on the maximum number the house can accommodate. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf) The standards do **not** say that residents must be allowed to use the machine for free, and the retrieved documents do not expressly prohibit coin-operated machines. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf)

However, if the rooming house operator charges an amount for a service, they must give you a **separate schedule of the amount before you take up residency**, and—if you use the service—an **itemised account showing your individual use**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

A special rule applies where the provider is **Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency**: it may impose a laundry service charge only where use cannot be accurately or practicably measured, and the charge **must not exceed the cost of providing the service or facility**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

Ask the operator:

- whether the coin charge was disclosed in the required **separate schedule of services** before you moved in; [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- for an **itemised account** showing your individual laundry use; [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- if the provider is Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency, for evidence that the charge does not exceed the cost of providing the laundry facility. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

So, based only on these documents: **coin-operated washing machines are not expressly banned, but the operator must comply with the applicable service-charge disclosure and itemisation rules.** The documents do not clearly establish whether a private rooming house operator may impose a coin charge in every circumstance.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered: one washing machine in good working order per 12 or fewer residents; 'The standards do not say that residents must be allowed to use the machine for free'; a 'separate schedule of the amount before you take up residency'; and the next step 'Ask the operator... whether the coin charge was disclosed in the required separate schedule of services before you moved in.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer avoids all three failure conditions: it says the standards 'do not say that residents must be allowed to use the machine for free', it states the operator 'must comply with the applicable service-charge disclosure and itemisation rules', and it limits the cost cap to where 'the provider is Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency'.

version-cited.reason: No. The answer names the Act as 'Authorised Version 111 (25 November 2025)' instead of the in-force Version No. 115 (13 October 2026). It also sources its service-charge schedule, itemised-account and Homes Victoria cost-limit rules (ss 109/120A) from version 110 (link 97-109aa110). Neither version was in force on 15 October 2026, and removing those rules would change the answer's substance. Only the Rooming House Standards Regulations version 002 is correct.

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
## What the law says

As at **1 October 2025**, the relevant document is **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 004, 1 July 2025**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

- The regulations say that **each room must be free from mould and damp caused by, or related to, the building structure**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)
- The retrieved documents **do not say whether a rental provider is prohibited from using a photograph showing apparent mould in a rental advertisement**. Therefore, I cannot say from these documents alone that the advertisement is unlawful.
- A photograph may be relevant evidence, but the documents **do not say that a photograph alone proves** the premises fail the minimum standard. In particular, the standard concerns mould or damp that is caused by, or related to, the building structure; the photo by itself may not establish that cause. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

## What the renter can ask or do

Before applying, the renter can ask the rental provider or agent:

1. **Whether the premises comply with the rental minimum standards**—this is information the provider must disclose to a rental applicant. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
2. **Whether the provider received a repair notice in the previous three years about mould or damp caused by, or related to, the building structure**—that information must also be disclosed to an applicant. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
3. For clarification or evidence, the renter can ask for details of the apparent mould, its cause, and any repair history. The retrieved documents do not prescribe any further advertising complaint process or specify what evidence is sufficient to prove non-compliance.

must-mention.reason: All three points are covered. The output states the mould and damp standard ('each room must be free from mould and damp caused by, or related to, the building structure'). It says the photo alone isn't proof: the documents 'do not say that a photograph alone proves the premises fail the minimum standard... the photo by itself may not establish that cause.' It also gives next steps, such as asking the agent whether the premises comply with the minimum standards and whether there was a prior repair notice.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer makes neither forbidden claim: it says the documents "do not say whether a rental provider is prohibited from using a photograph showing apparent mould in a rental advertisement" and "do not say that a photograph alone proves the premises fail the minimum standard."

version-cited.reason: No. The answer names "Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 004, 1 July 2025" but never names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 110. It also relies on 21-3sra002 (Regulations version 002, which was not in force on 1 October 2025) for the disclosure steps it gives the renter.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I let a friend move into my rental without telling the agent. Now I want them out. What do I have to do?
answer:
## What the law says

Under **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115**, incorporating amendments as at **13 October 2026**, you must not assign or sub-let all or part of the rented premises without the **residential rental provider’s written consent**. An unauthorised assignment or sub-letting is invalid unless VCAT has decided that consent is not required. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

If the arrangement with your friend amounts to an assignment or sub-letting, the rental provider may give **you** a notice to vacate under section 91ZV. The notice must give at least **14 days** before the termination date. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The retrieved documents do **not** say that simply allowing a friend to move in is necessarily an assignment or sub-letting. They also do not prescribe a process for a renter to remove that friend.

## What you can do or ask

- Ask your friend to leave voluntarily; the retrieved documents do not specify a notice period or formal procedure for doing this.
- If you want your friend to remain, seek the rental provider’s **written consent**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- If the provider withholds consent and you believe that is unreasonable, you may apply to VCAT for a determination that consent is not required. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- If the provider gives you a notice to vacate, the retrieved documents state that you may challenge it at VCAT, and the provider must obtain a possession order before a forcible eviction. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026, ss 81–82.  
[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026, s 91ZV.  
[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Authorised Version v009, 30 June 2026, Schedule 1 Form 6.

must-mention.reason: No. The answer covers written consent ('you must not assign or sub-let... without the residential rental provider's written consent') and says the outcome depends on whether the arrangement 'amounts to an assignment or sub-letting', but it never names a deciding fact such as exclusive space, what was agreed, or what the friend pays.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: none of the fail conditions are asserted. The only fixed period, "at least 14 days", applies to the rental provider's notice to vacate to the renter, not to ending the friend's occupancy, and the answer states that "the retrieved documents do not specify a notice period or formal procedure" for asking the friend to leave. It also does not suggest a lockout, say the friend has no rights, or say the friend can apply to VCAT to be added to the lease.

version-cited.reason: No. The answer names the Act correctly as "Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026", but citation [3] links to "21-3sra004", which is Regulations version 004, not the in-force version 009. The answer relies on that link for steps the user can take: challenging a notice to vacate at VCAT, and the requirement that the provider obtain a possession order before a forcible eviction. Deleting that material would change the answer's substance.

question: It is 1 November 2019. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?
answer:
## What the law said

The retrieved document is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, `rta-1997-v089-2019-12-04.pdf`, Authorised Version v089**. It is dated **4 December 2019**, so the documents provided do **not establish which version was in force on 1 November 2019**. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf)

On the law shown in that document:

- A notice to vacate had to be in the prescribed form, addressed to you, signed, state the reason, and state the termination date. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf)
- If the reason was repairs, the provider had to show that they intended to repair, renovate or reconstruct; had obtained necessary permits and consents; and could not properly do the work unless you vacated. The notice had to give at least **60 days’ notice** and be accompanied by supporting documentary evidence. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf)
- The Act expressly made a notice under **section 91ZK** ineffective if it was given in response to exercising, or proposing to exercise, a right under the Act. Section 91ZK concerns notices based on serious threats or intimidation. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf)
- The retrieved document does **not** state a general rule making every periodic/month-to-month notice invalid merely because the renter requested repairs. It therefore does not establish that your notice is retaliatory or invalid on that basis alone. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf)

## What you should check or ask

1. **Read the stated reason** on the notice. Check whether it claims repairs under section 91ZX, or instead alleges threats, intimidation, rent arrears, a breach, or another ground. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf)
2. **Check the termination date.** If it relies on repairs, it must be at least **60 days after the notice**. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf)
3. **Ask for the supporting evidence**, including the permits and consents and evidence showing why you must vacate for the work. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf)
4. **Preserve evidence of retaliation:** your repair requests, dates, responses, photographs of the leaking fixtures, and the timing of the notice. The documents do not specify what evidence is sufficient, so they do not permit a firmer conclusion.
5. If the notice is a repairs notice under section 91ZX, you may apply to the Tribunal challenging its validity **within 30 days after it was given**, and the Tribunal may determine whether it is valid. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf)
6. Do not treat the notice as withdrawn unless there is a written withdrawal signed by both the person who gave it and the person to whom it was given. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: No. The answer never says a no-reason notice is allowed with at least 120 days' notice, which is the first missing point. It also misses the second point, that a no-reason notice has no effect if given in response to the tenant exercising a right such as requesting repairs: it applies that rule only to section 91ZK and says the document 'does not state a general rule' of that kind. It also misses the third point, the 60-day VCAT challenge window, citing instead a 30-day window for repairs notices.

must-not-say.reason: No. The answer asserts that the notice had to 'state the reason' and gives a challenge deadline other than 60 days: 'you may apply to the Tribunal challenging its validity within 30 days after it was given'.

version-cited.reason: No. The answer never names Authorised Version No. 088, the version in force on 1 November 2019. It relies only on 'Authorised Version v089' (rta-1997-v089-2019-12-04.pdf, dated 4 December 2019, link 97-109aa089), a later version, and applies its rules as the law and as steps the user can take: the 60-day repair notice, the s 91ZK retaliation rule, and the 30-day Tribunal challenge. Its caveat about the version does not change this.

question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?
answer:
## What the law says

On **1 October 2025**, the applicable document was the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 — Authorised Version No. 110, dated 6 August 2025**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

- A rental provider or agent must advertise or offer the premises at a **fixed rent**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- They must not **solicit or otherwise invite** an offer higher than the advertised rent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- Advertising the property at a higher rent may also be unlawful if the original advertised rent was a **false or misleading representation**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- However, the version in force on 1 October 2025 did **not** contain the later provision expressly prohibiting acceptance of an unsolicited higher offer; that provision appears in the later version dated 25 November 2025 and cannot be used for the date in your question. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
## What the law says

The applicable document is the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115, dated 13 October 2026**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

You used the approved form, as required. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The rental provider must not unreasonably refuse consent to keep a pet. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

Crucially, the provider is **taken to have consented** unless, within **14 days** after receiving your request, they apply to the Tribunal for an order that refusal is reasonable. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Because you sent the request three weeks ago—about 21 days—the documents indicate that consent has arisen **unless the provider made a Tribunal application within those 14 days**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

An owner’s allergy is not specifically listed in the Act’s factors. The Tribunal may consider the type of pet, the character and nature of the premises and its fixtures, whether refusal is permitted under another Act, prescribed matters, and any other relevant matter. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The documents do not say that an owner’s infrequent visits, or an allergy alone, automatically makes refusal reasonable.

## What you can do or ask

Ask the agent in writing whether the residential rental provider applied to the Tribunal within the required **14-day period**, and ask for the application details or order. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

If no such application was made within 14 days, you can state that the provider is taken to have consented under section 71C(2). [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The documents do not set out a separate renter-initiated procedure for obtaining confirmation of that deemed consent, so they do not establish what application you could personally make if the agent continues to dispute it.

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
## What the law says

Applying the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (6 August 2025), Authorised Version 110**—the version in force on 1 October 2025—a notice to vacate for sale is permitted if the premises are to be **sold or offered for sale with vacant possession immediately after the termination date**. The notice must give at least **60 days’ notice** and be supported by the required documentary evidence. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

The buyer pulling out does **not automatically withdraw** the notice. Under section 91ZZQ, a notice is withdrawn only by a written notice of withdrawal signed by both the person who gave the notice and the renter. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

However, the documents do not establish whether your particular notice is still valid after the sale fell through. That depends on matters such as whether the landlord is still genuinely offering the property for sale with vacant possession, and whether the notice met all form, evidence and timing requirements. The notice is not necessarily invalid merely because that particular buyer withdrew. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

- Ask the landlord in writing to confirm whether the property is still being offered for sale with vacant possession and to give you a **signed written withdrawal** if they no longer intend to proceed. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- Check that the notice was in the prescribed form, stated the reason and termination date, and included supporting documentary evidence. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
- If you believe the notice is invalid, you may apply to VCAT to challenge it **within 30 days after it was given**, and in any event on or before the hearing of the landlord’s application for a possession order. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- If you do not leave on the termination date, the landlord must apply to VCAT for a possession order; they cannot personally force you out. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

So, **unless the landlord formally withdraws the notice or VCAT finds it invalid, do not assume that the buyer’s withdrawal cancels it**.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered. The answer ties validity to the sale ground and its evidence: it depends on "whether the landlord is still genuinely offering the property for sale with vacant possession, and whether the notice met all form, evidence and timing requirements." It states the 60-day minimum notice period. It says withdrawal requires a "written notice of withdrawal signed by both the person who gave the notice and the renter." It gives next steps: asking for a signed written withdrawal, or applying to VCAT "within 30 days after it was given."

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The output rejects automatic cancellation and requires both parties for withdrawal, saying the buyer pulling out "does not automatically withdraw the notice", that withdrawal requires "a written notice of withdrawal signed by both the person who gave the notice and the renter", and that the notice period is "at least 60 days' notice".

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
## What the law says

On **1 October 2025**, the applicable retrieved document is **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version v004 (1 July 2025)**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

You do **not** have to pay the higher rent merely because the agent emailed saying it would increase. The rental provider must use the prescribed **Notice of Proposed Rent Increase** form, and **a valid notice is required for every rent increase**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

The notice must give you **at least 90 days’ notice** and state the current rent, new rent, start date, and method used to calculate the increase. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) Delivery by email is specified only **if you have consented to email delivery**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

Therefore, on the documents provided, the higher rent cannot start until a valid notice has been given and the required 90-day period has passed. Because you never received an official notice, the documents do not establish any date from which the higher rent is payable. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

- Ask the agent to provide the prescribed notice, including the proposed start date and calculation method. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)
- Continue paying the current rent unless and until a valid notice sets a lawful commencement date. This conclusion follows from the requirement that every increase have a valid notice and at least 90 days’ notice. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)
- If you receive a valid notice and consider the increase excessive, you may apply **in writing within 30 days after the notice is given** for a free investigation by the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:
## What the law says

As at **15 October 2026**, the retrieved document is **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version v009 (30 June 2026)**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

Damage to the rented premises must be reported to the rental provider **in writing as soon as practicable**. The renter must also use a **suitably qualified person** for any repair, whether urgent or non-urgent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

Skirting-board damage is not identified in the document as an urgent repair. The urgent-repair provisions allow a renter to arrange repairs only after taking reasonable steps to have the rental provider arrange them immediately and the rental provider has not done so. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) The document separately says that for **non-urgent damage**, the renter must notify the rental provider in writing and the rental provider must carry out the repair within a reasonable time. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

Therefore, you should **not simply arrange a quick repair without telling the owner or agent first**. Doing so would not comply with the document’s requirement to notify them in writing as soon as practicable. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The retrieved documents do **not** say whether repairing the skirting boards without notice would affect the owner’s property insurance, or whether the owner must notify their insurer. **I cannot answer the insurance part from these documents.**

## What you can do or ask

Write to the owner or agent promptly, explain that the dog damaged the skirting boards, and provide photographs. Ask whether they want to arrange the repair themselves or approve your proposed suitably qualified tradesperson. The documents specifically require written notice of the damage and state that only a suitably qualified person may do repairs. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

Keep copies of the notice, photographs, quotes, invoices and any approval. The retrieved documents do not state that you have an automatic right to choose the contractor or recover the cost of repairing this non-urgent damage. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
## What the law said on 1 March 2023

The applicable document is **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version v002 (1 June 2022)**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

It **did not prescribe a minimum number of electrical circuits** for a rental, so the retrieved document does not establish that your rental must have a particular number of circuits. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

The electrical-safety minimum standard requiring all power-outlet and lighting circuits to have a compliant circuit breaker and residual-current device applied **from 29 March 2023**, not on 1 March 2023. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf) The documents do not say that a breaker tripping when a kettle and heater run together, by itself, breaches a particular circuit-number rule. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

## What you can ask for or do

- **Notify the rental provider in writing** that the breaker trips when the kettle and heater are used together, and ask them to have the electrical installation inspected and any necessary repair carried out. The rental provider must maintain the premises in good repair, and non-urgent repairs must be completed in a reasonable time. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
- Ask for the **date of the most recent electrical safety check**. The provider must conduct an electrical safety check of electrical installations, appliances and fittings they provide every two years and give you the date in writing if you request it. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
- You may also request a **copy of the most recent electrical-safety-check record**; it must be provided within **7 days** after the provider receives your written request. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
- If you notify the provider of the repair and it has not been completed within **14 days**, you may apply to VCAT for an order requiring the repair. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

The retrieved documents do not say that you can require the provider to install a specific number of separate circuits. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
## What the law says

The retrieved **Residential Tenancies Act 1997**, **Authorised Version No. 110** (incorporating amendments as at 6 August 2025), does **not expressly say whether an ordinary rooming-house operator may charge coins for using a washing machine**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

However, from **26 February 2024**, the **Residential Tenancies (Rooming House Standards) Regulations 2023**, **Authorised Version No. 002** (incorporating amendments as at 1 December 2024), requires a rooming house to provide **one washing machine in good working order for every 12 or fewer residents**, based on the maximum number the rooming house can accommodate. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf)

If the operator charges residents an amount for services, the Act requires the operator to give residents a **separate schedule of the amount relating to those services before residency begins**, and an **itemised account showing individual use** if the services are used. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

A special rule allows **Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency** to impose a service charge for laundry services or facilities only where it is not possible or practicable to measure individual use accurately; the charge must not exceed the cost of providing the service or facility. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

Ask the operator:

1. **What is the legal basis for the coin charge?**
2. **Was the laundry charge disclosed in a separate schedule before you moved in?**
3. **How is the charge calculated, and can you receive an itemised account?**
4. **Whether the operator is Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency.**

The retrieved documents do not provide enough information to conclude that coin-operated washing machines are automatically lawful or unlawful for an ordinary private rooming-house operator.

The hardest one, that the law doesn't say the machines must be free, is covered by "does not expressly say whether an ordinary rooming-house operator may charge coins for using a washing machine." question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
## What the law says

The relevant document for **1 October 2025** is **_Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021_, rt-regs-2021-v004-2025-07-01.pdf, Authorised Version No. 004** (dated **1 July 2025**). [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

- Each room in rented premises must be **free from mould and damp caused by, or related to, the building structure**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)
- The documents do **not** state that a rental provider is prohibited from using an advertisement photo that appears to show mould. They therefore do not establish that the advertisement itself is unlawful.
- A photo that appears to show mould is **not, by itself, enough to prove** that the premises fail the minimum standard. The legal test also requires the mould or damp to be caused by, or related to, the building structure; the documents contain no rule saying that an advertising photo conclusively proves that fact. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

## What the renter can ask or do

Before applying, ask the rental provider or agent:

1. **Whether the premises comply with the rental minimum standards**, which is information the provider must disclose to a rental applicant. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
2. **Whether the provider has received a repair notice in the previous three years concerning mould or damp caused by, or related to, the building structure**, and, if so, what happened. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
3. For clarification or an inspection of the bedroom, and keep the advertisement photo and any other dated photos. The prescribed condition-report form says photos may be useful in a dispute about the condition of the premises. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

The retrieved documents do not specify any further rule about the evidentiary weight of an advertisement photo or a particular procedure for challenging the advertisement.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered: the answer states the mould and damp standard ('free from mould and damp caused by, or related to, the building structure'). It says the photo alone does not prove a breach: 'A photo that appears to show mould is not, by itself, enough to prove that the premises fail the minimum standard'. It also gives next steps, such as asking the agent whether the premises comply and requesting an inspection of the bedroom.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer says neither forbidden claim: it states a photo is "not, by itself, enough to prove" non-compliance, and that the documents "do not state that a rental provider is prohibited from using an advertisement photo that appears to show mould."

Authorised Version No. 004' but never names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 or its 'Authorised Version No. 110'. It also bases its disclosure and repair-notice steps on '21-3sra002', the Regulations' Version 002, which was not in force on 1 October 2025.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I let a friend move into my rental without telling the agent. Now I want them out. What do I have to do?
answer:
## What the law says

As at **15 October 2026**, the retrieved material includes **_Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021_, Authorised Version v009, dated 30 June 2026**. question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?
answer:
## What the law said on 1 October 2025

The applicable document is **_Residential Tenancies Act 1997_, Authorised Version No. 110, dated 6 August 2025**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

- The rental had to be advertised or offered at a **fixed rent**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- The rental provider or agent must not **solicit or otherwise invite** an offer higher than the advertised rent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- Advertising the property at a rent that was false or misleading was prohibited. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- The Act also prohibited misleading or deceptive conduct, or a false or misleading representation about the rent, when inducing someone to enter a residential rental agreement. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- On the documents provided, the Act does **not specifically say** that an agent may not accept a higher offer made without being invited. The later version dated 25 November 2025 added that rule, but it was not the version in force on 1 October 2025. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

Therefore, if the agent encouraged someone to offer more than the advertised rent, or used a misleading advertised rent to attract applications, that may be a contravention. The documents do not establish whether the email saying you had withdrawn, the re-listing, or another applicant’s offer actually breached the Act. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

The retrieved documents do not state a specific complaint process, application procedure, remedy for a rejected rental applicant, or evidentiary requirements for challenging this conduct. They also do not say what records a renter must save. I therefore cannot identify a statutory process or evidence checklist from these documents.

You can, however, ask the agent or provider to explain in writing:

1. why your application was recorded as withdrawn;
2. who withdrew it and when;
3. why the property was re-listed at a higher rent; and
4. whether the agent solicited or invited any offer above the advertised rent.

Save the advertisement, the original advertised price, your application and submission confirmation, the email saying you withdrew, the later listing, and all messages about rent or competing offers—but the documents provided do not specify these as legally required forms of evidence.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
## What the law says

The applicable document on **15 October 2026** is the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115** (**rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf**). [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

A rental provider must not unreasonably refuse consent to keep a pet. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) A request must be made using the approved form, which you say you did. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The rental provider is taken to have consented **unless, within 14 days after receiving the request, they applied to the Tribunal** for an order that refusal is reasonable. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Because three weeks is 21 days, a simple refusal by the agent after that period does not by itself prevent the deemed consent from applying—**unless the rental provider made the required Tribunal application within the 14 days**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The owner’s allergy is not listed specifically in the Act’s stated considerations. The Tribunal may consider the type of pet, the character and nature of the premises and its fixtures, whether refusal is permitted under an Act, prescribed matters, and any other relevant matter. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The documents do not say that an owner’s infrequent visits, or an allergy in those circumstances, automatically makes refusal reasonable. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

Ask the agent in writing whether the rental provider applied to the Tribunal under **section 71D within 14 days** of receiving your form, and ask for the application details. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

If no such application was made within 14 days, you can state that consent is taken to have been given under **section 71C(2)**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) If there was an application, the Tribunal can decide whether refusal is reasonable and may order that you are permitted to keep the dog. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The retrieved documents do not state the procedure or deadline for you to make your own Tribunal application.

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
### What the law says

Under the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 110 (6 August 2025)**, a landlord may give a notice to vacate if the premises are to be **sold or offered for sale with vacant possession immediately after the termination date**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

The buyer pulling out does **not automatically withdraw** the notice. A notice to vacate is withdrawn only by a written withdrawal notice signed by both the person who gave the notice and the renter. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) Therefore, unless that has happened, the notice remains on foot—but its validity depends on whether the landlord still satisfies the statutory selling ground. If the property is no longer being sold or offered for sale with vacant possession, the documents do not say that the notice automatically becomes invalid; they provide a process for challenging its validity. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

You do **not** have to leave merely because the landlord says you must: if you do not vacate, the landlord must apply to VCAT for a possession order, and only Victoria Police can forcibly evict you under a warrant issued from a VCAT order. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

### What you can do or ask

- Ask the landlord in writing to confirm whether the property is still being offered for sale with vacant possession and to give you a written withdrawal notice if it is not. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- You may apply to VCAT to challenge the notice’s validity within **30 days after it was given**; the Act specifically allows this for a notice given under the selling ground. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- If the landlord applies for a possession order, you may challenge the notice **on or before the hearing**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- Check that the notice was in the prescribed form and accompanied by documentary evidence supporting the reason; otherwise, it is not valid under the Act. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

It does cover written withdrawal signed by both parties, the selling ground and its documentary evidence, and next steps such as seeking a written withdrawal or applying to VCAT within 30 days.
