question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
## What the law says

Under **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version v004 (1 July 2025)**, the rental provider **must use the prescribed “Notice of proposed rent increase” form**, and **a valid notice is required for every rent increase**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

Therefore, an agent’s informal email saying that the rent will increase—without giving the required notice—does **not** establish a valid rent increase on the documents provided. You do **not** have to pay the higher rent yet; continue paying the current rent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

A valid notice must give you **at least 60 days’ notice** and state the proposed new rent, start date, and method used to calculate the increase. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) The increase cannot start before the date specified in a valid notice and, based on the required 60-day notice period, cannot validly begin less than 60 days after that notice is given. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

The documents also say that rent must not be increased during a fixed-term agreement unless the agreement allows it, and must not be increased more than once every 12 months. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

Ask the agent to provide the prescribed notice, including:

- the current and proposed rent;
- the start date;
- the calculation method; and
- how the notice was delivered. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

The prescribed form may be sent by email **only if you have consented to email delivery**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) If you later receive a valid notice and consider the increase excessive, you may apply in writing to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria for an investigation **within 30 days after the notice is given**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

The retrieved document does not state a different consequence for an informal email beyond requiring a valid notice, so it does not provide a more specific answer about any attempted retrospective increase.

question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
## What the law says

The relevant document is **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 004, dated 1 July 2025** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

- Each room in rented premises must be **free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- Before entering the tenancy, the rental provider must disclose whether the premises comply with the rental minimum standards [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- The provider must also disclose whether, since **31 December 2021**, they have received a repair notice in the previous **3 years** relating to mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- The retrieved documents do **not** say that a rental provider is prohibited from putting a photograph showing apparent mould in a rental advertisement. They also do **not** establish that the photograph itself proves the premises fail the minimum standard.
- The prescribed condition-report form says photographs may be useful in a dispute about the condition of the premises, but it does not say that a photograph is conclusive proof .

## What the renter can do or ask

Ask the rental provider or agent, before applying or signing:

1. **Does the premises comply with the rental minimum standards?** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)  
2. **Has the provider received a mould- or damp-related repair notice in the last 3 years?** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)  
3. **Will the apparent mould be removed and the underlying building-related cause fixed before the tenancy begins?** The documents support the minimum-standard requirement, but do not specify this exact advertising or pre-tenancy process [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

Keep a copy or screenshot of the advertisement and photograph. If you inspect or rent the property, take dated, labelled photographs identifying the room; the prescribed form says such photographs may assist in a dispute .

question: It is 15 October 2026. I let a friend move into my rental without telling the agent. Now I want them out. What do I have to do?
answer:
## What the law says

The documents do **not** say exactly how to remove a friend who is merely an occupant or guest. They do say that if your friend has been given part of the premises to live in—amounting to a **sub-let**—you must not sub-let any part of the premises without the rental provider’s **written consent**. Without consent, the sub-letting is invalid unless VCAT has determined that consent was unnecessary. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

The applicable document is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version v110, dated 6 August 2025**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) The retrieved **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version v009, dated 30 June 2026**, provides the prescribed notice-to-vacate form, but it is a form for requiring a **renter who is a party to the residential rental agreement** to leave. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

You must not use force to remove someone. The retrieved form states that only Victoria Police can carry out a forcible eviction, and only under a VCAT possession order and warrant. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

- Ask the rental provider or agent **in writing** whether they consent to your friend occupying or sub-letting part of the premises, and if not, what action they require under the rental agreement.
- Ask your friend to leave voluntarily.
- If your friend will not leave, the retrieved documents do **not** specify the notice or VCAT procedure for removing a person who is not named as a renter. They therefore do not provide enough information to say what formal step you must take.
- Do not change the locks, remove belongings, or use force based only on these documents. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Vic)**, Authorised Version No. 110 (dated 6 August 2025), which was in force on 1 October 2025 [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf):

### Can you challenge what happened?
Yes, you can challenge this conduct. The law explicitly prohibits the behaviors you described:
* **Soliciting higher rents:** A rental provider or their agent must not solicit or invite an offer of rent that is higher than the advertised amount [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). 
* **False/misleading representations:** They must not make a false or misleading representation in relation to the rent for the premises [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
* **Deceptive conduct:** They must not induce a person to enter into a rental agreement by engaging in conduct that is misleading or deceptive, or by making false representations concerning the rent payable [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

Falsely claiming you withdrew your application to re-list the property at a higher price likely breaches these provisions. You can report this to Consumer Affairs Victoria or apply to VCAT, which has the authority to make orders regarding contraventions of these sections [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

### What evidence should you save?
To support a challenge, preserve the following:
* **The original advertisement:** Screenshots or links showing the property was advertised at the specific price and the date it was posted.
* **The fraudulent email:** The full email chain claiming you withdrew, including headers/timestamps to prove you did not send it.
* **Proof of your application:** Confirmation emails of your application submission, receipts for any application fees paid, or sent messages confirming your intent to rent at the advertised price.
* **The new listing:** Screenshots showing the property re-listed at a higher rent and the date of that change.

### Limitations of the provided documents
The retrieved documents do not specify whether a rental application itself is legally binding, nor do they outline a specific administrative process for contesting a "fake withdrawal" email beyond reporting it as a breach of advertising and soliciting rules.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Vic)**, Authorised Version **v115-2026-10-13**, which is in force on 15 October 2026 [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf):

**What the law says about your situation**
*   **Unreasonable Refusals:** A residential rental provider (the owner or their agent) must not unreasonably refuse to consent to you keeping a pet [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
*   **The 14-Day "Deemed Consent" Rule:** Because you submitted your official request form three weeks ago, more than 14 days have passed. Under the law, if the rental provider does not apply to the Tribunal within those first 14 days, they are legally **taken to have consented** to your request [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Their verbal "no" is effectively overridden by this timeline.
*   **The Allergy Argument:** While an owner's allergy might be a factor in a Tribunal hearing, the Tribunal considers multiple factors when deciding if a refusal is reasonable, such as the type of pet, the character and nature of the rented premises, and any other relevant matters [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Given that the owner "hardly ever visits," a blanket refusal based on an allergy is likely to be viewed as unreasonable.

**What you can do or ask**
1.  **Notify the agent in writing:** Inform the agent that under section 71C(2) of the Act, they are taken to have consented because more than 14 days have passed without them applying to the Tribunal [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
2.  **Keep the dog:** You are legally permitted to keep the pet on the premises [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3.  **If they escalate:** If the owner or agent attempts to evict you or penalize you for the dog, you can apply to the Tribunal yourself under section 71A(b) for a formal order permitting you to keep the pet [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You would cite the deemed consent rule and the fact that their refusal was unreasonable given the owner's lack of presence.

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Vic)**, Authorised Version No. 110 dated 6 August 2025, which was in force on 1 October 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf):

### Do you still have to leave?
**Yes.** Unless your landlord formally withdraws the notice or you reach a new agreement with them, the original notice remains legally valid and you are required to vacate by the termination date specified in it.

### Why the notice is still valid
Under section 91ZZB of the Act, a residential rental provider (landlord) may give a notice to vacate if they intend for the premises to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession immediately after the termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). 

The Act does not state that a notice automatically becomes invalid if a buyer pulls out or the sale falls through. Instead, section 91ZZQ dictates that a notice to vacate can **only** be withdrawn if a formal notice of withdrawal is provided [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). This notice of withdrawal must meet three strict requirements:
* It must be in writing;
* It must be signed by the landlord (the person who gave the original notice); and
* It must be signed by you (the person to whom the notice was given) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

Because your landlord has not provided this signed notice of withdrawal, the original notice remains fully effective.

### What you can do
* **Request a formal withdrawal:** Ask your landlord to provide the written and signed notice of withdrawal as required by law if they no longer intend to sell [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). 
* **Negotiate an extension:** If you need more time to find a new home, you can ask your landlord if they are willing to agree to a later move-out date.
* **Challenge at VCAT:** You have the right to apply to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) to challenge the validity of the notice within 30 days after it was given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). However, note that VCAT will determine whether the original reason for the notice (the genuine intent to sell) was valid when it was issued.

It does cover withdrawal requiring a written notice signed by both parties, and it gives next steps (request a formal withdrawal, challenge at VCAT within 30 days).

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
Based on the legislation in force on 1 October 2025, here is how Victorian residential tenancy law applies to your situation:

### 📜 Applicable Law
On this date, the governing document is the ***Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Authorised Version No. 4 as at 1 July 2025** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). 

### 💰 Do you have to pay the higher rent?
**No.** You are not legally required to pay the increased amount based on an email from your agent. 
* A formal written notice is mandatory: *"A valid notice of a proposed rent increase is required for all rent increases"* [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
* The law specifically requires the use of the official **'Notice of Proposed Rent Increase to Renter of Rented Premises' (Form 5)** [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). An informal email or verbal negotiation does not meet this legal threshold. Until you receive a properly completed and served Form 5, your current rent remains legally binding.

### 📅 From when can the increase apply?
Even if your agent serves a valid notice today, the new rent cannot start immediately:
* **90-Day Rule:** The rental provider *"must give you at least 90 days notice of any rent increase"* [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
* **Specified Start Date:** The official notice must include a specific *"Start date"* for the new rent [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). This date cannot be less than 90 days after the notice is given to you.
* **Fixed Term Protection:** If you are currently in a fixed-term agreement, the provider *"must not increase the rent during a fixed term... unless the agreement provides for an increase"* [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
* **Frequency Limit:** The provider *"must not increase the rent more than once every 12 months"* [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

### ✅ What you can do / Ask your agent
1. **Request the Official Form:** Reply to the email and state that under Victorian tenancy law, an informal email is not valid for rent increases. Ask them to serve the official Form 5.
2. **Check the Calculation Method:** Once you receive Form 5, verify that it includes *"the method by which the rent increase was calculated"* [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). The new rent cannot be higher than what this method calculates.
3. **Challenge if Excessive:** If you believe the proposed increase is excessive, you can apply for a free review by the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria within 30 days of receiving the notice [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). You may also apply to VCAT to declare the amount excessive [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (v009)** [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) and the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (v097)** [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa097%20authorised.pdf), which were in force on 15 October 2026, here is how the law applies to your situation:

### 1. Can you fix it without telling the owner?
**No.** You are legally required to notify your rental provider in writing as soon as practicable of any damage to the premises [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The Act reinforces this duty, stating that once you become aware of damage, you must give written notice to the landlord detailing both the fact and the nature of the damage [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa097%20authorised.pdf). 

Because your dog caused the skirting board damage, this falls under `"damage caused by a failure of the tenant to ensure that care was taken to avoid damaging the premises"` [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa097%20authorised.pdf). If you attempt to fix it secretly without reporting it:
* You would be breaching your statutory duty to notify the landlord.
* The landlord can issue a formal repair notice requiring you to fix the damage at your own expense within 14 days, or they can do it themselves and charge you for the reasonable costs [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa097%20authorised.pdf). 
* Hiding damage can severely complicate your bond claim later, as you are legally required to leave the premises in the same condition you entered (accounting only for fair wear and tear) [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa097%20authorised.pdf).

### 2. Would it affect the owner's insurance?
The provided legal documents **do not contain any information** regarding how repairing pet damage yourself would impact the property owner's insurance policy. You would need to consult a qualified insurance broker or contact Consumer Affairs Victoria directly for advice on insurance implications. 

Let me know if you need help drafting the required written notice to your landlord!

question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:

### Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs?
No. The regulations do not specify a minimum number of electrical circuits that a rental property must have [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). 

### What can you ask for regarding the tripping breaker?
While the law does not mandate a specific circuit count, you can rely on two key provisions to address your issue:

*   **Upcoming Electrical Safety Standards:** On and from 29 March 2023, all power outlets and lighting circuits in rental premises must be connected to a switchboard-type Circuit Breaker (complying with AS/NZS 3000) and a switchboard-type Residual Current Device (RCD) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). You can ask your provider to ensure your switchboard is upgraded to meet this standard before it takes effect.
*   **Maintenance Obligations:** Under the standard tenancy agreement, the rental provider must `"maintain the premises in good repair and in a fit condition for occupation"` [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). A breaker that trips when high-draw appliances (like a kettle and heater) are used simultaneously indicates the circuit is overloaded. You can ask your provider to arrange for a licensed electrician to assess whether the wiring or circuit capacity needs upgrading to safely handle modern appliance loads [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?

### What the Law Says
Under section 71C, a residential rental provider (the owner or their agent) **must not unreasonably refuse** to consent to you keeping a pet [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 

Because you sent your official request three weeks ago, the "deemed consent" rule applies. The law states that the provider is legally **taken to have consented** to your request unless they apply to the Tribunal within **14 days** of receiving it [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 

If the owner did apply to the Tribunal within that 14-day window to argue their refusal is reasonable, the Tribunal will make the final decision. When deciding, the Tribunal considers factors such as:
* The type of pet and the character/nature of the rented premises [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* Any other matter the Tribunal considers relevant [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

While an owner's allergy could be considered under "any other matter," the fact that the owner "hardly ever visits" is highly relevant. If the owner rarely occupies the apartment, it may be unreasonable for them to refuse consent based on an allergy they are unlikely to experience while you live there.

### What You Can Do or Ask
1. **Ask the agent in writing:** Request confirmation of whether they filed an application with the Tribunal under section 71D within 14 days of receiving your request [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
2. **If they did NOT apply to the Tribunal:** You can legally keep the dog, as the law deems their consent as given once the 14-day period passes without a Tribunal application [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **If they DID apply to the Tribunal:** You will need to attend the hearing and present your case. Argue that the owner's infrequent visits make the allergy an unreasonable ground for refusal, and explain how keeping the dog does not negatively impact the character or nature of the premises [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?

### What the law says about the situation
Under section 91ZZB of the Act, a landlord is entitled to give you a notice to vacate if the premises are to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). As long as your landlord has not formally withdrawn it, the notice remains legally valid and enforceable.

### What you can do or ask
Because the sale has fallen through, your landlord no longer needs vacant possession for a sale. You should take the following steps:

   A notice to vacate can only be withdrawn if a formal "notice of withdrawal" is given [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf). You should ask your landlord to provide you with this document, which must meet specific legal requirements:
   * It must be in writing;
   * It must be signed by the person who gave the original notice (your landlord); and
   * It must be signed by you (the renter) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf).

2. **Challenge the notice at VCAT**  
   If your landlord refuses to withdraw the notice, you have the right to challenge its validity at the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT). question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021** (S.R. No. 3/2021), Authorised Version Number **v004** (updated 1 July 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf), here is how the law applies to your situation as of 1 October 2025:

### Do you have to pay the higher rent?
**No.** Under Victorian tenancy law, a valid written notice of a proposed rent increase is required for all rent increases [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). An email from your agent does not satisfy this legal requirement. Until you receive an official **Form 5 (Notice of Proposed Rent Increase to Renter of Rented Premises)**, you are not obligated to pay the increased amount and should continue paying your current rent.

### From when would a new rent start?
If your landlord decides to proceed with a rent increase, they must follow strict timing rules:
*   **90 Days' Notice:** The rental provider must give you at least 90 days' notice of any rent increase [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). 
*   **Start Date:** The official Form 5 will specify a "Start date," and the new rent cannot take effect until that date arrives [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Because of the 90-day rule, this start date will be at least 90 days after you receive the notice.
*   **Frequency Limit:** Your landlord cannot increase your rent more than once every 12 months [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

### What can you do?
*   **Request the Official Notice:** Ask your agent to provide you with a properly completed Form 5. 
*   **Challenge the Increase:** If you receive the notice and believe the proposed amount is excessive, you have two options:
    1. Apply to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria for a free investigation by filling out the 'Rent increase investigation' section on the form [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
    2. Apply to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) to declare the rent amount excessive [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

*(Note: If you live in a rooming house or a caravan park/site agreement, different notice periods may apply—90 days for rooming houses and 28 or 90 days for site agreements depending on whether the increase is fixed or non-fixed—but the requirement for an official written notice remains the same.)*

Because of this mandatory notification requirement, you cannot simply arrange for someone to fix the skirting boards without telling the owner first.

question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?
answer:
Based on the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Vic) in force on 1 October 2025 (Authorised Version v110-2025-08-06) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf):

### The Law Regarding Advertised Rent
Under Victorian law, rental properties must be advertised at a **fixed amount**, and "rental auctions" or bidding are strictly prohibited [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Specifically:
* **No Soliciting Higher Offers:** A residential rental provider or their agent is prohibited from soliciting or inviting any offer of rent that is higher than the advertised amount [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). 
* **No Misleading Advertising:** It is an offence to make a false or misleading representation regarding the rent for the premises [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
* **No Deceptive Conduct:** A provider or agent cannot induce someone to enter a rental agreement through conduct that is misleading, deceptive, or likely to mislead or deceive [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

### Can You Challenge What Happened?
**Yes.** The actions you described (soliciting bids above the advertised price and falsely claiming you withdrew) appear to contravene the fixed-rent and anti-misleading provisions of the Act [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). 
* **VCAT Orders:** The Tribunal has the power to make orders regarding contraventions of the misleading conduct provisions in the Act [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
* **Penalties for Providers:** Breaching the fixed-rent and anti-misleading advertising rules carries penalties of 60 penalty units for individuals or 300 penalty units for body corporates [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
* **Australian Consumer Law:** These tenancy laws operate alongside the Australian Consumer Law (Victoria), which provides additional protections against misleading and deceptive conduct in trade or commerce [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
* You can report this conduct to **Consumer Affairs Victoria** for investigation, as they oversee compliance with residential tenancy regulations.

### What Evidence Should You Save?
The retrieved documents do not provide a statutory evidence checklist for this specific scenario. However, to prove the prohibited conduct outlined in the Act [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), you should preserve the following:
1. **The Original Advertisement:** A screenshot or saved copy of the listing showing the *advertised fixed rent* and the date it was posted.
2. **Proof of Your Application:** Copies of your rental application, payment receipts (if any), and confirmation emails showing you applied at the advertised price.
3. **The "Withdrawn" Email:** The exact email claiming you withdrew, including headers/timestamps to prove you did not send it.
4. **Proof of the Price Change:** Screenshots of the property listed at the new, higher rent and any messages indicating someone else offered more than the advertised price.
5. **All Correspondence:** Save every email, text, or call log with the agent/landlord regarding this property.

*Note: If you proceed to VCAT or Consumer Affairs Victoria, they will guide you on the specific procedural requirements for your application.*

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Vic)**, Authorised Version No. 115 (dated 13 October 2026), which is in force on your question date of 15 October 2026 [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf):

### Can they refuse?
No, not unreasonably. Under section 71C(1) of the Act, a residential rental provider **must not unreasonably refuse** consent to you keeping a pet [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This is also reinforced in the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, which state that a rental provider must not unreasonably refuse a request to keep a pet [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). 

### The "14-Day Rule" (Crucial for your situation)
Because you sent your official request form three weeks ago, the most important factor is whether the agent or owner took legal action within the first two weeks. Under section 71C(2), if the residential rental provider does not apply to the Tribunal within **14 days** of receiving your request, they are legally taken to have **consented** to you keeping the pet [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 

*   **If they did NOT file a Tribunal application within those 14 days:** Their verbal "no" is effectively void. You are legally permitted to keep your dog despite their objection [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
*   **If they DID file a Tribunal application within those 14 days:** The matter moves to the Tribunal, which will decide if the refusal is reasonable under section 71D [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### What factors does the Tribunal consider?
If the case goes to the Tribunal, it decides what is "reasonable" by weighing specific factors outlined in section 71E(2) [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf):
* The type of pet you propose to keep.
* The character and nature of the rented premises (your apartment).
* The character and nature of the appliances, fixtures, and fittings on the premises.
* Whether refusing consent is permitted under any other Act.
* Any prescribed matters.
* **Any other matter the Tribunal considers relevant** [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

While an owner's allergy can sometimes be a valid concern, the fact that they "hardly ever visit" means it may not directly impact you or the condition of the apartment. The Tribunal will weigh this against your right to keep a pet, but ultimately, the Tribunal makes the final call on what is reasonable [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### What you should do now
1. **Confirm if a Tribunal application was filed:** Ask the agent in writing whether they submitted an application under section 71D within the first 14 days of receiving your form. 
2. **If no application was filed:** You may proceed with keeping the dog, as the law deems them to have consented [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **If a Tribunal application was filed:** Prepare for a hearing. Gather evidence showing why keeping the dog is reasonable (e.g., pet training records, proof of hypoallergenic measures you take, or statements from your doctor regarding your own health needs) and argue that an owner who rarely visits does not suffer actual detriment from the pet [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 

*(Note: This information is based strictly on the provided Victorian tenancy legislation documents. For formal legal advice or representation at VCAT, you should contact a local Tenants' Union or legal aid service.)*

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021** (Authorised Version v004, effective 1 July 2025), which is the law in force on 1 October 2025:

### Do you have to pay the higher rent?
**No.** Under Victorian law, a valid, written notice of a proposed rent increase is required for *all* rent increases [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). An informal email from your agent does not satisfy this legal requirement. Until you receive the correct statutory form, the rent increase is not legally enforceable, and you are only obligated to pay your current rent.

### From when would it take effect?
The new rent can only start on the date specified in the official notice, provided that date respects the mandatory minimum notice period for your tenancy type:
* **Standard rented premises:** The provider must give you **at least 90 days' notice** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). 
* **Rooming houses:** The operator must give you **at least 60 days' notice** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
* **Caravan/site tenancies:** It is **28 days** for fixed-amount increases or **60 days** for non-fixed amount increases [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:
Based on Victorian residential tenancy law in force on 15 October 2026, specifically the ***Residential Tenancies Act 1997*** (No. 109 of 1997) and the ***Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*** (S.R. No. 3/2021, Authorised Version v009 as at 30 June 2026):

### What the law says about the situation
Under Victorian tenancy law, you have a strict legal duty to report damage caused by your pet. The law states that a renter who becomes aware of damage to the rented premises must give written notice to the residential rental provider "as soon as practicable" of both the fact that the damage has occurred and its nature [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). This requirement is reinforced in the regulations, which state you must notify the rental provider in writing as soon as practicable of any damage to the premises [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). 

Importantly, the law distinguishes between actual damage and "fair wear and tear" caused by a renter or their visitor, which is not considered actionable damage [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). However, skirting boards chewed by a dog typically fall under tenant-caused damage rather than fair wear and tear.

### What you can do (and should do)
You **cannot** simply fix the skirting boards secretly without telling the owner. If you fail to report the damage:
* The landlord is entitled to issue a formal repair notice requiring you to fix the damage at your own expense within 14 days [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa097%20authorised.pdf). 
* If you do not complete the repairs in a "tradesman-like manner" within that 14-day window, or if the landlord chooses to handle it themselves, they may carry out the repairs and charge you for the reasonable costs [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa097%20authorised.pdf).

**Recommended steps:**
1. Send written notice (email or text is legally acceptable under the Electronic Transactions Act) to your rental provider immediately, stating the fact and nature of the damage [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
2. Offer to arrange the repair yourself at your expense, or ask if they prefer to handle it directly [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa097%20authorised.pdf).
3. Keep a copy of your notification and any receipts for repairs you pay for, as this protects you from future disputes over the bond or additional charges.

### Would it affect the owner's insurance?
The provided legal documents **do not contain any information** regarding how tenant-caused damage impacts a landlord's property insurance. You would need to consult an insurance broker or ask the owner directly to understand how their specific policy handles accidental pet damage.

question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021** (Authorised Version No. v002 dated 1 June 2022), which was in force on 1 March 2023, here is how your situation is covered:

### Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs?
No. The regulations do not specify a minimum number of electrical circuits that a rental property must have [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). 

However, under the same regulations, from **29 March 2023** (just one month after your question date), all power outlets and lighting circuits in rented premises are required to be connected to:
* A switchboard-type Circuit Breaker complying with AS/NZS 3000; and
* A switchboard-type Residual Current Device (RCD) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

### What can you ask for?
While there is no mandated circuit count, the frequent tripping of your breaker suggests the electrical system may be overloaded or inadequate. Here is what you can request from your rental provider:

1. **Request an Electrical Safety Check Record:** You have the right to ask for a copy of the most recent electrical safety check record. The provider must supply this within 7 days of receiving your written request [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). 
2. **Request Repairs or Upgrades:** Your rental provider is legally obligated to maintain the premises in good repair and in a fit condition for occupation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). If an electrician determines that the current circuit capacity is unsafe, insufficient, or causing damage, you can formally ask them to arrange for a licensed electrician to inspect the installation and upgrade the circuit capacity or add additional circuits. 
3. **Escalate if Necessary:** If the provider refuses to address an electrical issue that makes the property unsafe or unusable, it may breach their maintenance obligations and the rental minimum standards, giving you grounds to apply to VCAT for a repair order [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

*(Note: While the regulations set safety hardware standards like RCDs, they do not dictate load capacity or circuit quantity. Dealing with overloaded circuits typically falls under general property maintenance and electrical compliance laws rather than tenancy circuit-count rules.)*

question: It is 1 November 2019. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?
answer:
## What the law says

On **1 November 2019**, the relevant document is the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 088, incorporating amendments as at 2 July 2019**. Authorised Version No. 089 is dated 4 December 2019, so it was not yet in force on the date asked [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)[[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf).

For a month-to-month tenancy, check whether the notice is a **section 263 “no specified reason” notice**. Such a notice had to give a termination date **at least 120 days after it was given** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

A section 263 notice has **no effect if it was given in response to your exercise, or proposed exercise, of a right under the Act** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Asking the landlord to repair leaking fixtures may involve such rights because:

- the landlord must maintain the premises in good repair [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf); and
- a malfunctioning landlord-provided appliance, fitting or fixture that uses or supplies water is an **urgent repair** if it results, or will result, in a substantial amount of water being wasted [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

The fact that the notice arrived on the same day as your repair follow-up may be relevant to whether it was given “in response” to your request, but the retrieved Act does not say that timing alone proves retaliation.

## What you can do or ask

1. **Check the notice’s section number and reason.** The retaliation protection in section 266(2) expressly applies to notices under **section 261 or section 263**. As you rent month to month, the provision to check in particular is section 263 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

2. **Check the termination date.** A section 263 notice must allow at least **120 days** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

3. **Keep the repair request and notice**, especially anything showing when you reported or followed up the leak and when the notice was given. The retrieved Act does not specify a particular evidence checklist.

4. **Apply to VCAT to challenge the notice’s validity within 60 days after it was given.** After that period, the Act says you are not entitled to apply to challenge a section 263 notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). You can ask VCAT to determine that the notice has no effect because it was given in response to your exercise or proposed exercise of repair rights under the Act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

5. **Continue pursuing the repair separately.** For urgent repairs, you may arrange repairs if you took reasonable steps to have the landlord or agent carry them out immediately but could not get them to do so; reimbursement was limited to the reasonable cost or **$1,000, whichever was less** [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). If you cannot meet the cost, the repairs exceed $1,000, or the landlord refuses reimbursement, you may apply to VCAT, which must hear the urgent-repair application within **2 business days** [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: Yes: all three points are covered. The answer says a section 263 'no specified reason' notice must give 'at least 120 days' and that such a notice 'has no effect if it was given in response to your exercise, or proposed exercise, of a right under the Act', which it links to repair requests. The hardest point is covered by 'Apply to VCAT to challenge the notice's validity within 60 days after it was given.'

answer:
## What the law says

Under the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 110, incorporating amendments as at 6 August 2025**, the buyer pulling out **does not automatically cancel the notice**. A notice is withdrawn only through a written withdrawal signed by both the landlord and the renter. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

However, a sale notice is authorised only if, immediately after the termination date, the premises are to be **sold or offered for sale with vacant possession**. Therefore:

- if the landlord still intends to sell or offer the property for sale with vacant possession, the notice may remain effective; but
- if the landlord no longer intends to sell or offer it for sale, you may challenge the notice’s validity. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

The landlord cannot physically evict you merely on the strength of the notice. They must obtain a possession order from VCAT. VCAT may make that order only if satisfied that the landlord was entitled to give the notice, it has not been withdrawn, you remain after the termination date, and making the order is reasonable and proportionate. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

1. **Ask the landlord to withdraw the notice in writing.** The withdrawal must be signed by both you and the landlord. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
2. **Ask whether the property is still being sold or offered for sale with vacant possession**, and request evidence of that intention.
3. If it is no longer being sold or offered for sale, **apply to VCAT to challenge the notice’s validity**. The Act says this application must be made within **30 days after the notice was given**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
4. If the landlord applies for possession, tell VCAT that the buyer withdrew and provide any evidence that the property is no longer being sold. VCAT must consider whether the landlord was entitled to give the notice and whether possession would be reasonable and proportionate. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

**In short:** do not assume the notice has disappeared, but you do not necessarily have to leave if its stated sale basis no longer exists. Seek a signed withdrawal or challenge it at VCAT.

It says the buyer pulling out "does not automatically cancel the notice" and that a withdrawal must be "signed by both the landlord and the renter."
