question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
## What the law says

**You do not have to pay the higher rent merely because the agent emailed you about it or refused to negotiate.** A valid increase requires at least **60 days’ notice in the prescribed form**. An increase that does not comply is invalid under section 44(5) of the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, **Authorised Version No. 110** (incorporating amendments as at 6 August 2025) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

The prescribed notice is **Form 5—Notice of Proposed Rent Increase to Renter of Rented Premises** under the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, **Authorised Version No. 004** (1 July 2025). It must state the current and new rent, start date, and the method and calculation used to reach the new amount [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). It may be delivered by email only if you consented to electronic service [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

Therefore, if the agent’s email was **not Form 5**, you continue paying your current rent. The higher rent can start no earlier than the date specified in a valid Form 5, which must allow at least **60 days’ notice** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Negotiating about the proposed increase does not replace that requirement [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

Also, rent generally cannot be increased more than once every **12 months**. During a fixed term, it cannot increase unless the agreement provides for an increase of a specified amount or by a specified calculation method [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

- Tell the agent you have not received the prescribed **Form 5** and will continue paying the existing rent until a valid notice takes effect [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- Ask them to provide Form 5 showing the new rent, start date, and full calculation method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- If you receive a valid notice and consider the increase excessive, apply in writing to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria for an investigation within **30 days after the notice is given** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four required points are present: Form 5, at least 60 days' notice, a next step, and the hardest point, which is covered by 'An increase that does not comply is invalid' and 'if the agent’s email was not Form 5, you continue paying your current rent.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes: none of the failure conditions is asserted. The answer says "You do not have to pay the higher rent merely because the agent emailed you," and it requires "at least 60 days' notice" from a valid Form 5 rather than from the email date. It also says notice "may be delivered by email only if you consented to electronic service," which permits email rather than banning it.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Act as "Authorised Version No. 110 (incorporating amendments as at 6 August 2025)" and the Regulations as "Authorised Version No. 004 (1 July 2025)", with matching 97-109aa110 and 21-3sra004 links. Both are the versions in force on 1 October 2025, and it relies on no other version.

question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:
## What the law says

Under the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026**, a renter must give the rental provider **written notice as soon as practicable** after becoming aware of damage, describing both the fact and nature of the damage. [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Therefore, you should **not repair the skirting boards without telling the owner or agent first**. [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

A renter must not intentionally or negligently damage the premises, excluding fair wear and tear, and must leave the property as far as practicable in the same condition as at the start, allowing for fair wear and tear. [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) If the owner treats this as damage caused by failure to take care, they may issue a written repair notice requiring you to repair it at your expense within **14 days**, in a **proper and tradesman-like manner**; otherwise, they may arrange the work and recover the reasonable cost from you. [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 009, incorporating amendments as at 30 June 2026**, state that only a **suitably qualified person** may perform urgent or non-urgent repairs. [[13]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The retrieved documents **do not say whether this damage or a privately arranged repair would affect the owner’s insurance**. That depends on the insurance policy, so I cannot answer that part from these documents.

## What you can do or ask

1. **Notify the owner or agent in writing now**, identifying the chewed skirting boards. [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)  
2. Ask whether they want to arrange the repair themselves or will approve you engaging a suitably qualified person. [[13]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)  
3. If they require you to repair it, make sure the work is completed properly and in a tradesman-like manner, and keep the invoice and photographs. [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered. The answer says written notice must be given 'as soon as practicable'. It says the renter must not damage the premises 'excluding fair wear and tear' and must leave the property 'in the same condition', with repairs at the renter's expense. It states 'The retrieved documents do not say whether this damage... would affect the owner's insurance'. It gives the next step 'Notify the owner or agent in writing now'.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. None of the three failure conditions is met: the answer rejects a quiet repair ("you should not repair the skirting boards without telling the owner or agent first"), states no insurance outcome as fact ("The retrieved documents do not say whether this damage or a privately arranged repair would affect the owner's insurance"), and never says the renter must pay the owner's insurance excess.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names both required documents with their in-force versions, 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026' (link 97-109aa115) and 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 009, incorporating amendments as at 30 June 2026' (link 21-3sra009), and relies on no other version.

question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
## What the law said on 1 March 2023

The applicable document is the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 002**, incorporating amendments as at **1 June 2022**. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

- The retrieved regulations **do not prescribe a minimum number of electrical circuits** for a rental property. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
- The electrical minimum standard requiring all power outlets and lighting circuits to be connected to compliant switchboard-type circuit breakers and residual current devices did **not begin until 29 March 2023**, so it was not yet in force on 1 March 2023. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
- However, the rental provider had to maintain the premises **in good repair and fit for occupation**. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
- They also had to arrange an electrical safety check of all electrical installations, appliances and fittings they provided **every 2 years**, conducted by a licensed or registered electrician. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

1. **Notify the rental provider in writing** that the breaker trips when the kettle and heater operate together, and ask for a suitably qualified person to inspect and repair the electrical installation. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
2. Ask for the **date of the most recent electrical safety check**. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
3. Ask in writing for a **copy of the most recent electrical safety-check record**; it must be provided within **7 days** of the request. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
4. You may ask the provider or electrician whether another circuit or other electrical work is needed, but the retrieved regulations do **not** give you an automatic right to a particular number of circuits. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
5. If treated as a non-urgent repair and it is not completed within **14 days after written notice**, you may apply to VCAT for an order requiring the repair. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

The retrieved document does not establish whether tripping only when those two appliances run together is an **urgent repair**; it states only that urgent repairs include failure or breakdown of an essential service or a provider-supplied appliance for hot water, cooking, heating or laundering. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both points are covered. Point 1 is met by "The retrieved regulations do not prescribe a minimum number of electrical circuits for a rental property," which the rubric accepts as stating no rule on the number of circuits. Point 2, the harder one, is met by "Notify the rental provider in writing... and ask for a suitably qualified person to inspect and repair the electrical installation" and "Ask for the date of the most recent electrical safety check."

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer asserts neither failure condition: it states the regulations "do not prescribe a minimum number of electrical circuits" and that the circuit breaker and RCD standard "did not begin until 29 March 2023, so it was not yet in force on 1 March 2023."

version-cited.reason: No — the answer names only the 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 002' (link 21-3sra002), which is the correct in-force version, but it never names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 or its Authorised Version No. 101, which the rubric requires.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
## What the law says

**Yes, they may charge for using the washing machines, but there are conditions.** The rooming-house standards require **one washing machine in good working order for every 12 or fewer residents**, based on the house’s maximum capacity. The standards do not say that use must be free [[13]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf).

Where an operator charges separately for a service, they must:

- give you a separate schedule showing the charge **before you take up residency**; and
- give you an **itemised account showing your individual use** if you use the service [[12]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

Therefore, a coin-operated charge is not automatically unlawful, but the retrieved documents do not establish that inserting coins, by itself, satisfies the itemised-account requirement.

If the rooming house is operated by **Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency** under the special declared-rooming-house provisions, a laundry service charge must not exceed the cost of providing the facility, and written notice must be given when the charge is imposed or changed [[12]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What you can ask

Ask the operator for:

1. the schedule of laundry charges that should have been supplied before you moved in; and  
2. an itemised account of your individual laundry use [[12]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

Also check the rooming house’s maximum capacity: **two machines satisfy the minimum only if it can accommodate no more than 24 residents** [[13]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf).

These conclusions use the versions in force on **15 October 2026**:

- *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, **Authorised Version No. 115**, dated 13 October 2026 [[12]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- *Residential Tenancies (Rooming House Standards) Regulations 2023*, **Authorised Version No. 002**, dated 1 December 2024 [[13]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: Yes: all four points are covered. The answer states the requirement of 'one washing machine in good working order for every 12 or fewer residents', says 'The standards do not say that use must be free', requires 'a separate schedule showing the charge before you take up residency', and gives as a next step asking the operator for 'the schedule of laundry charges that should have been supplied before you moved in'.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. None of the three failing claims is made: the answer says "Yes, they may charge for using the washing machines, but there are conditions," sets out rules on charges ("give you a separate schedule showing the charge before you take up residency" and "an itemised account showing your individual use"), and limits the cost cap to houses run "by Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency under the special declared-rooming-house provisions."

version-cited.reason: Yes: the answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as 'Authorised Version No. 115, dated 13 October 2026' (link 97-109aa115) and the Rooming House Standards Regulations 2023 as 'Authorised Version No. 002, dated 1 December 2024' (link 23-10sra002), and every rule it applies comes from these in-force versions.

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
## What the law says

**As at 1 October 2025, showing possible mould in the advertisement is not, by itself, prohibited.** The Act then in force was the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 110**, incorporating amendments as at 6 August 2025 [[15]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).  

A later provision—section 65B—prohibits advertising premises unless the provider or agent reasonably believes they meet the rental minimum standards, but that provision did **not commence until 25 November 2025**. It was therefore not in force on 1 October 2025 [[11]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[12]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

The applicable minimum standard was in the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 004**, incorporating amendments as at 1 July 2025 [[14]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). It required each room to be free from mould and damp **caused by or related to the building structure** [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

**The photo alone is not necessarily enough to prove non-compliance.** It may be useful evidence of the room’s visible condition, but the standard also requires proof that the substance is mould or damp and that it is caused by or related to the building structure. The prescribed condition-report guidance says photos “may be useful in a dispute”; it does not make them conclusive proof [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

Before entering the agreement, the provider must disclose whether the premises comply with the minimum standards. They must also disclose if, within the previous three years, they received a repair notice about mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

Ask the agent or provider in writing:

- whether the marks are mould or damp;
- what caused them and whether the cause is structural;
- whether the problem has been inspected or repaired;
- whether the premises comply with the rental minimum standards; and
- whether any relevant mould or damp repair notice was received in the previous three years [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

Keep a dated copy of the advertisement and photos. They may support your case, but further evidence—such as an inspection, condition report or evidence of a structural moisture problem—would be needed to establish the full minimum-standard test [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered: the answer states the minimum standard requires rooms to be 'free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure'; it says 'The photo alone is not necessarily enough to prove non-compliance'; and it gives a next step, 'Ask the agent or provider in writing' whether the marks are mould and whether the cause is structural.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer says the photo is not proof ("The photo alone is not necessarily enough to prove non-compliance") and raises the advertising ban only to say it does not apply on that date ("did not commence until 25 November 2025. It was therefore not in force on 1 October 2025").

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names both required documents with their in-force versions: "Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 110, incorporating amendments as at 6 August 2025" and "Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 004, incorporating amendments as at 1 July 2025". It cites the later Act versions (97-109aa111 and 97-109aa115) only to say s 65B was not in force on 1 October 2025, so it does not rely on them, and deleting that material would not change the answer's substance.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I let a friend move into my rental without telling the agent. Now I want them out. What do I have to do?
answer:
## What the law says

The applicable document on **15 October 2026** is the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Vic), Authorised Version No. 115**, incorporating amendments as at **13 October 2026**. [[11]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

Your legal position depends on whether your friend is a **sub-renter** or merely a guest/housemate:

- A renter must not assign or sublet any part of the premises without the rental provider’s **written consent**. An unauthorised assignment or subletting is invalid unless VCAT has determined that consent is unnecessary. [[11]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- Because you did not obtain consent, the rental provider may give **you** a notice to vacate for unauthorised assignment or subletting. That notice must provide at least **14 days** before the termination date. [[11]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- The fact that the subletting is invalid does **not**, in the retrieved Act, automatically authorise you to physically remove your friend or change the locks. [[11]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- If your arrangement with your friend is itself a residential rental agreement, it can be ended by agreement between the provider and renter. [[11]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Otherwise, a residential rental agreement may be terminated only as allowed by Division 9 or Parts 7 or 8 of the Act. [[11]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- A residential rental provider must not require or compel a renter to leave except in accordance with the Act. Forcible removal ultimately requires a possession order and warrant; the warrant authorises a police officer or other authorised person—not you personally—to remove occupants. [[11]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The special VCAT procedure for an unauthorised occupier does not clearly solve your situation while you still live there. It applies where premises are occupied **solely** by a person who is not a renter and who entered or remained without the applicant’s consent. [[11]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

1. **Ask your friend to agree in writing to leave on a specified date.** If your arrangement is a residential rental agreement, termination by agreement is expressly permitted. [[11]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
2. **Do not personally force them out or assume that the lack of the agent’s consent lets you change the locks.** If they are legally your sub-renter, the Act’s termination and possession procedures apply. [[11]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
3. **Be aware of the risk to your own tenancy:** the rental provider can give you a notice to vacate with at least **14 days’ notice** because of the unauthorised subletting. [[11]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
4. If your friend refuses, you need to establish whether the arrangement was a **sub-rental agreement or merely permission to live with you**. The retrieved documents do not provide enough information to determine that from “a friend moved in,” and they do not state a removal procedure for a housemate or licensee who remains while the renter also occupies the home. I therefore cannot say from these documents alone which notice or VCAT application you should use.

must-mention.reason: No: the answer says the outcome depends on 'whether your friend is a sub-renter or merely a guest/housemate' and that it is written-consent subletting, but it never names a deciding fact such as a space that is only theirs, what they pay, or what was actually agreed. It names only legal labels ('sub-rental agreement or merely permission'), not the facts that decide them, so the first point is missing.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer asserts none of the failing claims: it warns 'Do not personally force them out or assume that the lack of the agent's consent lets you change the locks', applies the '14 days' notice only to the rental provider's notice to the renter, says 'I therefore cannot say from these documents alone which notice or VCAT application you should use', and never says the friend has no rights or can apply to VCAT to be added to the lease.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Vic), Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026' (link 97-109aa115), which is the version in force on 15 October 2026, and every rule it applies is cited to that version alone.

question: It is 1 November 2019. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?
answer:
**Version used:** *rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf*, Residential Tenancies Act 1997, dated 2 July 2019 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The filename gives the version as "v088". The text I retrieved doesn't print an "Authorised Version No." line. This is the version in force on 1 November 2019. *rta-1997-v089-2019-12-04.pdf* is dated 4 December 2019, so it came after your date and I haven't applied it [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **The retrieved text has no retaliation rule.** I found no provision in the retrieved parts of v088 that deals with a notice given in response to a repair request. I also found nothing in it about repair duties or urgent repairs, so the documents don't answer that part of your question.
- **A notice must fit a listed ground.** v088 sets out specific grounds on which a provider may give a notice to vacate, each with its own minimum notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Only a few grounds allow a same-day notice.** The termination date can be the day the notice is given or later for these three [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf):
  - serious damage caused intentionally or recklessly (s 91ZI)
  - endangering safety (s 91ZJ)
  - premises unfit for human habitation or destroyed or unsafe (s 91ZL)
- **Other grounds need at least 14 days.** Examples include threats and intimidation (s 91ZK), non-payment of rent (s 91ZM), and breach of a Tribunal order (s 91ZO) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Some grounds need at least 60 days.** These include repairs/renovation (s 91ZX), demolition (s 91ZY), business use (s 91ZZ), and occupation by the provider or family (s 91ZZA) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **The repairs ground has extra conditions (s 91ZX).** The provider must intend to repair, renovate or reconstruct. They must have obtained all necessary permits and consents. The work must be impossible to carry out properly unless you leave [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Documents may be required.** Several grounds carry a note referring to s 91ZZO, which sets out requirements for accompanying documentary evidence [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

## What you can check or ask

1. **Which ground does the notice cite?** Ask for the section number if it isn't stated.
2. **Does the termination date meet that ground's minimum?** A notice given on the same day as your repair follow-up with a short deadline is only consistent with the damage, danger or unfit-premises grounds. Other grounds need at least 14 or 60 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
3. **If it relies on s 91ZX (repairs),** ask for proof of the permits and consents, and for the reason the work can't be done while you stay [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
4. **Is the required documentary evidence attached** where s 91ZZO applies [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)?
5. **Does the stated ground match the facts?** For example, the notice may claim damage or unfitness while the real issue is leaking fixtures you reported.

## Gaps in the documents

- The retrieved part of v088 stops at s 91ZZB (premises to be sold). I can't say from these documents whether other grounds follow.
- I didn't find where in v088 a renter challenges a notice or what the Tribunal can do.
- The later Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 forms say a renter may challenge a notice at VCAT if they believe it was given because they "tried to exercise your rights as a renter" [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)[[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)[[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Those regulations are dated 2022 or later, so they weren't in force on 1 November 2019. They don't show what the law said on that date.

Because the retrieved v088 text doesn't address retaliation, I can't confirm what protection applied to you on 1 November 2019. The documents are silent on that point. Consider getting advice quickly from a community legal service or Consumer Affairs Victoria.
