question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
## What the law says

I used the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf". It is Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). That was the current version on 15 October 2026.

- **No unreasonable refusal.** A residential rental provider "must not unreasonably refuse to consent" to a renter keeping a pet [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 71C(1)).
- **A "no" from the agent is not enough.** The provider is taken to have consented unless, within 14 days after being given the request, they apply to the Tribunal (VCAT) under s 71D [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 71C(2)). A note to s 71A says the same [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Your timing.** You sent the request three weeks ago, which is 21 days. If no Tribunal application was made within 14 days, the law treats the owner as having consented. This is true even though the agent said no.
- **Only the Tribunal can confirm a refusal.** The provider can apply for an order that refusing consent is reasonable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 71D(1)). The Tribunal can make that order only if it is satisfied the refusal is reasonable. Otherwise it can order that you may keep the pet [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 71E(1)).
- **Factors the Tribunal may consider.** These are the type of pet, the character and nature of the premises, the appliances, fixtures and fittings, whether refusal is permitted under any Act, any prescribed matters, and any other relevant matter [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 71E(2)).

## What you can do

1. **Find out whether a VCAT application was made.** Ask the agent and owner in writing whether they applied to VCAT within 14 days of receiving your request. If they didn't, you can tell them in writing that consent is taken to have been given under s 71C(2) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Check the request itself.** The Act requires the request to be made in the Director's approved form and "given to the residential rental provider" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 71B). You gave it to the agent. The text I retrieved doesn't say whether that counts as giving it to the provider, so I can't confirm it.
3. **If the owner does apply to VCAT,** you can argue the refusal is unreasonable. The Tribunal decides this using the s 71E(2) factors [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What the documents don't answer

- They don't say whether an owner's allergy, or the owner rarely visiting, makes a refusal reasonable. That is for the Tribunal to decide.
- They don't set out a step-by-step process for a renter to enforce deemed consent.
- The contents page lists s 91ZZG, "Notice to vacate when pet kept without consent" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). I didn't retrieve its text, so I can't say what it requires.

For next steps, VCAT or Consumer Affairs Victoria could advise you. I haven't retrieved anything from them.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. The output says the provider 'is taken to have consented unless, within 14 days after being given the request, they apply to the Tribunal (VCAT)'. It applies this to the user's timing: 'You sent the request three weeks ago, which is 21 days. If no Tribunal application was made within 14 days, the law treats the owner as having consented.' It gives the next step: 'Ask the agent and owner in writing whether they applied to VCAT within 14 days of receiving your request.' The caveat about whether giving the form to the agent counts as giving it to the provider is extra material and does not make the answer unclear.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. None of the failing claims is made: the answer rejects the agent's refusal ("A 'no' from the agent is not enough"), treats a VCAT application as the provider's step, not the renter's ("they apply to the Tribunal (VCAT) under s 71D"; "If the owner does apply to VCAT, you can argue"), and leaves the allergy open ("They don't say whether an owner's allergy... makes a refusal reasonable. That is for the Tribunal to decide").

version-cited.reason: Yes — the answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as 'Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026' (file rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf, link 97-109aa115), which is the version in force on 15 October 2026, and every rule it applies (ss 71A–71E) comes from that version.

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
**Version used:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf", dated 6 August 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The file name indicates version 110. The excerpt doesn't print the words "Authorised Version No.", so I'm relying on the file name. This was the latest retrieved version before 1 October 2025. The next one, v111, is dated 25 November 2025 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **The notice stays in force until a withdrawal is signed.** A notice to vacate is withdrawn "only if a notice of withdrawal is given" (s 91ZZQ). The withdrawal must be in writing and signed by the person who gave the notice (your landlord) and by the person who received it (you) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The buyer pulling out doesn't withdraw it. The documents I retrieved say nothing about a sale-based notice lapsing automatically when the sale falls through.
- **A sale notice can rest on an intended sale, not only a signed contract.** A landlord may give a notice if the premises are, immediately after the termination date, "to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession" (s 91ZZB(1)). If there is a contract of sale, the notice must be given within 14 days after the last condition is satisfied, or within 14 days after the contract is entered into (s 91ZZB(2)–(3)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). So a collapsed sale doesn't automatically make the notice invalid. The landlord could say they still intend to offer the property for sale.
- **Notice period (in force on 1 Oct 2025):** the termination date must be at least 60 days after the notice was given (s 91ZZB(4)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The later version, v111, raises this to 90 days, but that is dated after 1 October 2025 and doesn't apply to your question [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Validity requirements (s 91ZZO).** The notice is not valid unless all of these are true [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf):
  - It is in the prescribed form.
  - It is addressed to you and signed.
  - It states the reason.
  - It comes with supporting documentary evidence.
  - It specifies the termination date.
- **Fixed-term agreements.** A sale notice has no effect if its termination date is earlier than the end of your fixed term, subject to any early-termination clause in your agreement (s 91ZZI(1)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Re-letting restriction.** A landlord who gets possession after a sale notice (ss 91ZY–91ZZB) must not re-let the premises as a residence for 6 months after the notice date. The penalty is 150 penalty units for an individual or 750 for a company. Exceptions apply if the Tribunal allows the letting, or if it is let to the family members listed in s 91ZZA (s 91ZZH) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

1. **Ask the landlord for a written notice of withdrawal.** It must be signed by both of you (s 91ZZQ) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Don't treat a verbal or informal assurance as enough.
2. **Check the notice itself** against the s 91ZZO requirements, the 60-day minimum, and the fixed-term rule above [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
3. **Apply to the Tribunal to challenge validity.** You can do this on or before the hearing of a possession order application, but it must be made within 30 days after the notice was given (s 91ZZS). The Tribunal decides whether the notice is valid (s 91ZZT) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). If your 30 days have passed, the documents don't say whether you can still apply.
4. **Ask why the notice still stands.** You can ask the landlord to confirm whether they still intend to sell or offer the property for sale with vacant possession. That is the basis for a s 91ZZB notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

## Limits of these documents

The excerpts don't set out the steps by which a landlord must get a possession order before you can be required to leave. They mention possession orders only in passing [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). They also don't state whether you must leave on the termination date if the notice is still in effect. Please confirm that with the Tribunal or a tenancy advice service. This isn't legal advice.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered. The hardest one, that the answer depends on the ground and its evidence, is met by 'A sale notice can rest on an intended sale, not only a signed contract... So a collapsed sale doesn't automatically make the notice invalid', together with the requirements for a stated reason and supporting documentary evidence. The 60-day minimum, the written withdrawal signed by both parties (s 91ZZQ), and the next steps (seek a signed withdrawal or apply to the Tribunal within 30 days) are all stated.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer asserts none of the failure conditions, since it says "The buyer pulling out doesn't withdraw it", requires the withdrawal to be "signed by the person who gave the notice (your landlord) and by the person who received it (you)", and gives the period as "at least 60 days", mentioning 90 days only to say it "is dated after 1 October 2025 and doesn't apply to your question."

version-cited.reason: Yes: the answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as "rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf", dated 6 August 2025, with link 97-109aa110, and takes every rule it applies (ss 91ZZB, 91ZZO, 91ZZQ, 91ZZI(1), 91ZZS–91ZZT) from that in-force version; it mentions v111 only to say the 90-day period comes later and doesn't apply, so deleting that mention would not change the substance.

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
**What the law says (as at 1 October 2025)**

I've used the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf" (version 110, dated 6 August 2025). It was the latest version retrieved dated on or before 1 October 2025. The next one retrieved, v111, is dated 25 November 2025. The excerpt doesn't print the words "Authorised Version No.", so the number 110 comes from the file name.

- A rental provider must give the renter at least 60 days' notice, in the prescribed form, of a proposed rent increase [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- The notice must state the amount of the increase, how it was calculated, and the renter's right to ask the Director of Consumer Affairs to investigate within 30 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- A rent increase that breaks these rules is invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- The prescribed form is Form 5. In the Regulations version dated 1 July 2025 ("rt-regs-2021-v004-2025-07-01.pdf"), it says "a valid notice of a proposed rent increase is required for all rent increases" and that 60 days' notice is required [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- Form 5 allows delivery by email only if the renter has consented [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

**Your situation**

- **Do you have to pay the higher rent?** On these documents, no. An email from your agent that isn't a Form 5 notice does not meet the Act's requirements, so the increase is invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). Keep paying your current rent. Whether your email counts depends on whether it was actually a Form 5 notice with the required contents. You describe it as unofficial, so I've assumed it wasn't.
- **From when?** There is no date from which you must pay the higher rent until a valid notice is given. If the rental provider gives a valid Form 5 notice, the increase can take effect only after at least 60 days' notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The notice states the start date [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say how those days are counted when a notice is emailed.
- **Other limits:** Rent can't be increased at intervals of less than 12 months. Under a fixed-term agreement, rent can't go up before the term ends unless the agreement provides for it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do**

1. Ask the agent in writing for a valid Form 5 notice, and say you haven't received one.
2. If a valid notice arrives and you think the rent is excessive, apply in writing to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria within 30 days after the notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). After the Director's report you can apply to VCAT within 30 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
3. You can apply to VCAT without a report only with VCAT's leave, and only after the 30 days have passed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Form 5 says you must pay the increased rent from the date on the notice unless VCAT decides otherwise [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

**Limits of these documents**

- A later Regulations version dated 25 November 2025 ("rt-regs-2021-v005-2025-11-25.pdf") shows Form 5 requiring 90 days' notice [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). That postdates 1 October 2025, so it doesn't apply to your date.
- The documents don't say whether you could recover extra rent you've already paid. I haven't guessed.

must-mention.reason: Yes. Every point is covered: the answer says the prescribed form is Form 5 and requires at least 60 days' notice. For the hardest point, it states 'On these documents, no. An email from your agent that isn't a Form 5 notice does not meet the Act's requirements, so the increase is invalid.' It also gives next steps: 'Keep paying your current rent' and ask the agent in writing for a valid Form 5 notice.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: none of the failure conditions are asserted. The answer says "On these documents, no... Keep paying your current rent," gives 60 days' notice for this date, mentions the 90-day period only to say "it doesn't apply to your date," and states that "Form 5 allows delivery by email only if the renter has consented."

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names both required documents with their in-force versions: the Act as "version 110, dated 6 August 2025" ("rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf") and the Regulations as "rt-regs-2021-v004-2025-07-01.pdf" ("dated 1 July 2025"). It mentions the later v005 ("rt-regs-2021-v005-2025-11-25.pdf") only to say it postdates 1 October 2025 and does not apply, so it does not rely on any version that was not in force.

question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:
## What the law says

- **Damage and notice.** A renter and any visitor must not intentionally or negligently damage the rented premises. A renter who becomes aware of damage must give the rental provider written notice "as soon as practicable" of the damage and what it is. Those two rules are s 61 and s 62 in the 2022 text I retrieved (*rta-1997-v101-2022-09-07.pdf*, 7 Sept 2022) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The current version's extract refers to the s 61 duty not to damage [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), but it doesn't reproduce s 61 or s 62. The 2026 regulations' summary of renters' obligations also says the renter must avoid damaging the premises and, where damage occurs, notify the rental provider in writing [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Who does the repair.** The 2026 regulations say "Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs—both urgent and non-urgent" [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). If you hire someone, they should be properly qualified.
- **The owner's process for damage.** The owner can give you a written repair notice. It can require you to repair the damage at your expense within 14 days. If you don't repair it "in a proper and tradesman-like manner", the owner may repair it at your expense. Alternatively, the notice can say the owner is doing the repairs and you are liable for the reasonable cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Paying the owner back.** If you are liable, you must reimburse the reasonable costs within 14 days after the repairs are completed, once the owner gives you the cost particulars in writing [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You can apply to the Tribunal for more time, or give written notice of hardship to get an extra 14 days (you must provide proof of hardship if asked) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Pets.** The regulations say a renter must seek the rental provider's consent before keeping a pet [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Check whether your dog was approved.

## Can you just get it fixed without telling the owner?

The documents don't expressly say "you may not arrange a private repair". But a silent fix doesn't fit the framework above. The duty is to notify the owner in writing, and the repair-notice process puts the owner in control of how damage is repaired and costed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The owner may also be entitled to enter on 24 hours' notice if they reasonably believe you have breached your duties [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A hidden or poor repair could therefore be discovered.

Practical steps:
1. Notify the owner or agent in writing now, with photos.
2. Offer to have a suitably qualified tradesperson fix it before you leave, and ask for their agreement. This is my suggestion, not a procedure set out in the documents.
3. Keep the invoice and photos.

At the end of the tenancy, the final inspection and condition report must be done within 10 days after the end date. Fair wear and tear doesn't count as damage you caused [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## Insurance

The retrieved documents don't address whether repairs or damage affect the owner's insurance, so I can't answer that. You would need to check the owner's policy or ask the owner or agent.

## Version note

The in-force Act on 15 October 2026 is *rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf* (13 Oct 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The filename suggests "v115", but the extract doesn't state an Authorised Version number. The regulations in force are *rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf* (30 June 2026) [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). I haven't relied on the older *rt-regs-2021-v005-2025-11-25.pdf* [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Where I cite the 2022 Act for s 61 and s 62, the current extract doesn't contain that text, so check the current wording.

must-mention.reason: No. The answer never says the renter must leave the home in the same condition, and it only implies rather than states responsibility for the dog's damage. It covers the written-notice duty ('as soon as practicable'), the insurance gap ('The retrieved documents don't address whether repairs or damage affect the owner's insurance') and next steps ('Notify the owner or agent in writing now'). On the second point it does say the renter must not damage the premises, may be liable for repair costs, and that 'Fair wear and tear doesn't count as damage you caused', but 'If you are liable' is conditional and the leave-in-same-condition obligation is absent.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer never endorses a quiet repair ("a silent fix doesn't fit the framework above... Notify the owner or agent in writing now"), states no insurance outcome as fact ("The retrieved documents don't address whether repairs or damage affect the owner's insurance, so I can't answer that"), and never says the renter must pay the owner's insurance excess.

version-cited.reason: No. The answer names Act v115 ('rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf', 97-109aa115) and Regulations v009 ('rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf', 21-3sra009), but it applies s 61 and s 62 as the law using text from the superseded 2022 version ('rta-1997-v101-2022-09-07.pdf', 97-109aa101). This includes the 'as soon as practicable' written-notice duty, and the caveat to 'check the current wording' does not stop that from counting as reliance on a version not in force on 15 October 2026.

question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
## What the law says

I've used the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, file **rt-regs-2021-v002-2022-06-01.pdf** (dated 1 June 2022). It was the latest version retrieved that predates 1 March 2023. The file name shows "v002", but the excerpts I retrieved don't print the words "Authorised Version No." I can't confirm the number from the text itself.

- **No rule on the number of circuits.** Nothing in the retrieved text says how many circuits a rental must have or how power points must be split between them. Nothing addresses a breaker tripping under combined kettle and heater load.
- **The electrical safety standard starts after your date.** Schedule 4, clause 9 says that "on and from 29 March 2023" all power outlets and lighting circuits must be connected to a switchboard-type circuit breaker complying with AS/NZS 3000. They must also be connected to a switchboard-type residual current device (RCD) that meets one of the listed standards [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). On 1 March 2023 that requirement was not yet in force.
- **That standard is about protection devices, not capacity.** It covers breakers and RCDs, not how many circuits there are.
- **A residual current device is a prescribed safety device** under regulation 25 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

## What you can ask for

- **Electrical safety check records.** Your rental provider must keep records of electrical safety checks. These include the electrician's name and licence number, the date, the results, any repairs and actions taken, and an AS/NZS 3019 report. They must give you a copy of the most recent check within 7 days of your written request [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Asking for it would show whether the wiring and switchboard have been assessed.
- **A 2-yearly electrical check.** The duty to have a licensed or registered electrician check the electrical installations every 2 years, and to arrange a check if none has been done in the last 2 years, appears in Schedule 3 of the later version **rt-regs-2021-v005-2025-11-25.pdf** (25 November 2025) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). The 2022 excerpts I retrieved don't show that text, so I can't confirm it was in force on 1 March 2023.
- **From 29 March 2023.** You could then ask that the circuits comply with the breaker and RCD standard in Schedule 4, clause 9 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

## What the documents don't cover

- The Residential Tenancies Act 1997 wasn't retrieved. It would contain the repair and urgent repair rules and the VCAT process, which I can't describe from these documents.
- The retrieved text doesn't show whether a tripping breaker counts as a fault or urgent repair.
- A later standard-form summary (dated 1 July 2025) says rental providers must keep premises in good repair and carry out non-urgent repairs in a reasonable time [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). I can't confirm that applied on 1 March 2023.

For the circuit problem itself, the documents give you no specific right to extra circuits. The practical step is to ask in writing for the electrical safety check record and for an electrician to look at the overload.

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both points are covered. The answer says 'No rule on the number of circuits. Nothing in the retrieved text says how many circuits a rental must have.' For the harder next-step point, it says 'ask in writing for the electrical safety check record and for an electrician to look at the overload,' which covers asking about the last electrical safety check and amounts to requesting a repair.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer states no minimum and says the breaker/RCD standard was not yet in force, quoting "Nothing in the retrieved text says how many circuits a rental must have" and "On 1 March 2023 that requirement was not yet in force."

version-cited.reason: No. The answer names the Regulations' in-force version ('rt-regs-2021-v002-2022-06-01.pdf (dated 1 June 2022)'), but it never names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 Authorised Version No. 101, saying only 'The Residential Tenancies Act 1997 wasn't retrieved.' It also presents the 2-yearly electrical check from the later 'rt-regs-2021-v005-2025-11-25.pdf' under 'What you can ask for', which counts as relying on a version not in force on 1 March 2023 despite the caveat.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents I retrieved don't say whether a rooming house operator can or can't charge for coin-operated washing machines. They set out rules for any charge for services. They also set a laundry standard that doesn't mention fees.

**Source used:** I used *rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf* (Residential Tenancies Act 1997), dated 13 October 2026. It is the latest version I found, so it is the one in force on 15 October 2026. The file name indicates version 115. The text I retrieved doesn't print the words "Authorised Version No.", so I can't confirm that number from the content.

## What the law says

- **Charging for services generally (s 109):** If an operator charges an amount for services, they must give you a separate schedule of the amounts for those services before you take up the room. If you use a service, they must also give you an itemised account showing your individual use. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- **Utility charges outside rent (s 108):** An operator may charge for electricity, gas and water used in a room only if the operator pays for them and the room is separately metered. This doesn't apply to a shared room. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) It covers use in your own room and doesn't mention shared laundry machines.
- **Public and community housing (s 109A):** Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency may impose a service charge for "laundry… services or facilities". This applies only to a rooming house declared under section 19(2) or (3). It applies only if it isn't possible or practicable to accurately measure your use. The charge must not exceed the cost of providing the facility to you. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
  - They must give you written notice when they impose or change the charge. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
  - You can apply to the Tribunal to have the charge withdrawn or varied. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- **Laundry standard:** From 26 February 2024, a rooming house must have a washing machine in good working order for every 12 or fewer residents, plus a wash trough and a clothes line or other drying facility. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf) Two machines would meet this for up to 24 residents. The standard says nothing about fees.
  - The version I found is *rt-rooming-house-standards-regs-2023-v002-2024-12-01.pdf*, dated 1 December 2024. I can't confirm it was still the current version on 15 October 2026.

## What you can do or ask

1. **Ask your operator for the schedule of services and amounts** that you should have received before moving in (s 109(a)). If they haven't given you one, that is worth raising. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
2. **Ask for an itemised account of your own use** of the machines (s 109(b)). [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
3. **Find out who your operator is.** If it is Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency, ask for the written notice of the laundry charge. Check that it doesn't exceed the cost of providing the service. If you disagree, you can apply to the Tribunal to withdraw or vary it. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
4. **Check the number of machines.** Two machines is enough for up to 24 residents under the standard I found, so a shortfall is unlikely to be the issue. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf)

The retrieved documents don't answer whether a private operator can lawfully use coins to recover laundry costs, or how s 109A's "not practicable to measure" test applies to a coin meter. For a firm answer on your situation, you would need advice from a tenancy advice service or the Tribunal.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered. The hardest one, that the law doesn't say the machines must be free, is met by 'The documents I retrieved don't say whether a rooming house operator can or can't charge for coin-operated washing machines' and 'The standard says nothing about fees.' The answer also states the one-machine-per-12-residents standard, the s 109 schedule given 'before you take up the room', and the next step 'Ask your operator for the schedule of services and amounts.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes. None of the three is asserted: the answer says the documents 'set out rules for any charge for services' (s 109), never says the machines must be free, and limits the cost cap to public and community housing ('Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency... applies only to a rooming house declared under section 19(2) or (3)... must not exceed the cost of providing the facility').

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as 'rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf' (version 115, dated 13 October 2026) and the Rooming House Standards Regulations 2023 as 'rt-rooming-house-standards-regs-2023-v002-2024-12-01.pdf' (link 23-10sra002, version 002), and every rule it applies comes from these in-force versions.

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents I retrieved don't let me say for certain that the advertising rule was in force on 1 October 2025. A photo that looks like mould also doesn't prove the place fails the standard.

## What the law says

**Version caveat.** For 1 October 2025, the Regulations version in force appears to be *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, v004 (file dated 1 July 2025) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). The next version, v005, is dated 25 November 2025 [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). The file names give the version numbers. I didn't see an "Authorised Version" number printed in the extracts. For the Act, the retrieved versions are *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* v098 (29 March 2021) [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa098%20authorised.pdf), v111 (25 November 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) and v115 (13 October 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). None is dated in force on 1 October 2025. I haven't relied on v115 because it is dated after your question date.

**Advertising.**
- The advertising rule is s 65B. It says a provider or agent must not advertise or offer premises to let unless they reasonably believe the premises comply with the rental minimum standards at that time [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The penalty is 60 penalty units for a natural person and 300 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- s 65B is marked as inserted by No. 6/2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). It is absent from v098 [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa098%20authorised.pdf). It first appears in the retrieved v111, dated after your date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- The documents don't give its start date. I therefore can't confirm it applied on 1 October 2025, and I won't assume it did.
- If s 65B was in force, the test is the provider's or agent's *reasonable belief*. An ad showing apparent mould would make that belief hard to defend, but the retrieved text doesn't say so directly.

**The mould standard.**
- Schedule 4, clause 8 of the Regulations (v004) says each room must be "free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- Section 65A requires providers to meet the prescribed minimum standards by the day the renter moves in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**Is the photo enough?** The documents don't say what evidence is needed. They do show the standard is narrower than "any mould". It covers mould and damp *caused by or related to the building structure* [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). A photo can show visible mould. It doesn't show the cause. The retrieved documents say nothing about how a Tribunal would weigh photos.

## What the renter can do or ask

- **Ask for disclosure.** Regulation 16(2) lists information a provider must disclose to a rental applicant. It includes whether the premises comply with the rental minimum standards. It also includes whether the provider has received a repair notice in the last 3 years about mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Request urgent repairs after moving in.** If the premises don't meet the standards on or immediately after the day the renter moves in, the renter may issue a request for urgent repairs to bring them into compliance (s 65A(2)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **General duty to maintain.** The provider must keep the premises in good repair and in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation (s 68(1)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Records.** The later versions (v111, v115) require providers and agents to keep records showing compliance for advertised premises, and to produce them if the Director asks [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). That is a duty owed to the Director. It isn't a right of the renter. I also can't confirm it was in force on 1 October 2025.

**Not covered:** The retrieved documents don't cover how to complain about an ad, Tribunal remedies, or what evidence proves a breach.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered: the output quotes the standard that rooms be 'free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure', says 'A photo can show visible mould. It doesn't show the cause' (the hardest point), and gives next steps such as asking for disclosure under reg 16(2) and requesting urgent repairs after moving in under s 65A(2).

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer says neither forbidden thing. It does not claim the photo proves illegality ('A photo can show visible mould. It doesn't show the cause.'), and it does not assert the advertising ban applied on 1 October 2025 ('I therefore can't confirm it applied on 1 October 2025, and I won't assume it did').

version-cited.reason: No. The answer never names the in-force Act version (Authorised Version No. 110, dated 6 August 2025). Instead it relies on v111 ('97-109aa111', dated 25 November 2025) for rules it applies to the user, including s 65A, s 65B, s 68 and the urgent-repairs step. Deleting that material would change the answer's substance. It does correctly cite Regulations v004 ('21-3sra004').

question: It is 15 October 2026. I let a friend move into my rental without telling the agent. Now I want them out. What do I have to do?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved documents don't say how a renter removes a friend who has moved in. They do explain why the arrangement is a problem and what you can ask the rental provider for.

## What the law says
The current version is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", dated 13 October 2026. That is the version in force on 15 October 2026. The file name shows version 115, but the excerpt doesn't print an "Authorised Version No." in its text.

- A renter must not assign or sub-let the whole or any part of the rented premises without the rental provider's written consent (s 81(1)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- An assignment or sub-letting without that consent is invalid, unless the Tribunal has determined that consent is not required (s 81(3)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The retrieved text doesn't say whether a friend who moves in, perhaps without paying rent, counts as "sub-letting". It also doesn't cover a renter simply having a guest or other occupant.

## What you can do or ask
1. **Tell the agent.** The documents don't say you must, but the consent rule above is the reason to. If you want your friend to stay, you can ask for written consent. The rental provider must not unreasonably withhold it (s 81(2)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Don't pay a consent fee.** The rental provider can't demand or receive a fee for giving consent (s 84(1)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Apply to the Tribunal if consent is refused.** If consent is withheld and you think that is unreasonable, you can ask the Tribunal to determine that consent isn't required (s 82) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What the documents don't cover
- **How to make your friend leave.** The current Act excerpt has no step-by-step process for a renter removing an occupant. I can't tell you whether you need a notice, what period it must give, or whether you'd need the Tribunal.
- **Consequences for you.** The current version I retrieved doesn't include the termination provisions. An older, superseded version (rta-1997-v089, 4 December 2019) let a landlord give a tenant a notice to vacate, with at least 14 days' notice, for sub-letting without consent (s 253) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf). I can't confirm that the same rule applies in the 13 October 2026 version, so please don't rely on it as current.
- **Forcing someone out.** The Regulations' notice to vacate form (rt-regs-2021 v009, 30 June 2026) is for rental providers giving notice to renters. It states that rental providers can't personally use force to remove a renter, and that only Victoria Police can carry out a forcible eviction, and only on a VCAT order [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). It doesn't address a renter removing a friend, so I wouldn't treat it as a guide for your situation.

For the removal process, check the current termination provisions of the Act or contact Consumer Affairs Victoria (the form refers to 1300 558 181) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both points are covered: the answer says sub-letting requires 'the rental provider's written consent (s 81(1))', and it ties the outcome to the arrangement by naming payment as a deciding fact, saying the documents don't settle 'whether a friend who moves in, perhaps without paying rent, counts as "sub-letting"' as opposed to 'simply having a guest or other occupant'.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: none of the failure conditions is asserted. The answer says "I can't tell you whether you need a notice, what period it must give, or whether you'd need the Tribunal." The only notice period it mentions (14 days, s 253) comes from a superseded 2019 version and concerns a landlord's notice to a tenant, and the answer says "please don't rely on it as current." It never says the renter can lock the friend out or remove their belongings, that the friend has no rights, or that the friend can apply to VCAT to be added to the lease.

version-cited.reason: No. The answer names the Act's in-force version ('rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf', dated 13 October 2026, link 97-109aa115), but it also relies on a superseded version: under 'Consequences for you' it presents the rule from 'rta-1997-v089, 4 December 2019' (s 253, notice to vacate with at least 14 days' notice for sub-letting without consent) as a likely consequence for the user, and deleting that content would change the answer's substance despite the caveat.

question: It is 1 November 2019. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?
answer:
**Version used:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (file "rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf", version 088, dated 2 July 2019) [[10]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The next version I found is v089, dated 4 December 2019 [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf). That is after 1 November 2019, so I treated v088 as the version in force on your date. I inferred this from the file dates. The documents don't state commencement dates.

## What the law says

- **Notice with no reason.** A landlord may give a notice to vacate without giving a reason (s 263(1)). For a periodic tenancy the termination date must be at least 120 days after the notice is given, unless a different period is prescribed (s 263(2)) [[10]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Retaliation protection.** A notice under s 261 or s 263 is of no effect if it was given in response to the tenant exercising, or proposing to exercise, a right under the Act (s 266(2)) [[10]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Time limit to challenge.** For a s 263 notice, you can't apply to the Tribunal to challenge its validity after 60 days from the date it was given (s 266(3)(c)) [[10]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). From 1 November 2019, that points to about 31 December 2019. Please confirm the exact day.

## What to check

1. **Which section the notice relies on.** The retaliation protection in v088 names only ss 261 and 263 [[10]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). If your notice cites another ground, such as rent arrears or damage, the text I retrieved doesn't say s 266(2) applies. Those grounds have their own requirements [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf).
2. **The timing.** A notice given the same day you followed up repairs is the kind of link to point to when arguing it was "in response to" your request. The documents don't say what evidence the Tribunal requires.
3. **Whether the repairs request was a "right under this Act".** I didn't retrieve the repairs provisions, so I can't confirm that from these documents.
4. **The termination date.** For a periodic tenancy, check that it is at least 120 days after 1 November 2019 [[10]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
5. **The notice's form.** The form requirements (prescribed form, signature, reasons, termination date) appear in a later version, v090, dated 2 March 2020 (s 319) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf). The v088 text I retrieved doesn't include them, so I can't confirm what applied on 1 November 2019.

## What you can do or ask

- **Apply to the Tribunal within the 60-day limit** to challenge the notice as of no effect under s 266(2) [[10]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The retrieved v088 text doesn't set out the application steps.
- **If you stay, expect a possession application.** The landlord would have to apply to the Tribunal, which must be satisfied the landlord was entitled to give the notice. That wording comes from v089, a later document, so I can't confirm it for 1 November 2019 [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf).
- **Get advice quickly.** The 60-day limit is short. The later notice form (v090) also tells renters to seek advice, including from community legal organisations [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf).

The documents I retrieved don't answer how repairs requests work, what evidence proves retaliation, or the exact Tribunal procedure.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered: s 263 allows a no-reason notice with at least 120 days for a periodic tenancy; s 266(2) makes it of no effect if given 'in response to the tenant exercising, or proposing to exercise, a right under the Act'; and the answer says to 'Apply to the Tribunal within the 60-day limit'. The hardest point is retaliation: the answer hedges only on whether a repairs request counts as a right, and the core rule is still clearly stated.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer says "A landlord may give a notice to vacate without giving a reason (s 263(1))" and gives only a 60-day deadline: "you can't apply to the Tribunal to challenge its validity after 60 days from the date it was given (s 266(3)(c))". Its mention of "reasons" among the form requirements is tied to the later v090 version, and it says it cannot confirm these applied on 1 November 2019.

version-cited.reason: No. The answer names the in-force version ("rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf, version 088, dated 2 July 2019"), but it also relies on later versions. It presents v089's rule that the landlord must apply to the Tribunal for possession and the Tribunal must be satisfied the landlord was entitled to give the notice ("If you stay, expect a possession application"). It also lists v090's s 319 form requirements as item 5 under "What to check". Both are offered as law or steps despite caveats, and deleting them would change the answer's substance.

question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?
answer:
## What the law said on 1 October 2025

The version in force on that date was *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 110 (file "rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf", dated 6 August 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The next version in the documents is v111 (dated 25 November 2025) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). It was not in force on 1 October 2025.

- **Rent must be a fixed amount.** A rental provider or agent must not advertise or offer premises unless the rent is advertised or offered as a fixed amount [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **No inviting higher offers.** They "must not solicit or otherwise invite an offer of an amount of rent that is higher than the advertised amount." The penalty is 60 penalty units for a natural person and 300 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Accepting unsolicited higher offers is not in v110.** A separate rule against *accepting* an unsolicited or uninvited higher offer (s 30F(4)) appears only in v111 (25 November 2025) and later versions [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). I can't say it applied on 1 October 2025. v110's text of s 30F stops at subsection (3) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Misleading conduct and rent.** A rental provider or agent must not induce someone to enter an agreement by misleading or deceptive conduct, including false or misleading representations about the rent payable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). They also must not make a false or misleading representation about the rent when advertising [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**What this means for you.** "Someone else offered more" is only unlawful if the agent or provider *solicited or invited* that higher offer. Under v110, simply accepting an offer nobody asked for is not covered. The documents also don't address a false "withdrawn" email or a relisting at a higher rent. Raising the advertised rent is not prohibited in the text I retrieved. The email might support a misleading-conduct argument, but only if it was used to induce you or someone else to enter an agreement.

## What you can do

- **Ask the agent in writing** to explain the "withdrawn" email and say whether higher offers were invited. Ask them to confirm your application was at the advertised rent.
- **Raise a possible breach of s 30F(3).** This applies if there is evidence the agent or provider asked for or encouraged higher offers.
- **Apply to the Tribunal.** The Act says the Tribunal can make orders on an application about a contravention of s 30E (misleading or deceptive conduct) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The retrieved text doesn't say what orders the Tribunal can make for a s 30F breach, so I can't confirm a remedy there.
- **Report to the Director.** The Act, as set out in v111, lets the Director require a provider or agent to substantiate claims made about rented premises [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). It also lets the Minister or Director publish public warnings about conduct contrary to the Act [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). I only have these provisions in v111, not v110.

The documents don't cover other steps, such as contacting Consumer Affairs Victoria or the application process, so I can't advise on those.

## What to save as evidence

The documents don't list evidence. These suggestions are practical and tied to what you would need to show:

- **The original advertisement**, with the advertised rent, date and URL, as screenshots.
- **The current listing** at the higher rent, with date-stamped screenshots.
- **Your application and confirmation**, showing the rent you applied at and the date.
- **The "withdrawn" email**, with full headers and timestamps, and any replies or calls disputing it.
- **Any message from the agent** that mentions other offers, "best offers", or asks for higher rent.
- **Whatever shows where you heard about the higher offer**, such as the name and a written statement from the person.
- **A timeline** of dates, names and what was said.

If you need advice on remedies, speak to a tenancy advocate or legal service. The retrieved documents don't settle whether your situation is a breach.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered. The hardest one, the unsolicited higher offer, is settled by "Under v110, simply accepting an offer nobody asked for is not covered." The other three are covered by: "must not solicit or otherwise invite an offer of an amount of rent that is higher than the advertised amount"; "Raising the advertised rent is not prohibited in the text I retrieved"; and "The documents also don't address a false 'withdrawn' email."

must-not-say.reason: Yes. None of the three claims is made: the answer says "Raising the advertised rent is not prohibited in the text I retrieved" and "Under v110, simply accepting an offer nobody asked for is not covered," and it never says the applicant can force the agent to rent the property to them.

version-cited.reason: No: the answer names 'Authorised Version No. 110' (dated 6 August 2025), but its 'Report to the Director' step relies on provisions it sources only from v111 (25 November 2025), which was not in force on 1 October 2025, and removing that step would change the answer's substance.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
## What the law says

I used the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115** (file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf"). It incorporates amendments as at 13 October 2026, so it was in force on 15 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

- **Request form:** A renter must ask for consent to keep a pet in the form approved by the Director, and must give the request to the residential rental provider (s 71B) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **No unreasonable refusal:** A provider "must not unreasonably refuse to consent" to a pet (s 71C(1)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **The 14-day rule:** The provider is taken to have consented unless, within 14 days after being given the request, they apply to the Tribunal (s 71C(2)). A refusal alone does not stop this [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Only the Tribunal can make a refusal stick:** The provider can apply for an order that refusing consent is reasonable (s 71D(1)). The Tribunal can only make that order if it is satisfied the refusal is reasonable (s 71E(1)(b)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **What the Tribunal considers:** It may consider the type of pet, the character and nature of the premises, the appliances, fixtures and fittings, and "any other matter the Tribunal considers relevant" (s 71E(2)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Applying it to you

- **Timing:** You sent the request three weeks ago, which is 21 days. That is past the 14-day window. If neither the owner nor the agent applied to the Tribunal within 14 days of receiving your request, the owner is taken to have consented under s 71C(2), whatever the agent said [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Allergy:** The Act does not list an owner's allergy, or how rarely they visit, as a ground for refusal. Whether it would be a reasonable ground is for the Tribunal, under the open-ended "any other matter" factor [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say how the Tribunal would decide that, so I can't predict it.

## What you can do

1. **Check whether a Tribunal application was made.** Ask the agent in writing whether the owner applied to the Tribunal within 14 days of receiving your request. If not, you can point to s 71C(2) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Ask for written confirmation of consent.** Section 71A says you may keep a pet with the provider's written consent or a Tribunal order [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Act's note says the provider is taken to have consented when no application is made in time [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether deemed consent satisfies the "in writing" wording, so written confirmation is the safer route.
3. **Know the eviction protection.** An earlier version I retrieved (Authorised Version No. 110, 6 August 2025) says a notice to vacate for keeping a pet is only available after the Tribunal has made an order excluding the pet and 14 days have passed without the renter complying (s 91ZZG) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The No. 115 contents page lists s 91ZZG, but the retrieved text of the section is only from No. 110, so check it against No. 115 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Gaps in the documents

- They don't say whether giving the request to the **agent** counts as giving it to the provider. Section 71B(2) refers to the provider [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The 14-day clock may depend on that, so check the date the owner was actually given your request.
- They don't say whether a **renter** can apply to the Tribunal to force a decision. The pet applications in the Act are made by the provider (s 71D) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

This is general information from the retrieved text, not legal advice. Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenants' advice service could help you confirm the dates.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered, and the hardest one (point 2) is stated as: 'You sent the request three weeks ago, which is 21 days. That is past the 14-day window. If neither the owner nor the agent applied to the Tribunal within 14 days of receiving your request, the owner is taken to have consented under s 71C(2), whatever the agent said.' Point 1 is covered by s 71C(2) on deemed consent unless the provider applies to the Tribunal within 14 days, and point 3 by the step 'Ask the agent in writing whether the owner applied to the Tribunal within 14 days of receiving your request.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer says the opposite of each failure condition: the owner 'is taken to have consented under s 71C(2), whatever the agent said'; on the renter applying it says only that the documents 'don't say whether a renter can apply to the Tribunal'; and on the allergy it says 'Whether it would be a reasonable ground is for the Tribunal'.

version-cited.reason: No. The answer names the in-force 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115', but it also relies on 'Authorised Version No. 110, 6 August 2025' for the s 91ZZG eviction protection. It presents that rule as something the user should know and act on, with only a caveat to check it against No. 115. Deleting it would remove a substantive point from the advice.

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
**Short answer:** The buyer pulling out does not cancel the notice. Under the Act, a notice to vacate is withdrawn only by a signed written notice of withdrawal. The documents I found don't say what happens to a sale-based notice when the sale falls through.

## What the law says

**Version used.** The version in force on 1 October 2025 is *rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf* (Residential Tenancies Act 1997, file dated 6 August 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). I treat it as Version 110 because of its file name. The text I retrieved doesn't print the words "Authorised Version No." The retrieved text of that version also doesn't include the withdrawal, challenge or possession-order sections. For those I rely on the earlier and later versions below, so my conclusions on them are less certain.

**Sale notices (s 91ZZB, v110).**
- A landlord may give a notice to vacate if the premises are to be "sold or offered for sale with vacant possession" immediately after the termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- If there is a contract of sale, the notice must be given within 14 days after the contract is entered into, or within 14 days after the last condition is satisfied if the contract is conditional [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- The notice must give a termination date at least 60 days after it is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- Nothing in the retrieved text says the notice lapses if the buyer withdraws.

**Withdrawal (s 91ZZQ).**
- A notice to vacate is withdrawn "only if a notice of withdrawal is given" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa098%20authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- That notice must be in writing, signed by the person who gave the notice (the landlord), and signed by the person it was given to (you) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa098%20authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- This text is in the 2021 and 2022 versions, and the 2026 version repeats it [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The v110 excerpt cuts off before this section.
- Because the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice, it still stands.

**Do you have to leave?**
- The notice stays in place until it is properly withdrawn or found invalid.
- The landlord can still apply to the Tribunal for a possession order once they have given a notice to vacate [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa098%20authorised.pdf).
- The Tribunal can't decide that application before the termination date in the notice [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa098%20authorised.pdf).
- The Tribunal must make a possession order if it is satisfied of several things. These include that the landlord was entitled to give the notice, that the notice hasn't been withdrawn, that you are still in the premises after the termination date, and that an order is "reasonable and proportionate" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa098%20authorised.pdf).
- Those Part 7 provisions come from the March 2021 version. I did not retrieve them in v110.

## What you can do or ask

1. **Ask the landlord to sign a written notice of withdrawal.** You must sign it too [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa098%20authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
2. **Check the notice is valid.**
   - It must be in the prescribed form, signed, and state the reason, and it must give a termination date [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
   - A sale notice must also come with supporting documentary evidence [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
   - The termination date must be at least 60 days after the notice was given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
   - The notice must have been given within the 14-day windows above [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
3. **Challenge the notice at the Tribunal.**
   - You can apply on or before the possession-order hearing, and the application must be made within 30 days after the notice is given [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
   - The Tribunal can decide whether the notice is valid [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
   - These provisions are in the 2021 and 2022 versions, not the v110 excerpt.
4. **Argue "reasonable and proportionate" at any possession hearing.** The Tribunal must weigh the interests of both you and the landlord [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa098%20authorised.pdf).
5. **Know the 6-month letting restriction.** If the landlord gets possession under a sale notice, they must not re-let the premises as a residence within 6 months after the notice was given. Penalties apply, unless the Tribunal allows it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

## Caveats

- The later version, *rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf*, is dated after 1 October 2025, so I haven't applied it. It shows a 90-day minimum for sale notices (amended by Act No. 6/2025) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't show when that change took effect, so check which period applied to your notice's date.
- The documents don't say whether a landlord can rely on a sale notice after the sale collapses, or whether the Tribunal would treat the notice differently. Consider contacting Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy advocacy service for advice on your situation.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are present. The hardest one, that the outcome depends on the ground and its evidence, is covered: the answer separates notices for premises "to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession" from those where "there is a contract of sale" with its 14-day windows. It also says a sale notice "must also come with supporting documentary evidence" and tells the renter to check validity on these grounds. The answer also gives the 60-day minimum, says withdrawal must be "in writing, signed by the person who gave the notice (the landlord), and signed by the person it was given to (you)", and lists next steps: ask for a signed written withdrawal, or challenge at the Tribunal within 30 days.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer says the buyer pulling out "does not cancel the notice," that withdrawal needs a notice "signed by the person who gave the notice (the landlord), and signed by the person it was given to (you)," and that the termination date must be "at least 60 days after it is given"; it raises the 90-day minimum only as part of a later version it says "I haven't applied."

version-cited.reason: No. The answer names the in-force version ('rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf', link 97-109aa110), but it applies rules from versions not in force on 1 October 2025. Its core conclusion, that withdrawal requires a signed written notice (s 91ZZQ), comes from the 2021 and 2022 versions (97-109aa098, 97-109aa101). So do the possession-order and challenge steps it offers the user. Deleting that material would change the answer's substance, even though it carries caveats.

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
**Version applied:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf", Authorised Version 110, dated 6 August 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). It was the version in force on 1 October 2025. The next version I found (v111) is dated 25 November 2025, so it is later [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- A rental provider must give the renter **at least 60 days' notice, in the prescribed form**, of a proposed rent increase [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- The notice must state the amount of the increase, how it was calculated, and the renter's right to ask the Director to investigate within 30 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- A rent increase that contravenes section 44 is **invalid** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). An email or a refusal to negotiate is not a notice in the prescribed form.
- Other limits in section 44:
  - Rent cannot be increased at intervals of less than 12 months [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
  - Under a fixed-term agreement, rent cannot go up before the term ends unless the agreement allows it, either by a specified amount or by a specified calculation method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

## What this means for you

- **Do you have to pay the higher rent?** On what you describe, no. You have no official notice, so the documents give no basis for treating the increase as valid. I can't see the agent's email. If it did not comply with section 44, the increase is invalid.
- **From when?** The earliest an increase could apply is 60 days after a valid notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). If no valid notice has been given, there is no date yet. The documents don't say how the 60 days are counted, for example from sending or from receipt.
- **Version caveat:** The Form 5 text I found says 90 days' notice. It comes from regulations dated 25 November 2025 and later, which were not in force on 1 October 2025 [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)[[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). For the 1 October 2025 version of the Act, the documents show 60 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The regulations version in force on that date (the "rt-regs-2021-v004-2025-07-01.pdf" excerpt) did not show Form 5, so I can't confirm the prescribed form's wording for that date [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do

1. **Keep paying your current rent.** Ask the agent in writing for a formal notice of proposed rent increase.
2. **Check any notice you do receive** for:
   - the 60-day period
   - the amount and calculation method
   - the right to apply to the Director [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
   - whether it falls within 12 months of your last increase
   - whether it fits a fixed-term agreement, if you have one [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
3. **Challenge a valid notice if you think it is excessive.**
   - Apply in writing to the Director within 30 days after the notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
   - You can then apply to the Tribunal within 30 days after getting the Director's report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
   - Without a report, you need the Tribunal's leave, and you can only apply after the 30 days have passed. The Tribunal can grant leave if you had reasonable grounds for not asking the Director [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

The documents don't cover whether any rent you have already paid at the higher rate can be recovered, or how an email delivery would be treated on 1 October 2025.

The answer says notice must be 'at least 60 days' notice, in the prescribed form', mentions Form 5, and says 'An email or a refusal to negotiate is not a notice in the prescribed form'. For the hardest point it answers 'Do you have to pay the higher rent? On what you describe, no', which is clear enough despite the hedge that it cannot see the email. It gives next steps: 'Keep paying your current rent. Ask the agent in writing for a formal notice.'
