It mentions the 90-day Form 5 text from versions 005 and 009, and version 111, only to say they came later and were not in force on 1 October 2025. It applies the 60-day rule from version 110, so deleting the later-version material would not change the substance.

question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:
## What the law says

I relied on the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", dated 13 October 2026. That is the latest version I retrieved before 15 October 2026. The "v115" number comes from the file name. I could not see a separate "Authorised Version" number in the text I retrieved.

- **You must not damage the property.** A renter must not intentionally or negligently damage the rented premises. Fair wear and tear doesn't count as damage [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Dog chewing is more likely to be treated as damage than as fair wear and tear. That is my inference, because the Act doesn't mention pets.
- **You must tell the owner in writing.** A renter who becomes aware of damage must give the rental provider written notice "as soon as practicable". The notice must say that the damage has occurred and what it is. Email is allowed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Act gives no exception for damage you have already fixed, so repairing it quietly would not remove the duty to notify.
- **Repairs must be done by a suitably qualified person.** The regulations' prescribed rental agreement form says "Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs" [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). A quick unqualified fix is therefore risky.
- **The owner decides how the repair happens.** If the owner gives a written repair notice for damage you caused, they can require you to repair it at your expense within 14 days. Alternatively, they can say they are doing the repair and that you are liable for the reasonable cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
  - If you don't repair it "in a proper and tradesman-like manner" within 14 days, the owner may repair it at your expense [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
  - If the owner does the repair, you are liable for the reasonable cost once they give you the cost particulars in writing. You must reimburse them within 14 days after the repairs are completed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
  - You can apply to the Tribunal for more time, or give written notice of hardship to get an extra 14 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **The bond may be claimed.** The documents I retrieved that contain s 411AB are older versions: Authorised version dated 6 August 2025 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) and 29 March 2021 [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa098%20authorised.pdf). They let the owner claim from the bond "the reasonable cost of repairs to, or the restoration of" the property for damage caused by the renter, taking fair wear and tear into account [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa098%20authorised.pdf). I did not retrieve s 411AB from the 13 October 2026 version, so I can't confirm its current wording.

## Can you just get someone to fix it without telling the owner?

The documents don't support doing that. You have a written-notice duty [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), and repairs are meant to be done by a suitably qualified person [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The owner also has a statutory process for how damage is repaired and who pays [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Would it affect the owner's insurance?

The retrieved documents say nothing about insurance, so I can't answer that part. Check the owner's policy or ask the owner or agent.

## What you can do

1. **Email the owner or agent now.** Describe the skirting board damage and say the dog caused it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Offer to arrange a repair by a suitably qualified tradesperson.** Ask the owner to agree first. Keep photos, quotes and receipts. The documents don't expressly say an owner must accept this, but the repair-notice process shows owners can require the renter to repair [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3. **Expect a possible bond claim.** The owner may claim the reasonable cost from the bond [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa098%20authorised.pdf).
4. **Use the Tribunal for disputes.** In a compensation hearing, the earlier version (6 August 2025) lets the Tribunal consider "any action taken… to repair the damage at that person's own expense" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). I did not retrieve that provision from the 2026 version.

If the amount in dispute is large, get advice from Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy advice service.

must-mention.reason: No. The answer covers written notice 'as soon as practicable', says the documents 'say nothing about insurance', and gives next steps such as emailing the owner. It is missing the second point: it never says the renter must leave the home in the same condition (apart from fair wear and tear) when moving out. The closest it gets is the owner's ability to claim restoration costs from the bond and its own hedged 'inference' that dog chewing is damage, which doesn't state that duty.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. None of the three failure conditions are asserted: the answer rejects a quiet repair ("The documents don't support doing that"), states no insurance outcome ("The retrieved documents say nothing about insurance, so I can't answer that part"), and never says the renter must pay the owner's insurance excess.

version-cited.reason: No. The answer does name the in-force versions, the Act through 'rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf' and link 97-109aa115, and the Regulations through link 21-3sra009. However, it applies rules from versions not in force on 15 October 2026: the bond-claim rule in s 411AB comes from the 'Authorised version dated 6 August 2025' (97-109aa110) and 29 March 2021 (97-109aa098), and the Tribunal-consideration step comes from 'the earlier version (6 August 2025)'. These are presented as law and as steps the user can take ('Expect a possible bond claim', 'Use the Tribunal for disputes'), despite caveats. Deleting them would change the answer's substance.

question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
## What the law says

**Document applied:** *rt-regs-2021-v002-2022-06-01.pdf* (Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, dated 1 June 2022) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). This is the latest retrieved version dated on or before 1 March 2023. The retrieved text doesn't print an "Authorised Version No." The file name ("v002") suggests it is version 2. The later versions I found (v004, v005, v009) are dated 2025–2026, so they don't apply to 1 March 2023 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)[[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The v004 amendment table lists no changes between the 1 June 2022 amendment and December 2024, which fits v002 being in force on your date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

- **No circuit-count rule.** I found nothing in the retrieved regulations setting a minimum number of circuits or power points per circuit. They also say nothing about a breaker tripping when appliances run together.
- **Electrical safety standard.** Schedule 4, clause 9 says that "on and from 29 March 2023", all power outlets and lighting circuits must be connected to a switchboard-type Circuit Breaker complying with AS/NZS 3000. They must also be connected to a switchboard-type Residual Current Device (RCD) complying with the listed standards [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Timing.** On 1 March 2023 that requirement had not yet started, because it starts 29 March 2023 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). It is also about having a circuit breaker and RCD. It doesn't limit how many outlets share a circuit.
- **Safety devices.** A residual current device is a prescribed safety device [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

## What you can ask for

- **Electrical safety check record.** You can give your rental provider a written request for a copy of the most recent electrical safety check. They must provide it within 7 days [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The record must name the licensed or registered electrician and give the date and results, including repairs required and actions taken [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). This would show whether the wiring has been inspected.
- **Repairs or an upgrade.** I can't tell you from the 2022 regulations whether you can require extra circuits. The repair provisions of the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* weren't retrieved, so I can't say how they apply. A 2025 document (v004) summarises repair rights in its standard form, but it post-dates your date, so I haven't relied on it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

For a definitive answer, check the Act's repair provisions or ask Consumer Affairs Victoria.

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both points are covered: the answer says there is 'No circuit-count rule' in the regulations, and as a next step it says the tenant can 'give your rental provider a written request for a copy of the most recent electrical safety check', which records the check date, satisfying the 'and/or' next-step point.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never asserts a minimum number of circuits or that sharing a circuit is illegal ("I found nothing in the retrieved regulations setting a minimum number of circuits or power points per circuit"), and it says the circuit breaker/RCD standard does not yet apply ("On 1 March 2023 that requirement had not yet started, because it starts 29 March 2023").

version-cited.reason: No. The answer names the Regulations with a version ('rt-regs-2021-v002-2022-06-01.pdf' / '21-3sra002', dated 1 June 2022). It mentions the 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997' only without a version, and never identifies Authorised Version No. 101, so a required document is named without its version.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents I retrieved don't say outright that a coin-operated washing machine is allowed or banned. They do set rules on charging for services, and those rules give you some things to ask for.

## What the law says

**Version used:** the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", dated 13 October 2026. It is the latest version I found before 15 October 2026. The file name suggests version 115, but the extract doesn't print an "Authorised Version No.", so I can't confirm that number from the text.

- **Utility charges (s 108):** An operator can charge separately for electricity, gas and water used in your room, but only if the room is separately metered, and not more than the supplier charges [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This covers the room itself, so it doesn't clearly cover shared laundry machines.
- **Charges for services (s 109):** If an operator charges for services, they must:
  - give you a separate schedule of the amounts before you take up the room, and
  - give you an itemised account of your own use, if you use those services [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Public and community housing (s 109A):** Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency may impose a service charge for "laundry… services or facilities". This applies only if it isn't possible or practicable to accurately measure your use. The charge must not exceed the cost of providing the facility. They must give written notice of the charge and of any change. You can apply to the Tribunal to have it withdrawn or varied [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Laundry standard:** Under the *Residential Tenancies (Rooming House Standards) Regulations 2023* (version dated 1 December 2024), from 26 February 2024 there must be a washing machine in good working order for every 12 or fewer residents, based on the house's maximum capacity [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf). That version predates 15 October 2026, and I didn't find a later one. The regulation doesn't say whether the machine must be free or can be coin-operated.

## What you can do

1. **Ask the operator for the written schedule of service charges.** The operator must give you this under s 109 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Also ask for an itemised account of what you've been charged for using the machines [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Find out who runs the house.** If it's Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency, the laundry charge can't exceed the cost of providing it. You can apply to the Tribunal to challenge it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Check there are enough machines.** Two machines meet the standard for up to 24 residents at maximum capacity, using the one-per-12 rule [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf).

**Gap:** In the retrieved text for the current Act, I didn't find a provision that expressly allows or bans coin-operated machines in a privately run rooming house. I also didn't find a specific Tribunal route to challenge that charge. For a definite answer, check with Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy advice service.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered; the hardest one, that the law doesn't say the machines must be free, is covered by 'The regulation doesn't say whether the machine must be free or can be coin-operated.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes: none of the three claims is asserted, because the answer says the regulation "doesn't say whether the machine must be free or can be coin-operated," states the operator must follow rules on charges under s 109, and limits the cost cap to cases where "it's Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency."

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Act with its in-force version, via the file name 'rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf' (dated 13 October 2026) and the link '97-109aa115', and the Rooming House Standards Regulations as the 'version dated 1 December 2024' with the link '23-10sra002'; it relies on no other version for any rule it applies.

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
**Short answer:** Mould in an ad photo is not automatically unlawful. The advertiser's test is what they reasonably believe, not the photo itself. A photo alone doesn't prove the premises fail the minimum standards. The retrieved documents don't confirm that the advertising rule was in force on 1 October 2025, as explained below.

## What the law says

**1. The standard.** The rental minimum standards say each room "must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). This is clause 8 of Schedule 4 to the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*. The version in force on 1 October 2025 was the file titled **rt-regs-2021-v004-2025-07-01** (dated 1 July 2025). The next version in the results, v005, is dated 25 November 2025, so it came later [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). The wording of clause 8 is the same in both. The retrieved text doesn't print a separate "Authorised Version No." line, so I'm relying on the "v004" in the file title.

**2. Advertising.** Section 65B of the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* says a provider or agent "must not advertise or otherwise offer premises to let unless" they "reasonably believe the premises comply with the rental minimum standards". The penalty is 60 penalty units for a natural person and 300 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Caveat on dates:** I could only find this text in **rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13**, which is dated after your 1 October 2025 date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The version that was in force on 1 October 2025 is **rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06** (6 August 2025) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The portion of it I retrieved does not include section 65B.
- v115 notes that section 65B was inserted by Act No. 6/2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). None of the retrieved documents say when it commenced. So I can't confirm from them that the rule applied on 1 October 2025.

**3. Is the photo enough to prove non-compliance?** The documents don't set out any rules of evidence or proof. What they do say is:
- The standard only covers mould and damp "caused by or related to the building structure" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). A photo shows mould but not its cause, so on its own it doesn't establish a breach.
- The advertising test is the advertiser's *reasonable belief* in compliance [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Mould visible in their own photos could make that belief hard to defend, but the documents don't say so directly.
- Providers and agents must keep records sufficient to demonstrate compliance with section 65B, and the Director can ask for them (150 or 750 penalty units for failing to produce them) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). These provisions appear only in v115 (inserted by Act No. 46/2025), not in the version I retrieved for your date.

## What a renter can do or ask

- **Before signing:** I found no provision in the retrieved documents covering what a prospective renter can demand. The disclosure rules (regulation 16) that I retrieved are in the 2022 version [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf) and the later November 2025 version [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf), not the version in force on 1 October 2025. So I can't say what had to be disclosed on that date.
- **Provider's duty:** A provider must ensure the premises comply with the prescribed minimum standards on or before the day the renter moves in. The penalty is 60 or 300 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **After moving in:** If the premises don't comply on or immediately after that day, the renter may issue a request for urgent repairs to bring them into compliance [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs definition:** The definition in the Act (v110, in force 1 October 2025) includes "a failure to comply with any rental minimum standards" and "the presence of mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

I haven't found anything in the documents on a prospective renter's own complaint process or on what evidence a tribunal would require. For those, the documents don't answer the question.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered: the answer quotes the standard that rooms 'must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure', states 'A photo alone doesn't prove the premises fail the minimum standards... on its own it doesn't establish a breach', and gives a next step that 'the renter may issue a request for urgent repairs to bring them into compliance' after moving in.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer does not claim the photo alone proves illegality; it says "A photo alone doesn't prove the premises fail the minimum standards." It also does not say the advertising ban applies on 1 October 2025; it states "The retrieved documents don't confirm that the advertising rule was in force on 1 October 2025" and "I can't confirm from them that the rule applied on 1 October 2025."

version-cited.reason: No. The answer names 'rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06' and 'rt-regs-2021-v004-2025-07-01', but it applies rules taken from 'rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13', a later version not in force on 1 October 2025. These include the s 65B advertising rule and penalties, the provider's duty to comply by move-in, and the renter's right to request urgent repairs, presented as the law and as steps the user can take despite the date caveat. Deleting the v115 material would change the answer's substance.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I let a friend move into my rental without telling the agent. Now I want them out. What do I have to do?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents I retrieved don't set out any step-by-step process for a renter to remove a friend they've let move in. They do cover the rule you broke and the risk it creates for you.

I used *rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf* (Residential Tenancies Act 1997, dated 13 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). It is the latest version in the results and the one in force on 15 October 2026. The version number comes from the file name ("v115"). The extracted text doesn't print an "Authorised Version No." line.

## What the law says
- A renter must not assign or sub-let the whole or any part of the premises without the rental provider's written consent (s 81(1)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- A sub-letting without consent is invalid, unless the Tribunal has determined that consent isn't required (s 81(3)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- A rental provider can give a renter a notice to vacate if the renter has assigned or sub-let, or purported to, without consent. The termination date must be at least 14 days after the notice is given (s 91ZV) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**Caveat on s 91ZV:** The only text of s 91ZV I retrieved is from *rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf* (6 August 2025) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The v115 excerpt I have stops before that section. So I can't confirm from the documents that it reads the same in v115.

## What you can do or ask
- **Ask the agent for written consent.** This is the lawful route if the friend stays. The rental provider must not unreasonably withhold consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), and can't charge a fee for giving it (s 84) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Go to the Tribunal if consent is refused.** If the provider withholds consent and you think that's unreasonable, you can apply to the Tribunal for a determination that consent isn't required (s 82) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Ending the arrangement.** You say you want the friend out, so these two routes don't help you directly. They matter because the unapproved arrangement exposes you to a notice to vacate [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether the friend leaving, or you telling the agent, would stop the provider using s 91ZV.

## What the documents don't answer
- They don't say what notice, if any, you must give your friend, or how you can make them leave. This probably depends on whether they're a sub-tenant or just a guest, and the documents don't address that.
- They don't say whether the Tribunal can order a friend to leave at your request.

For those points, get advice from Consumer Affairs Victoria (1300 558 181) or a community legal organisation. Both are named in the Form 6 notice-to-vacate information sheet [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

question: It is 1 November 2019. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?
answer:
## What the law says for 1 November 2019

**The retrieved documents don't let me state the law in force on 1 November 2019.** None of them is dated on or before that day.

- The earliest is *rta-1997-v089-2019-12-04.pdf* (Residential Tenancies Act 1997, dated 4 December 2019; the file name suggests version 089). That is a month after your date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf). The file name is the only place a version number appears, so I can't confirm the formal Authorised Version number.
- The other Act versions are later still. *rta-1997-v090-2020-03-02.pdf* is dated 2 March 2020 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf), and *rta-1997-v098-2021-03-29.pdf* is dated 29 March 2021 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa098%20authorised.pdf).
- The v089 text I retrieved contains retaliation-style "notice of no effect" rules only for caravan park residents (s 206AZE) and Part 4A site tenants (s 207ZH). These don't cover an ordinary rented home [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf).

I therefore can't tell you whether a notice given on 1 November 2019 is invalid as retaliation, or what the deadline was to challenge it.

## What a later version says (not confirmed for your date)

*rta-1997-v098-2021-03-29.pdf* (29 March 2021) has these rules. Don't treat them as the law on 1 November 2019:

- A notice under s 91ZK is of no effect if it was given in response to the renter exercising, or proposing to exercise, a right under the Act [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa098%20authorised.pdf).
- A notice must be in the prescribed form and addressed to the renter. It must be signed, give the reason or reasons, and state the termination date [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa098%20authorised.pdf).
- Some notices must come with documentary evidence supporting the reason [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa098%20authorised.pdf).
- A renter can challenge certain notices at the Tribunal within 30 days after the notice is given [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa098%20authorised.pdf).

Whether any of this applied to your notice on 1 November 2019 isn't shown in the documents.

## What you can check and ask

Using the later version as a guide only:

1. **The reason stated on the notice.** Does it name a specific ground? Does it fit what happened?
2. **The form.** Is it addressed to you and signed? Does it give a termination date?
3. **Supporting evidence.** Was any required documentary evidence attached?
4. **Timing.** Note the date you were given the notice. Your repair follow-up and the notice were on the same day, which is relevant to showing it was a response to your request.
5. **Deadlines.** Find out the time limit for challenging the notice under the version in force on 1 November 2019, and act quickly.

The documents don't say which version applied on 1 November 2019, so I can't confirm the specific grounds or time limits for your notice. Get advice promptly. The later notice-to-vacate form directs renters to community legal organisations listed on the Consumer Affairs Victoria website, or to call 1300 558 181 [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). That form is from regulations dated 2022, so it isn't confirmation for your date.

must-mention.reason: No. The answer never says a no-reason notice is allowed with at least 120 days notice, and it never gives the 60-day VCAT challenge window. It cites only a 30-day Tribunal challenge from the 2021 version and declines to state the 1 November 2019 rules, so the first and third points are missing.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer ties both points to the 2021 version, saying "Don't treat them as the law on 1 November 2019" about "give the reason or reasons" and "within 30 days after the notice is given", and for 2019 says only to "Find out the time limit for challenging the notice under the version in force on 1 November 2019", so it never asserts that a reason was required or that a deadline other than 60 days applied on that date.

version-cited.reason: No. The answer never names the version in force on 1 November 2019 (Authorised Version No. 088, dated 2 July 2019). It names only later versions such as 'rta-1997-v089-2019-12-04.pdf' and 'rta-1997-v098-2021-03-29.pdf'. It also relies on v098 rules (s 91ZK retaliation, notice form requirements, the 30-day Tribunal challenge) as steps the user can take, despite the caveat that they may not apply on that date.

question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?
answer:
## What the law says (version in force on 1 October 2025)

I used **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf (version 110, dated 6 August 2025)** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The next version in the documents is v111, dated 25 November 2025, so v110 was the one in force on 1 October 2025 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The excerpt of v110 doesn't print the words "Authorised Version No."; I took the version number from the file name.

- **Fixed rent:** A rental provider or agent must not advertise or offer premises unless the rent is advertised or offered as a fixed amount. The penalty is 60 penalty units for a natural person and 300 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Inviting higher offers:** They must not "solicit or otherwise invite an offer of an amount of rent that is higher than the advertised amount." The penalties are the same [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Accepting unsolicited higher offers:** The v110 text I retrieved has no rule on this. A separate ban on accepting an unsolicited or uninvited higher offer (s 30F(4)) appears only in v111 (25 November 2025) and later versions, inserted by No. 6/2025 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). That is after your date, so I can't say it applied to you. If your agent only accepted a higher offer nobody invited, the v110 text doesn't clearly cover it.
- **False or misleading rent claims:** An agent or provider who promotes or advertises premises must not make a false or misleading representation about the rent. The penalties are the same [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Misleading conduct:** Section 30E bars misleading or deceptive conduct, or false representations about the rent, that induce someone to enter a rental agreement. The Act notes that the Tribunal can make orders for a contravention of that section [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Discrimination:** A provider must not refuse to let premises on the basis of a protected attribute under the Equal Opportunity Act 2010. A person who suffers loss from discrimination can apply to the Tribunal for compensation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Nothing you've described suggests this, so it only matters if you think that was the reason.

## What you can do

- **Ask for a written explanation.** Ask the agent or provider why the application is recorded as withdrawn and when and how that was recorded. The documents don't say this is required, but it is the obvious first step.
- **Challenge the facts.** If your application was recorded as withdrawn without your say-so, or the property was re-advertised higher after a higher offer was invited, this may fall within ss 30F(3), 30F(1) or 30G [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). If you believe the "withdrawn" email was a pretext for taking a higher offer, that is the point to raise.
- **Take it further.** The retrieved documents don't say how a renter enforces ss 30F or 30G, or whether you can apply to the Tribunal over them. I can't confirm that from these documents. The Tribunal-order note appears only for s 30E [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), and compensation is mentioned only for discrimination [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

## What to save as evidence

The documents don't list evidence. These suggestions are practical, not from the documents:

- The original advertisement showing the advertised rent and its date, such as screenshots or a saved page.
- The current listing at the higher rent.
- Your application and its confirmation.
- The "withdrawn" email, with full headers and timestamps.
- Any messages, calls or inspection notes, including anything where the agent asked for "best offers" or similar.
- Any evidence of the higher offer, and whether it was invited or unsolicited.
- Your own reply or objection.

The documents don't cover the "withdrawn" email itself or how to enforce these rules, so I can't say more on those points.

must-mention.reason: No. The answer never states that relisting at a higher fixed rent is not illegal by itself. It only says rent must be advertised as a fixed amount and that re-advertising higher 'after a higher offer was invited' may fall within the sections, so the first point is missing. The other three points are covered: inviting higher offers is banned, the v110 text 'doesn't clearly cover' accepting an unsolicited offer, and 'The documents don't cover the "withdrawn" email itself.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer makes none of the failing claims: relisting is tied only to an invited higher offer ('re-advertised higher after a higher offer was invited, this may fall within'), the unsolicited-offer ban is placed after this date ('appears only in v111 (25 November 2025)... That is after your date, so I can't say it applied to you'), and it never says the applicant can force the agent to rent to them.

version-cited.reason: Yes — the answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as 'version 110, dated 6 August 2025' (rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf, 97-109aa110) and applies only v110 rules (ss 30E, 30F, 30G). It mentions v111/v115's s 30F(4) only to say that rule came in after the user's date, and deleting that mention would not change the substance.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
**Short answer:** The agent's "no" doesn't settle it. Three weeks have passed, so unless the owner applied to VCAT within 14 days, the owner is legally taken to have consented.

I used *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 115 (file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026). This is the version in force on 15 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- A renter may keep a pet if the rental provider consented in writing or the Tribunal ordered that they may [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Requests must be made in the form approved by the Director and given to the rental provider [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You used the official form, so that step looks met.
- The rental provider **must not unreasonably refuse** consent to a pet [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The provider is **taken to have consented** unless, **within 14 days** of being given the request, they **apply to the Tribunal** under s 71D [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Refusing, or having the agent refuse, is not the same as applying to the Tribunal.
- Only the Tribunal can decide that a refusal is reasonable. A provider can apply for an order that refusing consent is reasonable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Applying it to you

- Your request was sent 3 weeks ago, which is 21 days. That is past the 14-day window [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- If the owner did not apply to VCAT within those 14 days, they are taken to have consented, whatever the agent said [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether the owner applied, so you need to check that.
- **The allergy:** The Act doesn't list an owner's allergy as a ground for refusal. If the owner did apply, the Tribunal may consider the type of pet, the character and nature of the premises, the appliances, fixtures and fittings, whether refusal is permitted under any Act, any prescribed matters, and any other matter it considers relevant [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say how VCAT would weigh an allergy, or the fact that the owner rarely visits, so I can't predict the outcome.

## What you can do

1. **Check whether VCAT proceedings were started.** Ask the agent in writing whether the owner applied to the Tribunal within 14 days of receiving your request.
2. **If no application was made,** tell the agent in writing that the owner is taken to have consented under s 71C(2) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Keep a copy of your request and proof of the date it was given.
3. **If an application was made,** you can put your case to the Tribunal. Relevant points include the type of dog and the premises, and the owner's rare visits as "any other matter" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**Gaps in the documents:**
- They don't say whether giving the request to the agent counts as giving it to the provider. Section 71B(2) says the request must be given to the rental provider [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If the agent received it, confirm that it reached the owner.
- They don't say how "taken to have consented" relates to the "consented in writing" wording in s 71A. For certainty, you could ask for written confirmation.

must-mention.reason: All three points are covered. Point 1: 'The provider is taken to have consented unless, within 14 days of being given the request, they apply to the Tribunal.' Point 2: 'Three weeks have passed, so unless the owner applied to VCAT within 14 days, the owner is legally taken to have consented.' Point 3: 'Ask the agent in writing whether the owner applied to the Tribunal within 14 days of receiving your request.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer says none of the failing claims: it states "The agent's 'no' doesn't settle it," it never says the renter must apply to VCAT (only that "If an application was made, you can put your case to the Tribunal"), and it treats the allergy as undecided rather than decisive ("The documents don't say how VCAT would weigh an allergy... so I can't predict the outcome").

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115' (file 'rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf', link 97-109aa115), the version in force on 15 October 2026, and every rule it applies is cited to that version only.

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
**Short answer:** Based on the documents I retrieved, the notice stays in force unless it is formally withdrawn. The documents don't say that a notice lapses automatically when a buyer pulls out. So you should not assume you can ignore it.

**Which version applies:** For 1 October 2025 I used the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf", dated 6 August 2025 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The file name indicates version 110. The excerpts I retrieved don't print an "Authorised Version No." line, so I'm relying on the file name for that number. The next version in the documents is v111, dated 25 November 2025, which is after your date [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **Sale notices.** A landlord can give a notice to vacate if the premises are, immediately after the termination date, "to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). If there is a contract of sale, the notice must be given within 14 days of the contract being entered into, or within 14 days after the last condition is satisfied [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Notice period.** The notice must give a termination date at least 60 days after it is given [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Later versions raise this to 90 days, but that is not the law on your date [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Paperwork.** The sale notice must be accompanied by supporting documentary evidence [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). This is covered by section 91ZZO, which the v110 text only cross-refers to in its notes [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **A buyer pulling out.** The retrieved text of v110 does not say what happens to a sale notice if the buyer withdraws. The ground is that the property is "to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). If the landlord is still selling or re-offering it, the ground may still apply. That is my reading, not something the documents state.
- **Withdrawing a notice.** The v110 excerpt I retrieved stops before the withdrawal section (91ZZQ), so I can't confirm its wording from v110. The same section appears in v101 (7 September 2022), which is earlier than your date, and in v111 (25 November 2025), which is later [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)[[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Both say a notice to vacate is withdrawn only if a notice of withdrawal is given. That notice must be in writing, signed by the person who gave the notice, and signed by the person it was given to [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)[[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). I haven't verified that v110 reads the same.

## What you can do or ask

1. **Ask the landlord for a signed notice of withdrawal.** Under the later and earlier versions, the landlord not formally withdrawing means the notice is not withdrawn. A withdrawal needs both your signature and the landlord's [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)[[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Check that v110 has the same wording.
2. **Consider challenging the notice at the Tribunal.** In v101 and v111, a renter who received a sale notice can apply to the Tribunal to challenge its validity, on or before the hearing of a possession order application. The application must be made within 30 days after the notice was given [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)[[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). I could not confirm this wording in v110 itself, so check it. If you are close to or past 30 days, act quickly.
3. **Check the notice itself.** Look at the termination date (at least 60 days after the notice was given), whether the notice was in time after the sale contract, and whether supporting documents were attached [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**Not covered by the documents:** I have no retrieved text on whether you must leave on the termination date, or on what happens if you stay. The part of v110 on possession orders was not in the excerpts. For advice on your specific situation, contact a tenancy advice service or Consumer Affairs Victoria.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are present. (1) The answer turns on the ground: the output explains the sale-with-vacant-possession ground and the contract-of-sale timing, says 'If the landlord is still selling or re-offering it, the ground may still apply', and tells the renter to check the supporting documents. (2) It states the 60-day minimum notice period. (3) The hardest point, written withdrawal signed by both, is covered by 'a notice to vacate is withdrawn only if a notice of withdrawal is given... in writing, signed by the person who gave the notice, and signed by the person it was given to'; the hedge about verifying v110 does not obscure which way it falls. (4) It gives next steps: ask for a signed withdrawal, or challenge the notice at the Tribunal within 30 days.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer avoids all three failure conditions: it says "The documents don't say that a notice lapses automatically when a buyer pulls out," states that "A withdrawal needs both your signature and the landlord's," and gives "at least 60 days," mentioning 90 days only to say "that is not the law on your date."

version-cited.reason: No — the answer names 'rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf' (version 110, dated 6 August 2025), but it takes the withdrawal rule (s 91ZZQ) and the 30-day Tribunal challenge from v101 and v111, which were not in force on 1 October 2025, and presents them as the law and as steps the user can take; removing them would change the answer's substance.

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents I retrieved don't include the version of the law in force on 1 October 2025 for this question, so I can't confirm from them whether you must pay the higher rent or from when.

## What the law says

**Versions in force on 1 October 2025**
- The Residential Tenancies Act 1997 version closest to that date is *rta-1997-v111-2025-11-25.pdf* (25 November 2025), which is after your date. The excerpts I retrieved from it cover only Part 4A (site agreements) and Part 12A (specialist disability accommodation). They don't include the ordinary rent increase section, section 44 [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (*rt-regs-2021-v004-2025-07-01.pdf*, 1 July 2025) was in force on 1 October 2025. The excerpt I retrieved covers Forms 9 to 18, not Form 5, the notice of rent increase for ordinary renters [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- Form 5 appears only in later versions: *rt-regs-2021-v005-2025-11-25.pdf* (25 November 2025) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf) and *rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf* (30 June 2026) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Both postdate your question, so I can't treat them as the law on 1 October 2025.

**Older versions of section 44 (not the law on your date)**
The only retrieved versions that include section 44 are *rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf* [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) and *rta-1997-v090-2020-03-02.pdf* [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf). Both say:
- A landlord must give at least 60 days' notice, in the prescribed form, of a proposed rent increase [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf).
- A notice can only provide for one rent increase [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf).
- A landlord must not increase rent at intervals of less than 12 months [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf).
- A rent increase that contravenes the section is invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf).

These are 2019 and 2020 versions, so they are not the law on 1 October 2025. Later documents show the rules changed. For example, the Form 5 in the November 2025 regulations says 90 days' notice [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). I can't say what the rule was on 1 October 2025.

## What you can do

- **Ask the agent** for the formal notice of proposed rent increase. The older versions of the Act say the notice must be in the prescribed form, and that an increase made without following the section is invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf). I can't confirm this applied on 1 October 2025.
- **Don't rely on an email alone.** The documents don't say an email like yours counts as a valid notice. The later Form 5 mentions email delivery only "if consent has been provided by the renter" [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). That form postdates your question.
- **Challenging the amount:** The older versions let a tenant ask the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria to investigate a proposed rent they think is excessive. The application must be in writing within 30 days after the notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf). Since you haven't received a notice, that clock may not have started, but I can't confirm this from the in-force law.

**To get a firm answer,** you would need the Act version and regulations version actually in force on 1 October 2025. I didn't retrieve them. Consumer Affairs Victoria or a community legal centre can confirm the position.
