question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents I retrieved point against repairing it quietly. They require you to tell the owner in writing about damage. They say nothing about the owner's insurance.

## What the law says

**Versions used**
- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997**, file *rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf* (13 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This is the latest version retrieved and the one in force on 15 October 2026. The file name indicates version 115, but the excerpts don't show an "Authorised Version" line, so I can't confirm the number from the text.
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021**, *rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf* (30 June 2026) [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- Some points below appear only in earlier documents. I say so each time.

**Your duty not to damage the premises.** The Act treats damage caused by a renter's failure to take care, under s 61(1), as a ground for the owner to give a repair notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**The owner's options.** The owner can give a written repair notice. It can require you to repair the damage at your expense within 14 days. If you don't repair it "in a tradesman-like manner", the owner can repair it at your expense (s 78) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Alternatively, the owner can say they will do the repairs themselves and that you are liable for the reasonable cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**Paying for it.** You are liable for reasonable repair costs once the owner gives you the cost particulars in writing. You must reimburse them within 14 days of the repairs being completed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If you can't pay in time, you can apply to the Tribunal for an extension. If you're in hardship, you can give written notice asking for an extra 14 days (s 79) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**Telling the owner and who does the repairs.** The standard rental agreement's rights summary says that where damage occurs, the renter "must notify the rental provider in writing". It also says non-urgent damage must be notified in writing as soon as practicable, and that "only a suitably qualified person may do repairs" [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). These clauses appear in *rt-regs-2021-v005-2025-11-25.pdf* (25 November 2025) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). The 30 June 2026 excerpts I retrieved don't reproduce them, so I can't confirm they are unchanged.

**Compensation.** The Tribunal rules on compensation for damage are in the earlier Act version, *rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf* (6 August 2025) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). I did not retrieve that part of the October 2026 version.
- When assessing a damage claim, the Tribunal may consider any action the person claimed against took to repair the damage at their own expense (s 211(g)) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- It may also consider money already recovered from the bond (s 211(c)) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- It must account for depreciation of the damaged part (s 211A) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**Fair wear and tear.** The condition report form (30 June 2026) says the owner must allow for fair wear and tear, which doesn't count as damage caused by the renter. Dog chewing is unlikely to be treated as fair wear and tear. That is my inference, not something the documents say [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## Would it affect the owner's insurance?

The retrieved documents don't address this. They say nothing about the owner's insurance policy, notification duties or claims. I won't guess, and you would need to check the owner's policy or ask the owner or agent.

## What you can do

1. **Tell the owner or agent in writing** about the chewed skirting boards, rather than fixing them quietly [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
2. **Offer to repair them.** The Act's repair-notice process contemplates the renter repairing "in a tradesman-like manner", and the rights summary says a suitably qualified person should do repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Ask the owner or agent to agree to the repair, and keep invoices and photos.
3. **Keep evidence.** Photos and receipts help if there is a dispute. The Tribunal may consider repairs paid for by the person being claimed against [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
4. **Check your options if you disagree.** If the owner claims more than you think is fair, the Tribunal can look at depreciation and the bond [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

I can't tell you from these documents that a quiet repair is unlawful. They do set a written-notice requirement and a qualified-person requirement, and the quickest safe route is to tell the owner.

must-mention.reason: No. Point 2 is only partly covered. The answer says the renter is liable for repair costs and that fair wear and tear 'doesn't count as damage caused by the renter'. It never says the renter must leave the home in the same condition (apart from fair wear and tear) when moving out, which is the key obligation for a renter about to leave. The written-notice point ('must be notified in writing as soon as practicable'), the insurance point ('The retrieved documents don't address this') and the next-step point ('Tell the owner or agent in writing') are all covered.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: none of the failure conditions are asserted. The answer says the documents "point against repairing it quietly" and advises "Tell the owner or agent in writing... rather than fixing them quietly". On insurance it states no outcome, saying only "The retrieved documents don't address this... I won't guess". It never says the renter must pay the owner's insurance excess.

version-cited.reason: No. The answer names the in-force versions, 'rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf' and 'rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf'. However, it also applies rules from versions not in force on 15 October 2026. It bases the written-notice and qualified-person requirements, including its step 1 advice to tell the owner in writing, on 'rt-regs-2021-v005-2025-11-25.pdf'. It bases the Tribunal compensation factors (ss 211, 211A) and steps 3 and 4 on 'rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf'. Deleting that material would change the substance of the answer.

question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
## What the law says (as at 1 March 2023)

The version in force on that date, among the documents I retrieved, is the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (S.R. No. 3/2021)**. Its file is rt-regs-2021-v002-2022-06-01.pdf, dated 1 June 2022 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The file name indicates version 002, but the text I retrieved doesn't print an "Authorised Version" number. The 2025 and 2026 versions are later, so they can't show the law on your date. Between v002 (June 2022) and v004 (July 2025), a v003 may exist that I didn't retrieve. I can't rule out that it was in force on 1 March 2023.

- **No rule on the number of circuits.** Nothing I retrieved sets a minimum number of circuits or a power-load requirement for a rental. The only electrical rental minimum standard is "Electrical safety" in Schedule 4, clause 9 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **That standard hadn't started yet.** It applies "on and from 29 March 2023". From then, all power outlets and lighting circuits must be connected to a switchboard-type circuit breaker complying with AS/NZS 3000 and to a switchboard-type residual current device (RCD) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). On 1 March 2023 it wasn't yet in force.
- **It covers protection devices, not capacity.** Even once it starts, it is about circuit breakers and RCDs. It doesn't say how many circuits a home needs or that a kettle and heater must run together without tripping.
- **No ruling on your situation.** The documents don't say whether a breaker tripping from overload counts as a defect.

## What you can ask for

The documents contain a standard-form agreement. The retrieved v002 text is Form 2 (agreements of more than 5 years), and I'm assuming the standard terms are similar for other agreements. It includes these terms:

- **Maintenance:** the rental provider must keep the premises in good repair and fit for occupation, and must ensure they meet the rental minimum standards [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Electrical safety check:** the provider must have all electrical installations, appliances and fittings they provided checked every 2 years by a licensed or registered electrician. On request, they must give you the date of the most recent check in writing [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). If no check has been done in the last 2 years when you occupy the premises, they must arrange one as soon as practicable [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Non-urgent repair:** you must notify the provider in writing, and they must do non-urgent repairs in a reasonable time. If they haven't done the repairs within 14 days of notice, you may apply to VCAT for an order [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs:** these include failure of an essential service or appliance for hot water, cooking, heating or laundering supplied by the provider [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The documents don't say a tripping breaker is an urgent repair.

**Practical steps:**
1. Write to the provider or agent describing the tripping, and ask for the date of the last electrical safety check.
2. Ask for a licensed electrician to inspect the circuit and say whether the wiring or switchboard needs work.
3. If nothing happens within 14 days, you may apply to VCAT.

I can't tell you from these documents whether the provider must add circuits.

must-mention.reason: Both points are covered: the answer says 'Nothing I retrieved sets a minimum number of circuits', and it gives next steps 'Write to the provider or agent describing the tripping, and ask for the date of the last electrical safety check' along with a non-urgent repair request.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer says neither. On circuits, it says "Nothing I retrieved sets a minimum number of circuits" and that the standard "doesn't say how many circuits a home needs." On the RCD standard, it says it applies "on and from 29 March 2023" and that "On 1 March 2023 it wasn't yet in force."

version-cited.reason: No. The answer names the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 in version 002 ("rt-regs-2021-v002-2022-06-01.pdf", link "21-3sra002"), which was in force on 1 March 2023. However, it never names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 101, so it leaves out a required document.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents I retrieved don't say that an operator may charge for coin-operated washing machines, and they don't say it is banned. They do set rules that apply if a charge is made.

## What the law says

The main source is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf" (version 115, dated 13 October 2026). It is the latest version I found before 15 October 2026.

- **Section 108** lets an operator charge separately for electricity, gas and water, but only where the operator pays the bills and the room is separately metered. It covers consumption "in the room" and cannot exceed the supplier's charge [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). It doesn't mention shared laundry machines.
- **Section 109** applies if an operator charges for services. The operator must:
  - give you a separate schedule of the amounts for the services before you take up residency; and
  - if you use those services, give you an itemised account of your individual use [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Section 109A** applies only to rooming houses run by Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency. They may impose a service charge for "laundry… services or facilities" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This applies only if it isn't possible or practicable to accurately measure your use [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The charge must not exceed the cost of providing the service or facility [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The charge can change only in line with changes in that cost [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Standards for laundries:** The *Residential Tenancies (Rooming House Standards) Regulations 2023* (file "rt-rooming-house-standards-regs-2023-v002-2024-12-01.pdf", dated 1 December 2024) set the laundry standard. From 26 February 2024, there must be a washing machine in good working order for every 12 or fewer residents, based on the house's maximum capacity [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf). The standard doesn't say whether the machine must be free. So two machines would meet it for up to 24 residents.
- **Prohibited terms:** The *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (file "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf", dated 30 June 2026) list prohibited terms. One is "a term which unreasonably limits the resident's use of utilities" [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The heading for that list is cut off in the excerpt I have. I can't tell from the documents whether a coin charge counts as such a term.

**Gaps:** Nothing I retrieved addresses coin-operated machines directly. The Rooming House Standards document I found is dated 2024, so I can't confirm it is the version in force in October 2026.

## What you can do or ask

1. **Ask for the written schedule of charges.** The operator must have given you one before you moved in if they charge for services [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If you use the machines, ask for an itemised account of your use [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Find out who runs the house.** If it is Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency, the s 109A limits apply. You can ask for the cost basis of the charge and for written notice of any change [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You can apply to the Tribunal to have the charge withdrawn or varied [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Check your agreement.** Look for any term about laundry charges and compare it with the prohibited terms list [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
4. **Check the machines.** They must work. The regulation requires a washing machine "in good working order" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf).

For a firm answer on a private operator, contact Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy advice service. I couldn't confirm the point from these documents.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are present: the standard requires 'a washing machine in good working order for every 12 or fewer residents'; it notes 'The standard doesn't say whether the machine must be free'; s 109 requires 'a separate schedule of the amounts for the services before you take up residency'; and the first next step is 'Ask for the written schedule of charges.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes: none of the three claims is made, since the answer says the standard "doesn't say whether the machine must be free", states that s 109 sets rules "if an operator charges for services", and limits the cost cap to s 109A, which "applies only to rooming houses run by Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency."

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as "version 115, dated 13 October 2026" (file rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf) and the Rooming House Standards Regulations 2023 by the file "rt-rooming-house-standards-regs-2023-v002-2024-12-01.pdf" and the link 23-10sra002. It also relies only on in-force versions, including the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 version 009 dated 30 June 2026. It does not apply any rule taken from a version that was not in force.

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
## What the law says

**Which versions apply on 1 October 2025**
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021**, file `rt-regs-2021-v004-2025-07-01.pdf`, dated 1 July 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). The next version in the documents is dated 25 November 2025 [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf), so it was not yet in force.
- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997**, file `rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf`, dated 6 August 2025 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The later versions are dated 25 November 2025 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) and 13 October 2026 [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The "v004" and "v110" labels come from the file titles. The text I retrieved doesn't print an "Authorised Version No." line, so I can't confirm the number from the text itself.

**Mould is a minimum-standards issue.** Under the regulations, each room "must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). Regulation 29(1) makes Schedule 4 the standard for most rented premises [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). Bedrooms are covered, because the standard applies to "each room" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

**Can they advertise it like that?** I can't confirm this from the documents for 1 October 2025.
- The advertising rule is section 65B. It says a provider or agent must not advertise premises unless they "reasonably believe" the premises comply with the rental minimum standards. The penalty is 60 penalty units for a natural person and 300 for a body corporate [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- That text appears only in the 25 November 2025 version [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) and the 13 October 2026 version [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Both are later than your date.
- The 6 August 2025 Act extract [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) doesn't include section 65B. I can't tell you from these documents whether it was in force on 1 October 2025, and I won't fill that gap from memory.
- If section 65B applies, the test is the provider's reasonable belief, not whether the premises actually comply [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Photos that look like mould could make that belief harder to defend, but that is my inference. The documents don't say so.

**Is the photo enough to prove the place fails the standard?** The documents don't say what evidence is needed.
- The standard covers mould "caused by or related to the building structure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). A photo shows mould is present. It doesn't show the cause, and the documents don't say how that is proved.
- Separately, section 65A requires premises to meet the minimum standards on or before the day the renter moves in. The penalty is 60 penalty units for a natural person and 300 for a body corporate [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

## What a renter can do or ask

- **Ask for disclosure before signing.** The prescribed information a provider must disclose to a rental applicant includes [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf):
  - whether the premises comply with the rental minimum standards;
  - whether the provider has received a repair notice in the last 3 years about mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure.
- **Request urgent repairs after moving in.** If the premises don't comply with the standards on or immediately after the day you enter, you may request urgent repairs to bring them into compliance [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The definition of "urgent repairs" covers both a failure to comply with any rental minimum standards and mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). That definition is in the 6 August 2025 Act [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Ask about records, with a caveat.** The 13 October 2026 version requires providers and agents to keep records showing compliance with section 65B, and to produce them if the Director asks [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). That version post-dates your question, so I can't say it applied on 1 October 2025.

The documents don't say how a renter would formally challenge an advertisement or what proof the Tribunal would require. For that, you'd need other sources.

It also gives next steps: ask for disclosure before signing and request urgent repairs after moving in.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I let a friend move into my rental without telling the agent. Now I want them out. What do I have to do?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved documents don't set out how a renter removes a friend who has moved in. They do cover what the law says about letting someone move in without the agent's consent.

## What the law says

The version in force on 15 October 2026 is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", dated 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The file name suggests version 115, but the retrieved text doesn't print an "Authorised Version No.", so I can't confirm that number from the text.

- A renter must not assign or sub-let the whole or any part of the rented premises without the rental provider's written consent (s 81(1)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- An assignment or sub-letting without consent is invalid, unless the Tribunal has determined that consent is not required (s 81(3)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The rental provider must not unreasonably withhold consent. It is unreasonable to withhold it on the basis of an attribute in section 6 of the Equal Opportunity Act 2010 (s 81(2), (2A)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- If the rental provider has reasonable grounds to believe the renter has failed to comply with their duties under the Act or the agreement, they may enter the premises (s 86(1)(e)). They must give at least 24 hours' written notice, and entry must be between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. on a day that isn't a public holiday (s 85(b)(iii)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**Gap:** The retrieved text doesn't say whether a friend simply staying with you counts as "sub-letting". It also doesn't say what the rental provider can do about an unconsented sub-let in the current Act. The only provision I found on that is in an older 2019 version (rta-1997-v089-2019-12-04.pdf) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf). It isn't the version in force now, so I haven't relied on it.

## What you can do or ask

- **Tell the agent.** The retrieved documents don't require this step. But the law centres on the rental provider's written consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), and the agent can already enter on 24 hours' notice if they suspect a breach [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Ask for consent instead, if you'd rather your friend stayed.** If consent is withheld and you think that's unreasonable, you can apply to the Tribunal for a determination that consent isn't required (s 82) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Check your own position first.** Under s 81 the risk sits with you as the renter, not your friend [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What the documents don't cover

They don't give a process, notice period or Tribunal procedure for a renter who wants an unauthorised occupant to leave. The regulations' Form 6 (rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf, dated 30 June 2026) is a notice to vacate from a rental provider to a renter, so it doesn't apply to your friend. It does state that rental providers can't use force to remove people. Only Victoria Police can carry out a forcible eviction, and only on a VCAT order [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). For the steps to remove your friend, I'd suggest contacting Consumer Affairs Victoria (1300 558 181, the number on the form [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)) or a community legal centre.

must-mention.reason: No: the point that the answer depends on the arrangement, with a deciding fact named (a space that's only theirs, what was agreed, or what they pay), is missing. The output only says the text 'doesn't say whether a friend simply staying with you counts as "sub-letting"', without naming any deciding fact. The written-consent point is covered by s 81(1).

must-not-say.reason: Yes. None of the four failure claims are asserted. The answer states the documents "don't give a process, notice period or Tribunal procedure for a renter who wants an unauthorised occupant to leave." The only notice period it gives ("at least 24 hours' written notice") concerns the rental provider entering the premises, not ending the friend's occupancy. It never suggests locking the friend out or removing their belongings. The line "the risk sits with you as the renter, not your friend" is about liability under s 81, not a claim that the friend has no rights. The only Tribunal application mentioned is the renter seeking a determination that consent isn't required (s 82), not the friend applying to be added to the lease.

The answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 by the file name 'rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf' and the link '97-109aa115', which is version 115, the version in force on 15 October 2026. It uses that version for every rule it applies, and the only other source it relies on is the in-force Regulations version 009 ('21-3sra009'). It mentions the 2019 version 089 only to say it has not relied on it, and it states no rule from that version.
